title: Modeling and steady-state limit cycles of the cardiovascular-autonomic negative feedback control dynamics: A system theoretic approach
abstract: Understanding the dynamical interplay between the cardiovascular function and the autonomic neural control is fundamental for studying homeodynamic regulation and for clarifying the mechanisms that sustain physiological stability. In this work, we present a novel electrical analog of the integrated cardiovascular–autonomic system, developed within a modular framework. Pulmonary and systemic circulations, together with the dynamics of the left and right ventricles, are modeled by using electrical circuits tailored to represent both linear and nonlinear physiological behaviors. This modular structure allows the individual subsystems to be combined into a unified, high-dimensional state-space model, providing a coherent system theoretic basis for formal closed-loop analysis. The model is implemented in the MATLAB/Simulink environment, and numerical simulations reveal persistent, self-sustained oscillations in the state variables. Phase-space analysis confirms the periodic nature of these oscillations and their convergence from different initial conditions, indicating that a stable limit-cycle arises from the system dynamics. By integrating a modular electrical analog with a system theoretic perspective, this framework reproduces realistic cardiovascular rhythms, highlighting emergent oscillatory patterns that are central to physiological regulation. The proposed modeling framework offers a rigorous platform for exploring the interactions between neural control and hemodynamics.

title: FG-ConvNO: A Geometry-Aware Neural Operator for Propeller CFD Prediction
abstract: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) is essential in contemporary engineering design, yet it remains expensive to compute and can take thousands of CPU/GPU hours or more for a single high-fidelity simulation. Recent developments in machine learning for scientific modeling have led to powerful surrogate frameworks that can approximate flow fields and physical quantities by using a fraction of the computational cost. However, most of these methods require largescale homogeneous datasets or simple geometries, exhibiting severe generalization gaps when applied to complex and data-scarce configurations. To address this, we propose the Factorized Geometry Convolutional Neural Operator (FG-ConvNO) for robust geometry-aware propeller pressure prediction under limited training data. We introduce geometryaware encoding, efficient interpolation-based decoding, and auxiliary global quantity supervision. In addition, we incorporate DISCO blocks that use discrete continuous convolutions to make the model discretization agnostic. In our experiments, FG-ConvNO achieves the highest accuracy for both surface pressure and global thrust prediction on a procedurally generated propeller CFD dataset. Geometry-aware encoding and architectural simplification improve stability, while random vertex subsampling enhances robustness. Overall, adding geometric priors to grid-based convolutional operators reduces overfitting on complex propeller geometries and improves generalization in low-data regimes.

title: Emerging trends in AI-driven mining hazard management
abstract: The management of geotechnical hazards in mining is critical for ensuring operational safety and sustainability, yet its practical implementation often struggles with the inherent geological uncertainty and the dynamic, non-linear nature of mining environments. Artificial intelligence (AI), and specifically machine learning (ML), has emerged as a transformative technology, offering a shift from reactive to proactive, data-driven hazard management. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the evolution and application of AI in mining hazard management, tracing this development from early statistical and ML models to recent advances in deep learning. The review finds that these advanced models have demonstrated significant success in tasks such as rockburst prediction, slope stability analysis, and gas outburst forecasting by identifying complex patterns in large, multi-source datasets from seismic, geological, and operational monitoring. Despite these successes, significant challenges persist: the efficacy of purely data-driven models is often limited by data scarcity, imbalanced datasets, and a lack of physical consistency; the black-box nature of many deep learning models has created a barrier to their interpretability and trustworthiness in safety-critical applications. The future of AI in mining hazard management lies not in isolated algorithms but in integrated, hybrid systems. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and explainable AI (XAI) are identified as critical frontiers. These approaches promise to create models that are not only more accurate and generalisable but also transparent and interpretable to engineering practitioners, bridging the gap between AI's theoretical potential and its practical application in creating safer mining environments.

title: Dynamic Position-Wise Competitive Word Generation and Reordering: A Framework for Competitive Lexical Selection and Sequence Reconstruction
abstract: Autoregressive language models typically generate text incrementally, conditioning each new token on a previously generated prefix. Although effective, this process couples lexical selection to a predetermined left-to-right generation trajectory. This paper proposes Dynamic Position-Wise Competitive Word Generation and Reordering (DPC-WGR), a conceptual framework in which candidate words compete dynamically for output positions before the final sequence is assembled. Instead of treating the next-token decision as the sole unit of generation, the framework maintains a set of candidate lexical items, evaluates their suitability for multiple positions, resolves competition among candidates and positions, and reconstructs the output sequence according to the resulting assignments. The proposed framework integrates five operations: candidate generation, position-conditioned evaluation, competitive allocation, iterative reassignment, and sequence reconstruction. A multi-criteria scoring function can incorporate contextual compatibility, task relevance, semantic contribution, dependency compatibility, redundancy, and positional coherence. A constrained assignment mechanism is introduced to prevent incompatible candidates from occupying the same position, while an iterative refinement process allows candidate replacement and position reassignment before finalization. The framework can operate as a modification of an existing autoregressive language model or as a more extensively redesigned iterative generation architecture. The paper formalizes the proposed mechanism, presents an optimization objective and an algorithmic procedure, and establishes an experimental protocol for evaluating its effectiveness against conventional autoregressive decoding and existing insertion-based generation methods. The central hypothesis is that competitive position assignment may improve global lexical organization in tasks where the importance of a word cannot be adequately assessed from its immediate left-to-right generation context. This hypothesis remains to be tested experimentally. The paper identifies the principal technical challenges, including combinatorial search, grammatical dependencies, candidate-set incompleteness, and the risk that local competition produces globally incoherent sequences.

title: Demographics-Informed Neural Network for Multimodal Spatiotemporal Forecasting of Urban Growth and Travel Patterns Using Satellite Imagery
abstract: Abstract Transportation planning requires anticipating how built environments, population characteristics, and aggregate travel indicators evolve over time. Conventional forecasting approaches often treat these dimensions separately, limiting their ability to represent spatial-demographic change. This study introduces the Demographics-Informed Neural Network (DINN), a deep learning framework that forecasts next-year county-level satellite imagery from historical image sequences while enforcing demographic consistency through a frozen demographic predictor. DINN combines an encoder-decoder image predictor, gated skip connections, demographic bottleneck fusion, and demographic consistency regularization. The frozen demographic encoder is then reused as a fixed feature extractor to estimate aggregate county-level commute-mode and vehicle-availability indicators. Experiments using US county data from 2012 to 2023 show that DINN achieves an MSE of 0.00379 and SSIM of 0.8342 for satellite image prediction. Across repeated grouped spatial splits, DINN provides modest but consistent improvements over ConvLSTM, transformer-based, and encoder-decoder baselines, with stronger performance on both image reconstruction and change-detection metrics. The demographic predictor explains approximately 80% of the variance in population characteristics from satellite imagery. Transfer learning results show higher accuracy for absolute travel-indicator counts than for scale-controlled shares, indicating that part of the signal reflects county population scale. Overall, the findings suggest that satellite-derived spatial representations capture built-environment and demographic correlates of aggregate travel indicators; however, the results should be interpreted as county-level predictive associations rather than causal behavioral inference.

title: Climate downscaling with likelihood functional flow matching
abstract: Decisions about heat, frost and flooding are made locally, yet reanalyses and climate models resolve tens of kilometres. Generative downscalers add kilometre-scale detail with uncertainty, but are tied to a grid, costly to sample and lack a tractable likelihood. Here we introduce CD-FFM, a functional flow-matching model that treats the high-resolution field as a continuous random field that one model can query at any location and resolution. Its velocity acts pointwise, so spatial variability comes from a noise prior fitted to the observed spectrum and every observation has an exact likelihood. Downscaling ERA5 to 1 km daily temperature over Fennoscandia, CD-FFM lowers the continuous ranked probability score by 27-31% against regression and 12-18% against a forty-times larger neural operator in each of three test years, and outperforms a CorrDiff-style diffusion model while sampling about fifty times faster. The same model transfers to precipitation and makes large kilometre-scale ensembles affordable.

title: Beyond Affine Reconstruction: Multi-Resolution Transformer DeepONets for the Radiative Transfer Equation
abstract: Radiative heat transfer plays a dominant role in fire simulations, where solving the radiative transfer equation (RTE) is a computational bottleneck. Neural operators can accelerate these computations by learning solution operators from offline simulation data. However, conventional DeepONet surrogates rely on fixed-grid inputs and affine reconstruction, limiting their flexibility across resolutions and their approximation accuracy at a fixed latent dimension. In this paper, we develop a transformer-based DeepONet for multi-resolution RTE surrogate modelling. The proposed approach combines a Perceiver encoder, which maps temperature and absorption coefficient fields at different spatial resolutions into a fixed-size latent representation, with a cross-attention decoder that enables non-affine reconstruction of the radiative intensity. This architecture allows a single model to process inputs at varying resolutions without resampling them onto a common grid. We formulate a computable empirical version of a previously derived theoretical lower bound for affine reconstruction, enabling direct comparison with model errors on the same dataset. Experiments on a two-dimensional pool-fire dataset demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms autoencoder-based DeepONets in predicting both radiative intensity and incident radiation, with fewer trainable parameters. Power spectral density analysis shows improved preservation of small-scale structures. Both affine baselines remain above the corresponding lower bound at all evaluated ranks, whereas the proposed model achieves a training error below it at one matched latent dimension, demonstrating the potential of non-affine reconstruction to overcome this representational limitation. Experiments on a dataset combining three spatial resolutions confirm the accuracy advantage of the approach at each input resolution.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Next-Generation Firewalls for Discriminating Cyber Attacks from Legitimate Service Traffic Surges
abstract: Next-generation firewalls (NGFWs) sit on the critical path between public networks and production services. Their most consequential error is no longer a missed signature; it is the inability to tell a malicious flood from a genuine surge in legitimate demand. Flash crowds, seasonal campaigns, media-driven spikes, and elastic microservice fan-out can resemble distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) traffic in volume while remaining economically and operationally valid. Static access-control lists, fixed rate limits, and signature catalogs therefore produce an unacceptable trade-off: either they under-block stealthy application-layer attacks or they over-block paying users. This article reviews, compares, and synthesizes peer-reviewed evidence from 2020 onward on machine-learning and deep-learning methods that can be embedded in NGFW and software-defined enforcement points to discriminate attacks from legitimate service-intensity bursts. We organize the literature into statistical filters, classical classifiers, representation-learning hybrids, sequential models, and two-tier designs that first cheaply detect a burst and then classify its intent. Published detectors regularly report accuracy above 98% on CICDDoS2019 and related traces, yet most benchmarks omit a dedicated flash-event class, which inflates apparent performance and leaves the operationally hardest decision under-tested. Building on that gap, we propose AID-NGFW, a three-tier architecture that couples entropy and cumulative-sum screening with a calibrated three-class discriminator (benign, flash crowd, attack) and a policy engine that drops malicious flows while scaling or shaping legitimate surges. Comparative tables and figures compile reported accuracies, F1-scores, datasets, and latency–accuracy trade-offs. We argue that the scientific and engineering priority is no longer binary attack detection in isolation, but reliable, low-latency, and explainable discrimination under encrypted traffic, class imbalance, concept drift, and adversarial mimicry.

title: An actively trained neural operator for near-explicit atmospheric chemistry
abstract: Earth-system models simplify atmospheric chemistry into condensed mechanisms, because near-explicit mechanisms such as the Master Chemical Mechanism (MCM) are too costly to solve in every grid cell. Neural emulators could lift this limit, but most advance the chemistry in small time steps and cover only a few species or a reduced mechanism. Here we introduce FNO-MoE, a Fourier neural operator with a mixture of experts that predicts the full near-explicit chemical state over 30 minutes in a single call. The same network also guides its own training, using the disagreement among its experts to select the most informative box-model simulations. At equal cost, this active sampling yields a more accurate emulator than random or evenly spread sampling. Fine-tuning on longer trajectories keeps it stable over multi-hour runs in which models trained on short simulations diverge. The resulting emulator reproduces the evolution of thousands of species with high fidelity, remains accurate for unseen chemical compositions and runs orders of magnitude faster than the numerical solver. These results open a new direction for emulating complex atmospheric systems: neural operators that predict the full chemical state over long windows and choose their own training data. Training under changing meteorology is the next step towards bringing near-explicit chemistry into Earth-system models.

title: Agentic and generative AI for intelligent autonomous vulnerability assessment and penetration testing: A systematic analysis
abstract: Context: Vulnerability Assessment and Penetration Testing (VAPT) is increasingly challenged by the scale, heterogeneity, and dynamic nature of modern digital infrastructures, particularly across enterprise IT, operational technology (OT), industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), and cyber–physical systems. Although Agentic AI and Generative AI have each shown promise for automating parts of security auditing, the current literature remains fragmented across isolated audit phases and is still dominated by conventional IT-centric perspectives. Objectives: This paper systematically analyses recent advances in Agentic AI, Reinforcement Learning (RL), Large Language Models (LLMs), and tool-augmented Generative AI for autonomous VAPT. It aims to synthesise how these paradigms support end-to-end security auditing, identify the principal technical, operational, and governance gaps in the literature, and derive an evidence-grounded reference model for trustworthy autonomous auditing across both IT and OT environments. Methods: A PRISMA-guided systematic review was conducted across major scholarly databases, covering publications from 2020 to 2025. From 1144 initially identified records, 72 studies were retained after deduplication, screening, and full-text eligibility assessment. Included studies were coded across five attributes and synthesised into thematic trajectories to derive the proposed framework. Study credibility was screened against three qualitative, non-instrumented criteria—venue and editorial process, presence of empirical or systematic conceptual evaluation, and explicit acknowledgement of limitations. Results: The review shows that agentic approaches are best suited to sequential and adaptive tasks such as reconnaissance orchestration, exploit-path selection, lateral movement, post-exploitation pivoting, and adaptive re-testing. In contrast, generative approaches are strongest in reasoning over unstructured evidence, interpreting configurations and advisories, contextualising vulnerabilities, assessing exploit feasibility, mapping compliance controls, and producing traceable audit reports. However, few studies integrate these capabilities into a governed end-to-end workflow, and real-world OT/Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) validation remains limited. Of the 72 coded studies, 56 apply classical machine or deep learning, 14 use generative/LLM techniques, and only 2 employ reinforcement-learning or agentic control; none is evaluated against a physical or emulated OT/IIoT target, and reported autonomy is strongly scaffolding-dependent (for example, 21% fully autonomous versus 64% human-assisted task completion on AutoPenBench, an external benchmark outside the coded corpus). To address these gaps, this paper derives a unified Agentic–Generative VAPT model comprising four tightly coupled layers: agentic decision-making, generative reasoning, structured tool interfaces, and validation–governance. It further introduces a formal threat and evaluation abstraction for Model Context Protocol (MCP)-style interface layers and proposes a five-dimensional VAPT Autonomy Benchmark for future empirical validation. Conclusion: Autonomous security auditing is evolving from isolated AI-assisted tasks towards integrated, policy-constrained, and auditable architectures. Nevertheless, major challenges remain in hallucination control, prompt injection, sparse reward design, explainability, safety-aware evaluation, and benchmark standardisation. Future research should prioritise tightly integrated agentic–generative systems, realistic and safety-aware IT/OT testbeds, and governance mechanisms that enable trustworthy human-in-the-loop deployment in operational environments.

title: A recommender framework for sustainable coastal disaster management using big data, maritime surveillance, and AIOps
abstract: Abstract The convergence of intensifying human activity and climate change is escalating the frequency, magnitude, and complexity of maritime disasters, while real-time situational awareness and coordinated response remain critical bottlenecks. This paper presents a recommender framework and its underlying Data and AI Integration Platform for sustainable coastal disaster management, integrating maritime surveillance, big-data pipelines, and MLOps/AIOps automation. The core technical contribution is a dual-path decision-support engine that couples a lightweight 1D-CNN time-series event classifier with a fine-tuned BART large language model, enabling simultaneous reasoning over structured sensor telemetry and unstructured maritime text. The classifier is validated on real-world AIS telemetry (MarineCadastre.gov) aligned with NOAA buoy data as well as a controlled synthetic corpus, attaining 93.9% accuracy and a 92.4% macro-F1 at ~ 5.3 ms per sample, and is benchmarked against LSTM, Bi-LSTM + Attention, Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN), Transformer, and Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) baselines. The BART summariser, fine-tuned on 2000 maritime documents, reaches ROUGE-1 73.4, ROUGE-L 68.7, and BLEU 65.2, outperforming GPT-2 and T5 baselines, and is assessed by five domain experts (Fleiss’ kappa = 0.71). Beyond component metrics, we report platform-level indicators, including end-to-end alert latency, situational-awareness gain, and analyst reading-time reduction, to demonstrate the operational benefit of the integrated system for Coast Guard and maritime authorities. The platform-level indicators are obtained from an explicitly documented replay protocol over 320 annotated incident scenarios of stated provenance, the real-world AIS labels are produced by a two-stage rule-plus-expert annotation procedure (Fleiss’ kappa = 0.78), and every model comparison is reported with bootstrap confidence intervals and McNemar significance tests. Results indicate that the framework advances the shift from reactive to proactive, transparent, and resilient maritime disaster response.

title: ZENO: Nonlinear filtering with Zakai Equation Neural Operators
abstract: State inference and parameter learning for nonlinear filters is a core computation for scientific machine learning with varied applications in engineering and neuroscience. The unnormalized filtering distribution is governed by the Zakai equation, a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) that combines the forward Kolmogorov operator (known as the Fokker-Planck equation) with observed likelihood updates. Although solving these high-dimensional SPDEs is often impossible analytically and intractable numerically, advances in operator learning and physics-informed machine learning have made it feasible. Harnessing these advances, we introduce the Zakai Equation Neural Operator (ZENO), a model that optimizes a neural operator against a Zakai Equation based physics-informed loss to approximate the exact unnormalized filtering distribution for latent stochastic dynamical systems. We use this ZENO-inferred posterior distribution in an expectation-maximization (EM) framework to perform parameter learning and state inference. We demonstrate ZENO's ability to accurately infer the posterior distribution and learn its corresponding SDE parameters in three simulated stochastic dynamical systems (Double-Well bistable system, Van Der Pol (VDP) oscillator, and Lorenz system) and compare its performance against established methods for latent SDE inference and learning. We show that ZENO recovers previously observed limit cycles representing forward and backward locomotion from a whole-brain imaging dataset of immobilized \textit{C. elegans} nematodes. ZENO is a novel approach to the problem of nonlinear filtering and dynamical inference through the lens of partial differential equations and operator theory.

title: When Does Dynamics Randomization Test Context Inference?
abstract: Environments with randomized dynamics are widely used to ask whether world models need explicit context inference. However, randomization can leave little predictive information for a context encoder to add, because distinct latent parameters may produce similar transitions at visited states, or those states may already reveal the active context. We formalize the remaining one-step information as predictive headroom and compare kernels under fixed and visited state--action distributions to distinguish changes in query coverage from changes in context weights. We analyze discrete and continuous environments and find low headroom both when kernels differ little and when visitation reduces an otherwise large discrepancy. At the same time, resetting state components increases headroom, showing that context evidence accumulates in state. We propose reporting this headroom alongside the randomized parameters, so that gains from explicit context inference can be interpreted relative to the information missing from the current state and action.

title: What is the Optimal Way to Lie? From Microscopic to Kinetic Descriptions of Consensus Control
abstract: Abstract We establish an approach for consensus control of opinion dynamics by introducing a liar to the classical system. The liar’s aim is to steer the population toward consensus at their goal opinion by showing ‘apparent opinions’, or ‘lies’, to members of the population. We analyse this as an optimal control problem for how best to lie to a population in order to guarantee the consensus that the liar desires. We consider a range of regularisations, each motivated by some social convention, such as the liar wanting to present an opinion close to their goal opinion. For each regularisation, we demonstrate the effect of instantaneous controls. Furthermore, we introduce a Boltzmann-type description for the corresponding kinetic system and present analysis and numerical results for the resulting Boltzmann and Fokker-Planck equations.

title: Thermal analysis of ternary hybrid nanofluids for advanced cooling of AI chips and data centers using dual numerical techniques
abstract: The problem of controlling the massive heat produced by high-performance AI processors has become more difficult due to the quick development of artificial intelligence (AI) and the exponential expansion of data centers. In addition to reducing processing efficiency, excessive heat endangers system dependability and energy sustainability. To mitigate this challenge, the present study investigates the application of ternary hybrid nanofluids (Tri-HNF: Al₂O₃–CuO–GNP/EG) as advanced coolants, comparing their performance with binary hybrid nanofluids (Di-HNF: Al₂O₃–CuO/EG) and mono nanofluids (NF: Al₂O₃/EG) in enhancing thermal regulation over a flat surface. The Collocation Chebyshev Method (CCM) and the Galerkin-weighted residual Method (GWRM), two separate numerical techniques included in Mathematica 11.3, were used to convert the governing nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) to ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and solve them numerically. The excellent agreement between the two methods demonstrates the consistency and accuracy of the numerical schemes. The effects of magnetic field, viscosity, suction, radiation, and heat generating factors on the flow and temperature fields were revealed using parametric experiments. Findings show that the Tri-HNF exhibits superior thermal performance due to the synergistic effects of Al₂O₃ (enhanced stability), CuO (excellent thermal conductivity), and graphene nanoplatelets (GNP) (exceptional heat transport efficiency). Compared to Di-HNF and NF, the Tri-HNF achieves higher Nusselt numbers, improved heat dispersion, and lower thermal resistance. In summary, this work demonstrates that Tri-HNF provide an efficient and reliable solution for cooling AI chips, microelectronics, and data centers, offering a pathway toward sustainable and thermally stable next-generation computing systems.

title: Solving and Learning Navier-Stokes Dynamics with the Neural Basis Method
abstract: Physics-informed machine learning has become a major direction in predictive modeling of fluid dynamics, combining governing physics with learned representations. Yet prevailing formulations neither guarantee that small PDE-residual losses imply small solution errors nor scale effectively with increasing problem size. Here we present the neural basis method (NBM) as a new approach for Navier--Stokes dynamics. NBM is built on a ``representation-then-projection'' principle: fixed neural bases define the representation space, while projection of the governing equations determines the expansion coefficients. The same bases define common coordinates for the parametric solution manifold, recasting operator learning as a parameter-to-coefficient mapping and enabling scalability by removing explicit spatial dependence. For incompressible flow, NBM yields a velocity-only formulation whose residual provides an a posteriori velocity-error estimate, establishing a certified, data-free training objective for coefficient learning. Theoretical analysis and numerical experiments demonstrate the accuracy, efficiency, generalization, and scalability of NBM, with substantial improvements over baselines.

title: Robust and Scalable LPWAN Architecture with Integrated Security for Industrial IoT Applications
abstract: Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) is revolutionizing the means of critical infrastructure through real-time monitoring, automation and making smart decisions. The Low-Power Wide-Area Networks (LPWANs) like LoRaWAN, Sigfox, and NB-IoT are highly essential in enabling low energy, long-range two-way communication in IIoT-related use cases. Nevertheless, current implementations of LPWAN usually have serious gaps related to scalability, robustness, and security applied in an industrial world. In this study, a powerful and scalable framework of LPWAN is suggested combined with lightweight, multiple-layered security solutions depending on the specific requirements of IIoT communication. The framework provides hierarchical and intelligent adaptive network topography, dynamic clustering and intelligent gateway coordination. Its security is enforced by using symmetric encryption, key exchange on Elliptic curve and Device authentication using HMAC. Scalability and resilience are achieved by the architecture by incorporating adaptive channel allocation, fault-tolerant routing, and anomaly detection with edge intelligence in real-time. NS-3 simulation-based assessment with realistic industrial traffic patterns shows that a packet delivery ratio is more than 95 percent, latency reduces by up to 40 percent in crowded settings, and cryptographic overheads are less than 5 percent. The offered solution enhances the resistance to seemingly typical IIoT attacks (jamming, replay, node impersonation, etc.) considerably without affecting energy and latency consumption. The resultants substantiate the architecture in its ability to support secure and scalability of IIoTs and further research will integrate the architecture with real-life applicative industrial testbeds and blockchain efficient trust mechanisms.

title: Model predictive quantum control: A modular approach for efficient and robust quantum optimal control
abstract: Abstract Model predictive control (MPC) is one of the most successful modern control methods. It relies on repeatedly solving a finite-horizon optimal control problem and applying the beginning piece of the optimal input. In this paper, we develop a modular framework for improving efficiency and robustness of quantum optimal control (QOC) via MPC. We first provide a tutorial introduction to basic concepts of MPC from a QOC perspective. We then present multiple MPC schemes, ranging from simple approaches to more sophisticated schemes which admit stability guarantees. This yields a modular framework which can be used 1) to improve efficiency of open-loop QOC and 2) to improve robustness of closed-loop quantum control by incorporating feedback. We demonstrate these benefits with numerical results, where we benchmark the proposed methods against competing approaches.

title: Mean-Field Limit of Non-exchangeable Multi-agent Systems Over Hypergraphs with Unbounded Rank
abstract: Interacting particle systems are known for their ability to generate large-scale self-organized structures from simple local interaction rules between each agent and its neighbors. In addition to studying their emergent behavior, a main focus of the mathematical community has been concentrated on deriving their large-population limit. In particular, the mean-field limit consists of describing the limit system by its population density in the product space of positions and labels. The strategy to derive such limits is often based on a careful combination of methods ranging from analysis of PDEs and stochastic analysis, to kinetic equations and graph theory. In this article, we focus on a generalization of multi-agent systems that includes higher-order interactions, which has largely captured the attention of the applied community in the last years. In such models, interactions between individuals are no longer assumed to be binary (i.e., between a pair of particles). Instead, individuals are allowed to interact by groups so that a full group jointly generates a nonlinear force on any given individual. The underlying graph of connections is then replaced by a hypergraph, which we assume to be dense, but possibly nonuniform and of unbounded rank. For the first time in the literature, we show that when the interaction kernels are regular enough, then the mean-field limit is determined by a limiting Vlasov-type equation, where the hypergraph limit is encoded by a so-called UR-hypergraphon (unbounded-rank hypergraphon), and where the resulting mean-field force admits infinitely-many orders of interactions.

title: LogLook: Execution-Grounded Memory for Frontier-Model Robot Planners
abstract: Many manipulation tasks require a robot to remember what it has done and what it has seen. Frontier vision-language models can plan such tasks without task-specific training, but how such a planner should remember an episode is an open question. We argue that its memory must keep track of what the planner has done and learned, and must let the planner choose what to look at, since every frame costs tokens; a note rewritten at every step meets both poorly. We propose LogLook, whose execution-grounded memory lets the system keep the record, an execution log and the model's earlier notes, while the model decides where to look: frames are returned only where it expects a change, and demonstrations are skimmed before it inspects the parts it chooses. Measured with the benchmark's motion planner, LogLook matches the success of a note-only memory with 43% fewer tokens and less than half the images, and fails far fewer episodes through what it remembered or saw. With direct control, LogLook solves 93.5% of the RoboMME test set.

title: Lie Algebra-Based Quantum Optimal Controls Interpolation
abstract: Abstract We present a framework combining Lie group theory and feed-forward neural networks to efficiently generate quantum optimal control pulses for arbitrary unitary operations in superconducting qubit systems, bypassing the need for explicit optimization at inference time. The exponential scaling of the Hilbert space dimension with qubit number makes standard optimization approaches computationally prohibitive when large ensembles of distinct propagators must be processed, a bottleneck that is particularly acute in Trotterized quantum simulation. Our method addresses this limitation by pre-computing a representative set of control pulses via Lie group theory and training neural networks to map target propagators to their corresponding pulses. We demonstrate the approach on superconducting qubit systems of 2, 3, and 4 qubits, finding high reconstruction fidelity for specific combinations of Lie algebra parameters. As a physically motivated benchmark, we apply the methodology to reconstruct control pulses for the Trotter propagators of a neutrino system undergoing collective flavor oscillations. The successful generalization across system types demonstrates that a single model -trained once on hardware-specific random propagators -can serve as a universal control-pulse generator for any target quantum system of compatible Hilbert space dimension, offering a promising route toward scalable quantum simulation.

title: Hybrid AI-Mathematical Modelling for Nonlinear Dynamical Systems
abstract: Nonlinear dynamical systems underpin phenomena across fluid mechanics, epidemiology, climate science, and engineering, yet their inherent complexity renders classical analytical methods insufficient for real-world applications. This paper proposes and evaluates a Hybrid AI-Mathematical Modelling (HAIMM) framework that synergistically integrates physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), symbolic regression, and reservoir computing with traditional mathematical constructs such as ordinary and partial differential equations. The framework preserves the interpretability and physical consistency of mathematical models while harnessing the pattern-learning capacity of modern machine learning. Through four representative case studies Lorenz attractor forecasting, epidemic compartmental modelling, fluid boundary-layer prediction, and structural vibration identification we demonstrate that HAIMM achieves up to 94.3% prediction accuracy with a 40% reduction in computational overhead compared to purely numerical baselines. A structured comparison across model families is presented via tabular benchmarks, and key dynamical behaviors are illustrated through system-generated flow diagrams. The results suggest that hybrid approaches represent a principled, scalable pathway for taming the complexity of nonlinear dynamics in science and engineering.

title: How does community of inquiry matter? Mediating effects and configurational pathways linking project-based learning design to learning engagement
abstract: The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AIGC) has reshaped animation students’ skill profiles and the conditions of instructional design in project-based learning (PBL) studios. We examine whether and how perceptions of PBL design are associated with Learning Engagement (LE), treating AIGC-assisted PBL studios as the research context rather than testing generative AI as a model variable. Drawing on Community of Inquiry (CoI) theory, we examine Problem Driven (PD), Project Design (PDe), Project Implementation (PI), and Project Evaluation (PE) as antecedents; Cognitive Presence (CP), Social Presence (SP), and Teaching Presence (TP) as statistical mediators; and LE as the outcome. We analyzed two-wave survey data from 490 upper-year animation students using PLS-SEM and fsQCA. PBL and CoI were measured concurrently at T1, and LE at T2; indirect effects therefore represent indirect statistical associations rather than mediation with a fully established temporal sequence. PD, PDe, and PI showed significant positive direct associations with LE. PE’s zero-order and single-predictor associations were positive, but its direct path coefficient became significantly negative after controlling for the other PBL dimensions and CoI mediators. The coefficient was sensitive to model specification, suggesting possible statistical suppression; it should not be interpreted as evidence that evaluation itself inherently inhibits engagement. The three CoI dimensions showed significant statistical mediation associations across all 12 indirect paths. TP and SP had relatively higher point estimates of indirect statistical associations, but differences between indirect effects were not formally tested; no dimension is claimed to be optimal. PE’s positive indirect associations through CoI partially offset its negative net direct association without reversing the total association after adjustment. The extent of this offset may depend on the degree to which CoI-related experiences are concurrently reported. fsQCA identified seven high-engagement configurations. No individual PBL dimension was indispensable. CoI dimensions appeared as core or peripheral conditions, although not every configuration included all three. These findings clarify the dual pathways linking evaluation and engagement through indirect statistical associations and configurational conditions, and provide guidance for optimizing PBL under different resource constraints. Conclusions are limited to AIGC-assisted PBL studios and do not establish the instructional effects of generative AI.

title: HGWM: Hierarchical Graph-Guided World Model for Zero-Shot Object Navigation via Graph Matching
abstract: Zero-shot object navigation requires an embodied agent to choose where to search while retaining evidence from previous observations. HGWM couples an LLM-generated room-anchor prior with persistent spatial-semantic memory. A coarse stage assigns visual-semantic scores to candidate headings on a 0-10 scale; a fine stage measures symbolic compatibility between observed objects, room context, and the goal prior. Phase-dependent fusion combines these scores with an LLM direction recommendation before local action selection. On HM3D v0.1, the reported HGWM configuration achieves 62.6% success rate (SR) and 31.5% success weighted by path length (SPL), compared with 58.1% and 31.2% for WMNav. On MP3D, the corresponding values are 46.8% and 17.9%, compared with 45.4% and 17.2%. The results indicate higher success point estimates and modest path-efficiency gains. On HM3D v0.2, the full model obtains 74.4% SR and 31.9% SPL. Additional component ablations reduce SR by 0.9-2.3 percentage points and SPL by 0.6-1.5 points. These are author-reported aggregate measurements. The accompanying implementation repairs pass offline tests; episode-level rerun records are not available. Evaluation is confined to simulation.

title: Functional Analysis and Partial Differential Equations in Spectral Barron Spaces
abstract: Abstract. Spectral Barron spaces, constituting a specialized class of function spaces that serve as an interdisciplinary bridge between mathematical analysis, partial differential equations (PDEs), and machine learning, are distinguished by the decay profiles of their Fourier transform. In this work, we shift from conventional numerical approximation frameworks to explore advanced functional analysis and PDE theoretic perspectives within these spaces. Specifically, we present a rigorous characterization of the dual space structure of spectral Barron spaces, alongside continuous embedding in Hölder spaces established through real interpolation theory. Furthermore, we investigate applications to boundary value problems governed by the Schrödinger equation, including spectral analysis of associated linear operators. These contributions elucidate the analytical foundations of spectral Barron spaces while underscoring their potential to unify approximation theory, functional analysis, and machine learning.

title: Discontinuous Galerkin Finite Element Operator Network for Solving Non-Smooth PDEs
abstract: Abstract. We introduce the Discontinuous Galerkin Finite Element Operator Network (DG–FEONet), a data-free operator learning framework that combines the strengths of the discontinuous Galerkin (DG) method with neural networks to solve parametric partial differential equations (PDEs) with discontinuous coefficients and non-smooth solutions. Unlike traditional operator learning models such as DeepONet and Fourier Neural Operator, which require large paired datasets and often struggle near sharp features, our approach minimizes the residual of a DG-based weak formulation using the symmetric interior penalty Galerkin (SIPG) scheme. DG-FEONet predicts elementwise solution coefficients via a neural network, enabling data-free training without the need for precomputed input-output pairs. We provide theoretical justification through convergence analysis and validate the model’s performance on a series of one- and two-dimensional PDE problems, demonstrating accurate resolution of discontinuous coefficients, sharp features, and interface-induced non-smoothness, strong generalization across parameter space, and reliable convergence rates. Our results highlight the potential of combining local discretization schemes with machine learning to achieve robust, non-smooth-feature-aware operator approximation in challenging PDE settings.

title: DT-JEPA: Learning to Predict Future Representations for Decision-Making
abstract: Decision Transformer (DT) has demonstrated strong performance in various offline reinforcement learning (RL) tasks by conditioning action generation on expected future returns and historical trajectories. However, treating expected future returns as the condition provides an incomplete description of the future, as trajectories with different state transitions and behaviors may share similar returns. Moreover, expected future returns inherently depend on task-specific reward functions, which makes policy learning reliant on reward-labeled datasets and restricts its scalability to tasks with similar but unseen rewards. Recently, Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA) have emerged as a promising paradigm of self-supervised learning-based world models, which learn predictive representations of future dynamics in latent space rather than reconstructing future states in the original space. Inspired by JEPA, we propose DT-JEPA, an offline pretraining and online fine-tuning framework that learns general knowledge from reward-free offline trajectories and achieves excellent adaptation to unseen tasks. Instead of predicting a single deterministic future embedding, we design a novel probabilistic predictor to model the conditional distribution of future representations in the latent space, thereby capturing both predictive information and uncertainty about future dynamics. Theoretically, we show that 1) the JEPA objective seeks to maximize a variational lower bound on the mutual information between historical representations and future trajectories; and 2) predictive future-conditioned policy learning admits a finite-sample performance bound with an O(N-1/4) estimation term. Experiments on D4RL benchmarks demonstrate that DT-JEPA achieves efficient adaptation across varying offline RL tasks, outperforming traditional DT-based and other offline RL methods.

title: Conditional Neural Processes for Self-Supervised Goal Discovery in Action Imitation
abstract: Inspired by infants' ability to learn novel tasks by imitating others, in this work we evaluate to what extent Conditional Neural Processes can autonomously learn representations of actions that are informative about their underlying goal. We show that the addition of an attention mechanism in the hidden space fosters the emergence of robust goal representations early on in the observation of an action sequence, making it a promising model for a robotic self-supervised general learner.

title: Conditional Flow Models for Offline Maximum Entropy Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Offline maximum entropy reinforcement learning seeks to estimate the optimal soft action-value function \(Q^*\) from a fixed dataset without further interaction with the environment. Although \(Q^*\) is characterized by the soft optimal Bellman equation, the corresponding Bellman operator cannot be evaluated directly because both the reward distribution and the transition kernel are unknown. Consequently, estimating \(Q^*\) requires the joint treatment of environment modeling and value function learning. We propose a framework that addresses these tasks separately. Conditional diffusion models based on probability flow ODEs estimate the conditional reward distribution and transition kernel. The resulting distributional estimators define a data driven approximation of the soft optimal Bellman operator, whose empirical Bellman residual is minimized over a class of deep neural networks to estimate \(Q^*\). We establish nonasymptotic guarantees for the proposed method. For operator learning, we derive total variation error bounds for the conditional flow estimators that account explicitly for score estimation, numerical discretization, and terminal smoothing. For soft value learning, we first use the soft Bellman equation to show that $Q^*$ inherits Hölder regularity from the conditional reward and transition densities. For any Hölder index $β$, the value learning stage achieves an excess Bellman residual risk bound of order $\widetilde{\mathcal O}\big(n^{-\frac{2β}{d+2β}}\big),$ where $d$ is the total dimension of the state and action spaces. In contrast to many existing theoretical analyses of deep reinforcement learning, our results do not require Bellman completeness. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

title: CoPiT: A conditional Position-induced Transformer for aerodynamic field prediction on unstructured meshes
abstract: High-fidelity Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) simulations remain a standard tool for aerodynamic analysis, yet each solve on an unstructured mesh is computationally expensive, making many-query tasks such as design exploration, optimization, and multi-condition evaluation costly. Neural operators provide mesh-flexible surrogates for mapping geometry and operating conditions to flow fields; however, in many existing architectures, global parameters such as the freestream state and design variables are concatenated with pointwise inputs, leaving their influence on intermediate features implicit. This paper proposes CoPiT, a \textbf{Co}nditional \textbf{P}osition-induced \textbf{T}ransformer that builds on the Position-induced Transformer (PiT) as its geometric backbone and injects a global condition vector through multi-stage feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM), thereby making parametric modulation explicit while preserving geometry-based attention weights. The model is evaluated on two-dimensional AirfRANS airfoil fields, including scarce-data and extrapolation regimes, and on three-dimensional BlendedNet++ blended-wing-body surfaces. On the AirfRANS full-data test set, CoPiT reduces surface and volume losses by approximately 54\% and 24\% relative to Transolver, respectively, and achieves the lowest overall normalized test MSE among the compared baselines on BlendedNet++. Matched ablations show that FiLM conditioning generally improves upon input concatenation, while the preferred placement is task-dependent. CoPiT thus provides a practical operator-learning surrogate for parametric aerodynamics on unstructured meshes.

title: Branch‐and‐Cut POPMUSIC for the Electric Vehicle Routing Problem With Time Windows
abstract: ABSTRACT Advancements in computer hardware and commercial software have enabled the use of branch‐and‐cut (BC) methodologies to address medium‐scale vehicle routing problems (VRPs). Despite the introduction of efficient heuristics in the literature, tailoring these approaches to suit various VRP variants, such as the electric vehicle routing problem with time windows (EVRPTW), remains a difficult task. EVRPTW is an extension of the classic VRP with time windows in which internal combustion engine vehicles are replaced by electric vehicles. In this study, we develop a POPMUSIC matheuristic to solve the EVRPTW that relies solely on BC (termed BC‐POPMUSIC), and can be implemented using commercial optimisation software such as Gurobi. We introduce new battery infeasibility inequalities, along with capacity cuts, reachability cuts, ‐path cuts and polar cuts, and incorporate them into Gurobi to tighten the linear programming (LP) relaxation of the mixed integer linear program (MILP) model. Through extensive experiments, we show that this tightening can improve the quality of solutions. Since the EVRPTW requires visits to recharging stations when the battery is depleted, we propose an improvement heuristic to efficiently manage these recharging stops. We demonstrate the effectiveness of BC‐POPMUSIC on known benchmark instances of EVRPTW and compare it with state‐of‐the‐art exact solutions. Our result shows that the approach achieves comparable or better performance, especially on larger problems. In addition, we present new best known solutions for several benchmark instances.

title: Adaptive World-Models for Anomaly Recognition (AWARE): A Framework for Robot Dynamics Prediction and Introspection
abstract: Unrecognized anomalies in critical infrastructure can rapidly cascade into catastrophic physical or operational failures. Current anomaly detection approaches often rely on direct access to the monitored system by utilizing onboard sensors, such as motor encoders, to detect anomalous states. However, legacy hardware often lacks these sensors, or strict security protocols may prohibit access altogether. We therefore present AWARE, a world model framework that is capable of anomaly detection using only external camera monitoring via system dynamics estimation and state prediction. Evaluated across 240 real-world robotic crane trajectories, including payload collisions and motor degradations, AWARE demonstrates a 26% improvement in anomaly classification over our strongest baseline under noisy, camera-only state estimation. Furthermore, the inferred dynamics parameter can be decoded to identify the source of faults, localizing the degrading motor with 88% accuracy.

title: $Ψ$-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in a Unified Vision-Language World Model
abstract: Humans reason about the physical world by flexibly combining different forms of inference as a problem unfolds. Achieving this flexibility is a major open challenge in AI: capabilities often remain separated across specialized models, limiting how they can be composed and jointly adapted to a task. We introduce $Ψ$-0.6, a unified vision-language world model that adaptively composes perception, language, geometry, and simulation within a shared reasoning process we call streams of thought. These streams interleave images, text, and explicit representations of geometry and motion, all of which the model can generate and interpret through a shared token interface. $Ψ$-0.6 surpasses leading open-weight models zero-shot on multi-view spatial reasoning, with further gains from reasoning through geometric intermediates. It also supports counterfactual simulation: generating and interpreting imagined scenes to determine, for example, whether moving an object would obstruct a pathway. Reinforcement learning from task feedback jointly optimizes the selection, generation, and use of intermediate representations, improving visual question-answering accuracy with gains that transfer to unseen benchmarks. $Ψ$-0.6 offers a path toward adaptive physical reasoning -- not only predicting the physical world but also choosing the representations through which to reason.

title: Skeleton-Grounded Latent Action Model for Robot World Models
abstract: Robot world models simulate how environments evolve in response to robot actions. Latent action models enable learning dynamics from videos by encoding visual transitions as proxy actions. However, reconstruction-driven latent actions mix robot motion with object responses and other scene changes, complicating their correspondence with robot controls. We propose SkeLAM, a skeleton-guided latent action model for controllable robot world modeling. SkeLAM decomposes latent actions into a kinematic component grounded by robot skeleton supervision and a residual component retaining complementary visual dynamics. Cross-modal swap reconstruction encourages RGB-derived and skeleton-derived kinematic representations to be interchangeable during video reconstruction. The world model incorporates both components through separate conditioning pathways, while branch dropout reduces its dependence on future-derived residual information. A lightweight adapter maps robot actions to the kinematic space, and subsequent world-model fine-tuning adapts generation to these predicted conditions. At inference, the model generates future observations from the current observation and robot actions. On DROID, SkeLAM reduces end-effector ADE by 19.5% and LPIPS by 11.1% compared with DreamDojo. Motion probing supports kinematic specialization, while qualitative results demonstrate zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer in generated rollouts. Policy evaluation shows agreement between predicted success rates and those measured in real robot executions.

title: Sensorimotor Alignment: A Platonic Proxy for Embodied Policy Success
abstract: Robot foundation models are typically evaluated through costly closed-loop rollouts, motivating low-cost offline proxies for model capability. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests that as representations improve, modalities such as vision and language converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. We ask whether motion trajectories form another such modality: as embodied models become more capable, should their sensory representations converge toward the structure of physical motion? To test this, we propose Sensorimotor Alignment ($S^2$), a training-free offline metric that measures how well a model's sensory representation aligns with the geometry of physical motion. We find that $S^2$ correlates positively with downstream robot task success across model families, making it a low-cost offline proxy for prioritizing models before closed-loop evaluation. $S^2$ can also identify promising vision-language model (VLM) backbones before costly fine-tuning into vision-language-action models (VLAs). Beyond this correlation, $S^2$ offers representation-level explanations for phenomena observed in VLAs and world action models (WAMs). With $S^2$, we extend PRH to robotics and make sensorimotor alignment measurable, offering a low-cost, representation-level view of robot foundation models that closed-loop success rates alone cannot reveal.

title: See What I Need, Dream What I Want: A Navigation Foundation Model on a Self-Constructed Representation Space
abstract: What visual representation should a navigation policy act on? Navigation policies built on vision foundation models largely leave representation design to the encoders' pretraining objectives. We present RepresentNav, a navigation foundation model built on a self-constructed representation space: a visual representation constructed by the policy's own objectives from vision foundation models. RepresentNav builds this space with Representation Residuals, a compact three-layer transformer that attends over features spanning the full depth of multiple complementary vision foundation models, so that the policy learns to see what it needs for navigation. In the same space it dreams what it wants: before every action a latent chain-of-thought predicts the representation of the scene a moment ahead. The dream is trained end-to-end with the policy as a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), with a next-representation prediction loss and a regularizer on its targets. RepresentNav sets a new state of the art on VLNVerse, VLN-CE R2R, EVT-Bench, and two point-goal benchmarks, and its gains carry over to a physical robot amid clutter and moving people. On VLNVerse fine-grained, RepresentNav achieves 83.80% success, outperforming the previous state of the art by 20.05 percentage points, and on EVT-Bench distracted tracking it reaches 85.5% with a single camera (+10.1). With the same encoders, the self-constructed space clearly outperforms concatenating their outputs and learns to weight their layers unevenly, and a dream in it cuts collisions by a quarter. A single dreamed latent decodes into the depth, semantics, and 3D occupancy of the scene a moment ahead, more accurately than pretrained encoders applied to the real future frame, although occupancy is never supervised, and the rollout tracks the robot's own motion over the next second: the dream emerges as a compact latent world model.

title: RheOPT: Few-Shot Non-Newtonian Flow Prediction via Newtonian Pretraining of RheOFormer
abstract: Despite advances in numerical methods, non-Newtonian flow simulations remain computationally expensive because velocity and stress must be advanced together through rate- and history-dependent constitutive dynamics. Neural-operator surrogates reduce inference cost after training, but their training data require the same expensive simulations they aim to replace, making data-efficient learning essential when only a few non-Newtonian simulations can be afforded. Here, we introduce the Rheological Operator Pretrained Transformer (RheOPT), which pretrains a transformer-based neural operator on inexpensive Newtonian simulations and fine-tunes it on a small number of non-Newtonian samples. Rather than transferring the Newtonian constitutive response itself, RheOPT reuses geometry-conditioned transport structure that remains useful after the stress model changes. We evaluate RheOPT in two geometry-matched settings: a $4{:}1$ contraction channel for Giesekus, Oldroyd-B, and Bingham fluids, and the oscillatory wake behind a triangular obstacle for Oldroyd-B flow. In the contraction, Newtonian pretraining substantially improves few-shot prediction, and a model fine-tuned on four target samples can match or exceed a from-scratch model trained on four times as many. This benefit is reliable under reversible instance normalization (RevIN) but dataset dependent under Global normalization, a difference we trace to the dynamic range of each fluid's velocity and stress fields. In the wake, where relative $L_2$ error alone cannot verify that vortex shedding is recovered, phase-insensitive diagnostics show that pretraining recovers the shedding frequency and wake fluctuation amplitude that are suppressed by the from-scratch model in the few-shot regime. Overall, RheOPT establishes Newtonian simulation as a physically grounded pretraining source for data-efficient non-Newtonian operator learning.

title: Pixels to precision: Deep learning in dental imaging
abstract: Dental imaging is fundamental to diagnosis, treatment planning, and follow-up in Oral Medicine and Maxillofacial Radiology. Although conventional radiographic interpretation remains dependent on professional expertise, diagnostic performance may be influenced by observer variability, image quality, workload, and the subtle nature of early pathological changes. The development of Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning (DL), has introduced new approaches for automated analysis of dental and maxillofacial images. This narrative review discusses the evolution, principles, applications, clinical relevance, limitations, and future directions of deep learning in dental imaging, with emphasis on intraoral radiography, panoramic radiography, cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT), and related imaging modalities. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have demonstrated applications in dental caries detection, periodontal bone assessment, periapical lesion detection, tooth identification and numbering, jaw lesion analysis, anatomical segmentation, and treatment planning. More advanced architectures, including U-Net, residual networks, object-detection models, three-dimensional CNNs, and emerging transformer-based systems, have expanded the scope of automated image interpretation. However, the rapid growth of research has also highlighted important limitations, including small and heterogeneous datasets, inconsistent annotation, retrospective study designs, limited external validation, algorithmic bias, and difficulties in explaining model predictions. Importantly, high algorithmic accuracy does not necessarily translate into clinical effectiveness. Future research should therefore focus on diverse multicentre datasets, external and prospective validation, explainable AI, multimodal systems, ethical governance, and meaningful human-AI collaboration. Deep learning is most appropriately viewed as an adjunctive clinical decision-support technology that complements rather than replaces professional diagnostic judgment.

title: Optimal daily allocation between vocabulary and grammar in second- language study: a normative control model
abstract: Abstract Foreign-language learners with a fixed daily study budget divide their time between vocabulary and grammar and decide when to stop memorising words. Published guidance often places that stopping point near 98% coverage of the running words in a text. This paper treats the decision as a finite-horizon optimal-control problem. The state is mastered word families and a grammar-mastery index. A Zipf–Mandelbrot frequency distribution converts the first into text coverage, and comprehension is a constant-elasticity-of-substitution aggregate of coverage and grammar mastery, so the two skills are complementary but not perfectly substitutable. Forgetting is exponential; reading maintains some vocabulary at no cost, while grammar rehearsal is discounted by a modelling parameter. Four coverage conventions are fitted and carried through every analysis, each solved over a Latin-hypercube parameter box. Three findings hold across all four conventions. A 98% target is optimal in only 1.67% to 4.17% of the parameter box. The drivers of the optimal target are ranked identically every time: the free rehearsal that reading supplies for vocabulary, then vocabulary retention, then the horizon, with grammar-side parameters and the substitution elasticity nearly inert. One negative result is reported: the grammar rehearsal weight shifts the objective level, not the policy structure. Because the level of the optimal target depends on the coverage convention while its drivers do not, no point estimate is offered. The analysis is a normative model, not a prescription for individual learners.

title: OPTIMIZATION OF TOURIST ROUTES IN BATAM CITY USING INTEGER LINEAR PROGRAMMING WITH DESTINATION CATEGORY CONSTRAINTS
abstract: Tourist route planning plays an important role in improving travel efficiency and visitor experience in urban tourism areas. Batam City offers numerous tourist destinations with diverse characteristics, making route planning under realistic constraints a challenging task. Classical Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) models assume that all destinations must be visited, which is often impractical in real-world tourism scenarios. Therefore, this study proposes an optimization model for tourist route planning in Batam City using Integer Linear Programming (ILP) with destination category constraints. The proposed model allows a subset of destinations to be selected from a larger candidate set while determining the optimal visiting sequence. The objective function minimizes the total travel distance based on fixed driving distances obtained from digital map services. The model incorporates several constraints, including route continuity, subtour elimination, and category restrictions that limit the number of destinations selected from specific categories, such as beaches, shopping malls, and cultural sites. The model is implemented in Python using the PuLP optimization library and evaluated across four scenarios with varying category constraint settings. In the main scenario, the model produces an optimal route visiting 11 destinations with a total travel distance of 123.6 km. Scenario analysis further demonstrates that destination category selection significantly affects the total travel distance, with differences of up to 53.8% across scenarios despite a constant number of selected destinations. These findings indicate that ILP provides a flexible and effective framework for constrained tourist route optimization in urban tourism contexts. Furthermore, category-based constraints offer valuable insights into the trade-off between destination diversity and route efficiency.

title: Numerical Analysis Applications in Improving Engineering Models
abstract: Numerical analysis serves as the fundamental pillar of modern engineering modeling, providing the mathematical and computational tools necessary to transform complex physical equations into practical numerical solutions. This study reviews contemporary applications of numerical analysis in enhancing engineering models, focusing on methodological advancements in solving partial differential equations, data-driven model order reduction techniques, adaptive mesh methods, and machine learning-based surrogate models. The study employs a synthetic analytical approach that combines a review of recent literature with an analysis of empirical results from various numerical methods, addressing hybrid models that integrate traditional techniques with artificial intelligence. The analysis demonstrates that combining traditional numerical analysis methods with artificial intelligence and reduced-order models has revolutionized the ability of engineers to simulate complex multiphysics systems with unprecedented accuracy and computational efficiency; hybrid models have achieved computational speedups ranging from 72 to 522 times compare to traditional methods. Furthermore, the study addresses challenges related to computational cost and solution sensitivity to initial conditions, examining cutting-edge innovative solutions such as physicsinformed neural networks and causality-based learning. The study concludes that future trends in this field are shifting towards the development of hybrid models that combine analytical accuracy with computational speed, with an increasing emphasis on generalization capabilities beyond the training data. This opens up broad prospects for digital engineering and digital twin applications across the industrial, energy, and infrastructure sectors. The study offers a comprehensive perspective on the development of engineering models using advanced numerical analysis techniques and identifies promising future research directions in this vital field.

title: Measurement-driven quantum approximate optimization
abstract: Algorithms based on non-unitary evolution have attracted much interest for ground state preparation on quantum computers. One recently proposed method makes use of ancilla qubits and controlled unitary operators to implement weak measurements related to imaginary-time evolution. In this work we specialize and extend this approach to the setting of combinatorial optimization. We first generalize the algorithm from exact to approximate optimization, taking advantage of several properties unique to classical problems. In particular we show how to select parameters such that the success probability of each measurement step is bounded away from $1/2$. We then show how to adapt our paradigm to the setting of constrained optimization for a number of important classes of hard problem constraints. For this we compare and contrast both penalty-based and feasibility-preserving approaches, elucidating the significant advantages of the latter approach. Our approach is general and may be applied to easy-to-prepare initial states as a standalone algorithm, or deployed as a quantum postprocessing stage to improve performance of a given parameterized quantum circuit. We then propose a more sophisticated variant of our algorithm that adaptively applies a mixing operator or not, based on the measurement outcomes seen so far, as to speeds up the algorithm and helps the system evolution avoid slowing down or getting stuck suboptimally. In particular, we show that mixing operators from the quantum alternating operator ansatz can be imported directly, both for the necessary eigenstate scrambling operator and for initial state preparation, and discuss quantum resource tradeoffs.

title: Learning from Next-Frame Prediction: Towards Unified and Scalable Visual Representation Learning
abstract: Video provides a natural source of supervision: what happens next serves as a learning signal for visual world modeling. Yet masked video pretraining focuses on recovering missing content from surrounding context rather than predicting the future from the past. Autoregressive methods instead predict forward one token at a time, but have yet to match joint-embedding methods in representation quality. This gap motivates us to revisit the granularity and space of future prediction. In this work, we introduce VANE, a self-supervised visual pretraining framework built on next-frame prediction in embedding space. A causal encoder summarizes past observations for a state predictor that infers the representation of the entire next frame, making temporal evolution the primary learning signal. This prediction is carried out in a fixed embedding space provided by a frozen semantic tokenizer, emphasizing scene content and structure. To retain fine-grained spatial detail alongside semantic content, a lightweight auxiliary generative decoder reconstructs future-frame patches conditioned on the predicted representations. To unify visual modeling across images and videos, we construct a local-to-global crop sequence for still images, allowing the same encoder to predict newly revealed regions from earlier crops under the same objective. Experiments show that VANE improves with model and data scaling, achieving SOTA on most anticipation, recognition, and dense perception benchmarks among unified encoders. Especially on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 action anticipation, it surpasses V-JEPA 2.1 by 7.1 points in mean-class recall@5. These results demonstrate that next-frame prediction in embedding space is effective and scalable for visual world modeling.

title: Kernel methods in the deep Ritz framework: theory and practice
abstract: Abstract In this contribution, kernel approximations are applied as ansatz functions within the Deep Ritz method. This allows to approximate weak solutions of elliptic partial differential equations with weak enforcement of boundary conditions using Nitsche’s method. A priori error estimates are proven in different norms leveraging both standard results for weak solutions of elliptic equations and well-established convergence results for kernel methods. This availability of a priori error estimates renders the method useful for practical purposes where theoretical guarantees are important. The procedure is described in detail, meanwhile providing practical hints and implementation details. By means of numerical examples, the performance of the proposed approach is evaluated and the theoretical findings are verified. We further apply two-layered kernels in a high-dimensional test case, which goes beyond a purely linear method. To the best of our knowledge, this paper contains the first extensive numerical studies and discussions comparing kernel interpolation, the kernel Galerkin method, the deep Ritz method with kernels and the “classical” deep Ritz method with neural networks. We numerically verify advantages and disadvantages of the particular methods and show under which assumptions the individual approaches are beneficial.

title: Inside-JEPA: From Prediction to Relational Grounding in Latent World Models
abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models in latent space, enabling efficient planning but leaving their states opaque. We introduce Inside-JEPA, which places relational channels for ordered entity pairs inside the JEPA latent state and shows that an inverse-dynamics loss can ground these channels without relation labels when its head reads them, either alone or as part of the full state. On Something-Something V2, latent prediction alone performs no better than a random relation head, while inverse-dynamics supervision that recovers actions from channel changes improves relational AUROC by .065-.103 across ten settings with annotated boxes, by .081 on RH20T robot episodes with held-out tasks, and by .050-.061 across five relations using off-the-shelf detection and tracking. An inverse head on entity latents decodes actions more accurately but barely improves relational grounding; shuffled labels, two label-free objectives, and action labels on only 5% of the pairs also fail to ground the channels. Given an action, predicted relational changes approach the quality of observed future relations (AUROC .599 vs .621). For one-step relational goals, a supervised readout of the 16 channels ranks the correct action among the top five of 65 in 43% of cases, compared with 24% for prediction-only latents and 17% for a frequency prior.

title: In-Context Learning World Models for Robot Dual-Arm Manipulation of Soft Garment with Partial Observations
abstract: Robust manipulation of soft objects, such as garments, is a critical skill for service and household robots to adopt, but remains challenging due to its high-dimensional state space, and material-dependent deformations. Humans address this challenge by using mental world models that "imagine" the shape and material properties from partial observations, which enables them to predict how actions affect future states. As such, embedding such world models in robots allows for better generalization in manipulating a wide variety of garments in the real world. However, learned world models typically require large amounts of real world data that is strenuous to collect, and a mechanism to infer latent properties that govern dynamics. We present a Soft-Object World Model that performs generative full-state estimation and action-conditioned dynamics prediction using a transformer backbone trained on large-scale simulated soft object interactions, with measures to mitigate the sim-to-real gap. By learning to infer latent shape and material cues through in-context learning over a variable-length partial point-cloud history, the model generalizes across robot embodiments, material parameters, garment types and shapes, and manipulation coordination modes without weight updates. The world model is then integrated with a Goal-Conditioned action planner for motion synthesis. We validate the approach in simulation and real world for bimanual garment folding, reporting improvements in reconstruction fidelity, prediction accuracy, and task success.
