title: Economic lifetime-aware wind farm control
abstract: Abstract. We present the economic lifetime-aware formulation of wind farm control (WFC), a novel approach that incorporates the current state of damage of turbines – either provided by a digital twin or estimated from operational data – to compute control policies that optimize the long-term life management of a wind farm. The optimization is guided by an economic value function that balances power capture (taking into account variable spot market prices) with operation and maintenance (O&M) costs, including potential revenue losses due to turbine downtime. The optimization process is subject to constraints ensuring that the target lifetime of selected turbine components is met, considering varying inflow conditions. This results in optimal control setpoints for each turbine as functions of ambient conditions. After introducing the economic lifetime-aware WFC approach, the paper analyzes two case studies. The first is a synthetic scenario with a simplified set of environmental conditions, designed to demonstrate the behavior of the new control strategy and its impact on fatigue loads. The second case features the more realistic setup of a small wind farm, with wind climate data derived from a real meteorological mast. The benefits of the proposed methodology are highlighted by comparing it to a range of reference control strategies, which either ignore component damage or address fatigue loads in alternative simplified ways. When compared to greedy and power-maximizing WFC strategies, results show that only the lifetime-aware formulation ensures the achievement of the desired lifetime targets. Additionally, it also results in the best economic performance.

title: Echo: Coupled Action and Task Status Signal Denoising for Vision Language Action Models
abstract: Recognizing task completion and failure enables robots to stop upon success and initiate recovery or replanning after failure. Existing methods augment Vision Language Action (VLA) policies with task status signal prediction to support these execution decisions. However, learning and integrating these signals can require fine-grained supervision, external monitoring models, or complex architectural designs. Moreover, the potential of task status signals to directly guide action generation remains underexplored. We present Echo, a framework that combines task status signal learning without frame-level progress annotations with a compact design for status prediction and action generation within a single VLA. Specifically, Echo represents task status with stop and failure signals, added as two dimensions of each action chunk and denoised together with robot actions. Their combination distinguishes ongoing execution, successful completion, and failure. To learn these signals without fine-grained progress annotations, Echo constructs successful, failed, and recovery trajectories with complementary supervision properties. To enable status signal-guided action generation, Echo controls interactions between the signals and actions and denoises the signals faster than the actions. These allow later action denoising steps to condition on cleaner status estimates while preserving accurate signal prediction. Extensive real-world manipulation experiments show that Echo accurately predicts task status and consistently improves policy performance.

title: Dynamic client selection in federated learning using particle swarm optimization for medical image classification
abstract: Abstract Federated Learning (FL) enables decentralized medical institutions to collaboratively train predictive models without sharing sensitive patient data. However, conventional FL pipelines commonly rely on random client selection, which ignores the heterogeneous and unequal contributions of local data across institutions. This limitation can slow the convergence and reduce the model performance in non-IID clinical scenarios. To address this problem, we propose a dynamic client selection strategy based on Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). The proposed method formulates client selection as a combinatorial optimization problem and uses PSO to identify high-utility client subsets at each communication round without modifying local training or the aggregation mechanism. We evaluated the method on three public medical imaging datasets, LC25000, Biglycan, and ALL-IDB, using four CNN architectures under heterogeneous federated settings. The evaluation compares FedAvg, Oort, PyramidFL, and a GA-based baseline, and includes ablation, PSO grid search, Dirichlet non-IID analysis, and statistical validation. The results show that PSO-driven client selection improves model performance mainly in configurations with limited client participation and lightweight architectures, such as SqueezeNet and MobileNet. We demonstrated that the proposed method benefits mainly from empirical client utility, operates reliably within practical PSO parameter ranges, and remains most effective in heterogeneous settings with sufficient client participation. Overall, these findings suggest that optimization-guided client selection can improve federated medical image classification while preserving compatibility with standard FL aggregation pipeline.

title: Dual Exam: Controlled Evaluation of Multimodal Agents and World Models
abstract: World Models (WMs) can support Multimodal Agents (MAs) through simulated experience, while Agent trajectories can inform World Model refinement. Evaluating this interaction requires separate evidence about action selection and state evolution. We introduce Dual Exam, which tests Agents under fixed environment response mechanisms and World Models under fixed action interventions across physical, digital, social, and scientific domains. The Agent track compares 10 configurations on 1,088 items in 15 reporting categories. The World Model track contains 400 cases across eight scenarios; 15 configurations have full coverage and one covers six scenarios. GPT 6 Astra leads the case-weighted Agent Index at 31.3, and GPT-Image-2 leads the full-coverage WM Overall at 21.7. These scores use different tasks and metrics and are not directly comparable. A 150-case pilot of one coupled pairing records zero task successes and motivates component-level diagnosis. Results reveal uneven task performance and failures to preserve task-relevant state. Their value for predicting coupled success or sustained reciprocal learning remains to be established.

title: DiffDreamer: Coupling World Models with Differentiable Simulation for Agile Quadrotor Control
abstract: Tasks such as quadrotor dynamic-gate racing require agents to anticipate external motion while maintaining precise high-frequency control. World-model-based reinforcement learning provides a natural solution by learning latent dynamics for future imagination, yet it often entangles environmental evolution and the robot's own dynamics in a single learned rollout, where model bias can affect policy optimization efficiency. We propose DiffDreamer, a differentiable reinforcement learning framework that tightly couples a learned world model with differentiable simulation for actor optimization. In one optimization step, the learned world model propagates latent states that capture external dynamics and history-dependent features, while the differentiable simulator propagates the robot's explicit physical state. We further decompose the actor objective into a critic-driven pathway for non-differentiable task rewards and a simulator-driven pathway for differentiable motion rewards. Experiments on aggressive tracking and dynamic-gate racing show that DiffDreamer improves training convergence over the model-free, model-based, and differentiable-RL baselines, and final performance over these baselines and classical planning and control methods. Additional experiments assess reward decomposition and the odometry-conditioned relative-state representation through ablations. We also provide proof-of-concept real-world flight experiments for validation.

title: CAFM v4: a cascaded anchor-dominant residual fusion model for multi-scale brain tumor classification from magnetic resonance imaging
abstract: Inroduction Brain tumor classification using Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is critical for diagnosis and treatment planning in neuro-oncology. The CAFM v4 framework introduced in this study incorporates a novel Anchor-Dominant Residual Fusion (ADRF) mechanism for brain tumor MRI classification. Methods CAFM v4 combines ConvNeXt V2, Swin-Base, and EfficientFormerV2-S0 for feature extraction using deep supervision, knowledge distillation, class-balanced focal loss, and progressive training. Stochastic weight averaging and test-time augmentation are incorporated to support optimization, training stability, and benchmark performance. The proposed framework was evaluated on five public brain tumor MRI datasets: Br35H (binary), FigShare (3-class), 4-class, 15-class, and 30-class datasets. Results The proposed CAFM v4 framework achieved classification accuracies of 99.78%, 98.01%, 96.75%, 95.79%, and 97.73% on the Br35H, FigShare, 4-class, 15-class, and 30-class datasets, respectively. The model demonstrated strong benchmark performance across five independently trained datasets with different class distributions, sample sizes, and classification complexities. The learned fusion gates showed similar convergent values across training runs, indicating consistent information integration from the three backbone networks. Discussion CAFM v4 demonstrated strong performance relative to a majority of contemporary CNN-based, transformer-based, and hybrid frameworks. The results indicate that the proposed fusion strategy supports binary and multi-class brain tumor classification. However, these independently trained benchmark experiments do not establish external or cross-institutional generalization. Further patient-level external validation using independent multicenter datasets is necessary before establishing clinical utility.

title: Anticipating Social Consequences with Distributional World Models
abstract: Social world models predict how interactions develop after an action, helping agents negotiate, cooperate and mediate. In these situations, one action can lead to several plausible futures, hence predicting only one future can overlook consequential alternatives, while exploring them through repeated simulations increases inference cost. We propose DSWM, a Distributional Social World Model that predicts alternative responses, their probabilities and immediate and final outcome values in one output per candidate action. We train a 4B model on repeated simulations using supervised fine-tuning and GRPO. At inference time, the actor uses these possible consequences to choose an action. Across three seen and two unseen environments, with interaction backbones absent from training collection, DSWM achieves the best average performance on 13 of 15 metrics. Ablations show that retaining multiple futures and their predicted probabilities improves outcomes in all five environments.

title: An Introduction to World Models for Generalist Agents
abstract: World models have recently emerged as a promising direction toward developing generalist agents capable of understanding, predicting, and interacting with diverse environments. However, despite growing interest, the concept of a world model remains loosely defined, encompassing approaches ranging from predictive dynamics models and learned simulators to models that jointly generate future observations and actions. This introductory paper aims to clarify the concept of world models and provide a unified perspective on their role in developing generalist agents. Starting from the partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) framework, we connect world modeling to classical control, dynamical systems, signal processing, and reinforcement learning. We introduce different approaches to world modeling, emphasizing the knowledge they capture, their learning objectives, and how they support decision-making. We further explore the relationship between world modeling and policy learning, highlighting how these capabilities can be unified through conditional prediction without requiring separate models. Rather than offering an exhaustive survey of existing methods, this paper focuses on fundamental concepts, modeling principles, and connections, with the goal of providing an accessible and unified introduction to world models for generalist agents.

title: Airway image analysis systems: a review of datasets, evaluation methodologies, and deep learning approaches
abstract: Airway image analysis systems play an increasingly important role in computer-assisted diagnosis, quantitative airway assessment, intervention planning, and respiratory disease management. However, the development of robust airway analysis methods remains challenging due to the complex geometry of airway structures, strong class imbalance, variability in imaging protocols, and the need to preserve anatomical connectivity across multiple spatial scales. Recent advances in topology-aware learning, transformer-based architectures, and foundation-model adaptation have substantially changed the landscape of airway image analysis, motivating an updated review focused specifically on airway-oriented systems. In this narrative review, we provide a comprehensive overview of the datasets, evaluation methodologies, and computational approaches that underpin modern airway image analysis systems. We discuss the imaging modalities and publicly available datasets commonly used for airway analysis and examine their strengths, limitations, and implications for algorithm development and benchmarking. Particular attention is given to evaluation methodologies, including overlap-based, surface-distance, and topology-aware metrics that assess both segmentation accuracy and structural correctness. We further review the evolution of computational approaches, covering convolutional neural networks, transformer-based architectures, hybrid methods, topology-aware and tubular-aware networks, foundation-model adaptations, and data-efficient learning strategies. Finally, we discuss current challenges related to dataset availability, annotation quality, model generalization, topology preservation, and clinical deployment, and outline future research directions toward robust, interpretable, and clinically deployable airway image analysis systems.

title: A Physics-Informed Fourier Neural Operator Framework for Zero-Plating Fast Charging of Lithium-Ion Batteries via Real-Time Electrochemical State Estimation and Barrier-Riding Optimal Control
abstract: Extreme fast charging of lithium-ion batteries is critically limited by internal lithium plating at the negative electrode-separator interface, driving rapid degradation and thermal hazards. Real-time mitigation is fundamentally impeded because the interfacial plating overpotential (ηplating) is inaccessible to non-invasive sensors, leaving conventional protocols blind to metallic lithium deposition. While high-fidelity Doyle–Fuller–Newman (DFN) models resolve these dynamics, their computational cost (∼ 8 s) precludes embedded closed-loop control, whereas empirical equivalent circuit models lack the spatial resolution to detect plating. To resolve this trade-off, we develop a physics-informed 1D Fourier Neural Operator (FNO-1D) surrogate incorporating an explicit cumulative charge integral Q(t) = ∫ I dt to preserve mass conservation. Trained on 7,771 continuum DFN trajectories, the surrogate achieves a 4, 349× speedup (1.84 ms inference) with high fidelity (V RMSE = 5.40 mV, η plating , RMSE = 2.24 mV). Coupled with an Ensemble Smoother with Multiple Data Assimilation (ESMDA), the framework filters sensor noise (±10 mV to 5.94 mV) and reconstructs unobservable plating dynamics (RMSE = 4.12 mV, 95% CI = ±3.22 mV), establishing continuous closed-loop observability. A Barrier-Riding Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC) policy then maximizes charging current along the degradation boundary. Across a 10% - 80% SOC window, it cuts charging time by 21.7% (33.7 min vs. 43.0 min CC-CV)while strictly preventing lithium plating (η plating ≥ +14.81 mV > +5.0 mV), limiting peak temperature to 38.5◦C, and decreasing SEI growth by 21.5%. Finally, transferability is experimentally validated across two phys ical cycler benchmarks: cross-chemistry transfer on Oxford pouch cells, and chemistry-matched validation on commercial RWTH Aachen Sanyo 18650 NMCcells, achieving a terminal voltage tracking RMSE of 33.02 mV (86.0% error reduction over zero-shot transfer) providing an experimentally grounded paradigm for degradation-free fast charging.

title: Tactile-Based Robotic Manipulation: From Mechanics-Driven to Data-Driven Perspectives
abstract: Tactile sensing provides robots with direct access to physical interactions at the contact interface, making it a critical modality for robust and dexterous manipulation. Over the past several decades, tactile-based manipulation research has evolved from mechanics-driven approaches, which explicitly interpret tactile signals through contact mechanics and task-specific reasoning, to data-driven approaches that learn tactile representations and manipulation policies directly from data. This paper reviews the development of tactile-based manipulation from these two complementary perspectives. We first introduce the fundamentals of tactile sensing, and then review, from a mechanics-driven perspective, how those signals form manipulation-relevant state representations and subsequently influence the robot action. We then examine the recent advances in data-driven tactile manipulation, covering imitation learning, reinforcement learning, vision-language-action models, and predictive models. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future opportunities toward scalable, generalizable, and robust tactile-enabled robotic systems.

title: Steering Black-Box Large Language Model Agents with Pitfall Anticipation World Model
abstract: Frontier black-box Large Language Model (LLM) agents are proficient at long-horizon reasoning and precise action generation. However, when it comes to a specific agentic task, they have no internalized knowledge of how that particular environment unfolds. A world model offers a natural remedy, providing the agent with environment specific knowledge by foreseeing how the environment will respond to the action it is about to take. Prior world models for LLM agents mainly predict next observations at each step, which is costly and often uninformative because individual observations provide limited task-relevant guidance and not every step requires call for foresight. This raises a key question: what a world model should predict and when should it be invoked for agentic tasks? Our pilot study suggests that world model guidance is most useful when it anticipates pitfalls within a bounded multi-step future. Motivated by this, we introduce Pitfall Anticipation World Model (PAWM), which selectively intervenes when a potential pitfall arises and predicts the impending failure to steer the agent away from it. PAWM is trained in two stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on synthetic data labeled with agent pitfalls, followed by GRPO co-training with a black-box LLM to further optimize it in the target environment. PAWM improves Claude Sonnet 4.5 performance by 24.3% on ScienceWorld and 7.7% on WebArena-Lite, outperforming a range of baselines. These results demonstrate that PAWM provides an effective form of world model guidance for black-box LLM agents.

title: Spatial metabolomics-guided deep learning framework for dissecting immune evasion mechanisms in fungal infection microenvironments
abstract: Invasive fungal infections cause high mortality in immunocompromised patients, yet the spatially organized metabolic circuits that enable pathogens to evade host immunity remain poorly understood. Here we present an integrated computational–experimental framework coupling high-resolution spatial metabolomics with attention-enhanced deep learning to dissect immune evasion mechanisms within fungal infection microenvironments. We constructed a spatial metabolic atlas from MALDI-MSI and DESI-MSI data acquired on murine invasive pulmonary aspergillosis tissue sections, identifying 1,847 reproducible metabolite features across histologically distinct tissue compartments. A multi-scale convolutional network with fused channel and spatial attention modules was designed for automated segmentation of infection core, immune infiltration zone, and a transitional boundary zone, not previously resolved spatially in this infection model, that is enriched in immunosuppressive metabolites including kynurenine, prostaglandin E₂, and gliotoxin, achieving a mean Dice coefficient of 0.887 against expert pathologist annotations. To reconstruct the dynamic regulatory wiring underlying immune evasion, we developed a variational graph autoencoder coupled with neural ordinary differential equations, which inferred temporally evolving metabolite–immune interaction networks across 24, 48, and 72 h post-infection with an area under the precision-recall curve of 0.782 against KEGG and Reactome benchmarks. Network analysis ranked kynurenine as the highest-centrality hub metabolite at 48–72 h, and Neural ODE interpolation placed a putative metabolic tipping point between 36 and 48 h, marked by abrupt activation of tryptophan catabolism edges and a concurrent loss of Th1-associated signaling connectivity. Ablation experiments showed that the dual attention mechanism contributed the largest gain in segmentation and the second-largest in network inference, after the Neural ODE temporal coupling. This framework offers a hypothesis-generating, data-driven paradigm that recasts immune evasion as a spatially encoded and temporally dynamic process, and it yields prioritised candidate targets and therapeutic windows that remain to be tested by perturbation experiments before any antifungal intervention strategy can be built on them.

title: Safe World Model for Joint Trajectory and Beamforming Design of Mobile Base Stations
abstract: Mobile base stations (MBSs), including aerial and ground-based platforms, provide flexible wireless coverage through adaptive positioning. However, jointly optimizing their trajectories and digital beamforming is challenging because movement changes channel conditions and interference, while beamforming determines the resulting signal and interference powers. These coupled decisions also account for how current movements affect future positions and communication performance under mobility and safety constraints. We formulate this problem as a constrained Markov decision process that maximizes the time-averaged sum signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR), subject to mobility, restricted-zone avoidance, and transmit-power constraints. To support long-term planning and reduce the extensive environment interactions required by model-free reinforcement learning, we develop a SafeDreamer-based world model framework that learns latent system dynamics from experience and optimizes a joint trajectory and beamforming policy through imagined trajectories. Feasibility-preserving action mappings and safety cost signals incorporate operational constraints into policy learning. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework improves the time-averaged sum SINR by an average of 7\% and 9\% compared with proximal policy and deep Q-network baselines, respectively, while achieving higher sample efficiency and more reliable constraint satisfaction.

title: SP-HLM: Sparse-Pose-Driven Motion Generation and Whole-Body Control for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires an effective interface between high-level task policies and whole-body control. Existing interfaces typically rely on a single action representation for both task intent and whole-body coordination. This may burden the high-level policy or leave one aspect underspecified. We present SP-HLM, a framework built on a sparse-pose-driven interface. The interface combines five task-critical body poses with a learned latent motion prior to represent spatial intent and whole-body coordination in complementary forms. SP-VLA, a vision-language-action model, first predicts task-relevant sparse poses and finger joint positions from multimodal observations and language instructions using asynchronous action-chunk inference. Given these sparse targets, SP-MGM, a motion generation model trained through two-stage distillation, reconstructs coordinated full-body motion in real time. A pretrained motion encoder maps this motion to a compact latent representation. SP-GMT, a general motion tracker, then integrates the explicit sparse targets with this implicit motion prior for whole-body control. Experiments in simulation and on a real humanoid robot demonstrate improved motion tracking, whole-body coordination, and loco-manipulation success over existing approaches. Additional results and videos are available on our \href{https://sp-hlm.github.io/}{\textcolor{blue}{project page}}.

title: Physics-enforced neural ordinary differential equation for chemical kinetics optimization in reaction-diffusion systems
abstract: Calibrating chemical kinetics in a reaction–diffusion system is challenging because of complex dynamics governed by tightly coupled chemistry and transport, while experimental observations are often sparse and noisy. We propose a physics consistent diffusion-chemistry coupled neural ordinary differential equation (Diff-Chem Neural ODE) that embeds Arrhenius-structured reaction neurons into a fully differentiable streamline formulation and explicitly accounts for diffusion coupling. This design enables direct gradient-based analysis of kinetic parameters without sampling-based pretraining. We validate this method on burner-stabilized flat and stagnation reacting flows using mechanisms spanning different stiffness ranges. The proposed method reproduces species profiles with near-reference accuracy, whereas a pure chemistry Neural ODE that neglects diffusion coupling may misplace ignition and generate an incorrect thin reaction zone. Diff-Chem Neural ODE is more robust than pure chemistry Neural ODE and provides substantial speedups for gradient evaluation compared with fully discretized computations. In kinetics refinement, optimizing only a limited set of “primal” species reduces the loss by over 98 % and simultaneously recovers unobserved variables, demonstrating physically consistent global control. Finally, tests with 1–20 % noise in the objective show stable convergence without local overfitting, supporting its applicability under noisy measurements.

title: PhysiCalWorld: In-Context Physics Calibration for World Models
abstract: Existing world models typically perceive a scene through current visual frame or a narrow history window. However, these observations may not reveal the physics properties that determine transition dynamics, such as an object's mass distribution, joint damping, or surface friction. Without calibrating these physics factors for world models, predictions tend to regress toward an empirical prior and induce severe drift in novel test scenes. To this end, we propose PhysiCalWorld, which calibrates action-conditioned world models to the instance-specific dynamics via in-context prompting, without fine-tuning or analytical physics modeling. Our method encodes an exploratory interaction clip collected within the test scene into a compact physics descriptor token, which grounds subsequent predictions in the scene's actual physical behavior. PhysiCalWorld is trained end-to-end with the latent prediction loss alone, without physics labels. At inference time, the descriptor token is extracted once and can be reused across rollouts with negligible compute overhead. We evaluate PhysiCalWorld across four environments covering diverse physics variations and show that it substantially improves rollout prediction accuracy and visual planning success rate. The learned descriptors also form a physically structured latent space and generalize beyond the physics ranges seen during training.

title: OccJEPA: Occlusion as Masking for Amodal Video Segmentation
abstract: Amodal video segmentation asks for the complete mask of an object in every frame, including the parts hidden behind other objects. The best current methods generate these masks with fine-tuned video diffusion models, which need many denoising steps and an extra depth network, and give a different answer for every sample. Self-supervised video world models of the JEPA family are trained on a closely related task: predicting the representation of masked space-time regions from the visible ones. We therefore treat occlusion as masking. The tokens that the object's visible mask does not cover are dropped, the pre-trained V-JEPA 2.1 predictor fills them in, and a light head decodes the observed and predicted features into amodal masks. The resulting model, OccJEPA (Occlusion-as-masking JEPA), is deterministic and 33.5x faster than the diffusion-based state of the art, and more accurate on SAIL-VOS, on TAO-Amodal, including a held-out test split (+4.00 AP50) and visible masks tracked by SAM2, and on Kubric. Controlled experiments trace the gain to the predictor's pre-trained weights rather than to its capacity, for world models from 87M to 1.85B parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/zgp110/occjepa.

title: Model Predictive Control for Magnetically Actuated Cellbots
abstract: This article presents a control strategy for, which are magnetically actuated, micron‐scale robots embedded into living cells. Our approach combines model predictive control, which provides low computational complexity and adaptability to changing environments, with Gaussian Processes (GPs), which are used as disturbance estimators for precise path tracking. To address the challenges posed by unmodeled dynamics, we integrate data‐driven modeling with model‐based control to accurately track desired trajectories using relatively small data. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to integrate data‐driven modeling with model‐based control for magnetically actuated cellbots. The GP effectively learns and predicts unmodeled disturbances, providing uncertainty bounds as well. The experimental results show that our controllers perform very well, even in environments cluttered with cells.

title: Local and Sparse Kernel Operator Learning for Incompressible Flows: An Operator Lagrange Formulation
abstract: We present a local and sparse kernel method for learning the solution operators of incompressible flows. It builds on our earlier property-preserving kernel method, whose global output reconstruction and dense operator regression scale poorly. Our method replaces the global output reconstruction by local divergence-free interpolants with divergence-free polynomials of any degree, solved in parallel on the GPU. These interpolants are divergence free, periodic on periodic domains, and, with a multiscale kernel, approach Kolmogorov statistics under refinement. A compactly supported kernel, positive semidefinite in any input dimension, makes the operator regression sparse. Its support radius, and hence the sparsity, is fitted to data, and optional affine polynomials in the input capture global trends. Operator Lagrange weights join the two. They cost one sparse solve per new input and act on the training fields before the output reconstruction, so their local coefficients are never formed. We show that, unlike direct evaluation, Lagrange evaluation does not amplify solve errors by the cancellation among spatial coefficients. On ten fluid benchmarks, validation selects sparse matrices nearly everywhere, with densities that mostly decrease as the training set grows, and affine augmentation lowers the error by more than an order of magnitude for forced isotropic turbulence. These sparse models are at least as accurate as our earlier dense method and more accurate than neural operators. Lagrange evaluation is as accurate as direct evaluation with local output reconstructions, and up to nearly three orders of magnitude more accurate with global ones. We also present GPU timings and storage.

title: LLM-Based Exogenous World Modeling for Dynamic Scheduling
abstract: Dynamic scheduling requires dispatching online arrivals while anticipating future jobs, as poor decisions can compound downstream costs under nonlinear tardiness objectives. We show that a pretrained large language model (LLM) can serve as the exogenous component of a structured world model, forecasting uncertain future job arrivals. Specifically, we exploit an afterstate decomposition, which separates known deterministic shop transitions from uncertain exogenous job arrivals, enabling the LLM to forecast only the latter through a compact belief representation. Building on this, we develop Afterstate World-Model Planning (AWMP), which combines an evolved, belief-conditioned dispatching strategy with short scenario-based rollouts. A surprise-triggered refresh mechanism queries the LLM only when newly observed arrivals deviate sufficiently from previous forecast, and online residual self-calibration further conditions the LLM on its recent forecast errors to handle nonstationary arrivals. Across diverse arrival distributions, AWMP reduces weighted tardiness by 6-21% on dynamic job-shop and 22-46% on flexible job-shop benchmarks, relative to the best of eight classical priority-dispatching rules.

title: How Representational Priors Shape Generalization in World Action Models
abstract: World action models (WAMs) are shown to substantially diverge under generalization performance based on their generative backbones. We investigate this gap through the representational geometry that WAMs inherit from their backbones and how policy training reorganizes it. Our central hypothesis is that a useful representational prior would structure geometry that separates nuisance information from the in-distribution manifold in advance of training as a policy. We quantify this with nuisance orthogonality; orthogonality of the feature under visual variation outside the empirical in-distribution manifold. Across various image and video backbones, we show that a higher orthogonality from the representational prior is associated with stronger robustness to visual variations after WAM training, enabling policy generalization measurable prospectively for world models. In addition, analyzing the resulting robust WAMs reveals nuisance suppression; relative suppression of feature displacement caused by such variations and robust action generation of the policy. Together, these findings provide a geometric perspective on how the representational prior of the world model shapes the generalization performance of WAMs.

title: GeoMem-VLA: Internalizing 3D Scene Understanding into Temporal Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Geometric structure is essential for robotic manipulation and understanding the 3D world. Most VLA models rely on 2D representations of current observations, while geometry-aware approaches often require additional 3D information. However, geometry inferred independently from individual observations is often discarded rather than accumulated into a persistent task representation. Our key insight is that action generation needs a compact, task-relevant geometric abstraction that can be continuously updated, rather than a complete, renderable 3D reconstruction at every step. We introduce GeoMem-VLA, a VLA framework that internalizes explicit 3D supervision into dedicated geometric tokens and maintains them as temporal memory for action generation, without directly aligning the VLM's native visual embeddings with the teacher feature space. During training, a frozen geometry foundation model supervises learnable GeoPlan tokens through a geometric flow-matching objective over the current scene point map and future end-effector tracks. These tokens are integrated with the memory of observation representations, where historical information is retrieved, adaptively fused with current observations, and consolidated to retain event frames as the task progresses. At inference, the policy retrieves historical representations and fuses them with the current working representation to predict actions, without invoking the 3D teacher or explicitly reconstructing the scene. After benchmark-specific downstream adaptation, GeoMem-VLA achieves 98.9% average success on LIBERO and 91.10% / 91.24% on RoboTwin's clean/randomized settings. Across five real-world tasks, GeoMem-VLA achieves 78.0% average success. These results suggest that internalizing and remembering 3D scene understanding is a promising approach to robot control.

title: From Single-Actor Environments to Multi-Actor Event Worlds: Can LLMs Be Event World Models?
abstract: World models help agents assess the consequences of their actions before acting. Many real systems, however, involve multiple actors who make their own decisions, can evolve even when the agent takes no action, and are only partially observed through event logs. We formalize these systems as event worlds and ask whether large language models can predict future observations from the log and the agent's proposed actions. We build complementary benchmarks from human Diplomacy games and real Polymarket trades. Our hierarchical framework compares prediction with and without other actors' actions, then tests multi-step rollouts, predictions for actions never taken, and usefulness to agents. Fine-tuning and more data improve prediction when all actors' recorded actions are given. With only the agent's action, models struggle when other actors strongly affect the outcome, and larger models and longer histories help little. This gap also limits multi-step prediction and agent decisions, with models overestimating plan success. Yet imagined experience and initialization from world models can still improve policy learning. Anticipating other actors' actions remains a central challenge for event world modeling.

title: Events, Not Pixels: Where World Models Get the Return Wrong
abstract: World models are increasingly used for planning, where a planner ranks candidate actions by returns imagined by the model. However, these models are judged mainly by how well they render frames, even though a visually faithful rollout can still assign the wrong return. To identify where this mismatch arises, we introduce a transition-level diagnostic that replaces imagined transitions with real ones and measures the reduction in return error against a budget-matched random control. Our analysis yields two findings. (1) Event transitions, the few steps where a reward is earned or an episode ends, are rendered as well as other steps (median pixel-error ratio 0.85), yet restoring them removes a median of 70% of the return error. In contrast, restoring transitions with the largest MSE, SSIM or LPIPS error removes less than a random choice. Across the 44 Atari-100k model--collection pairs that pass our reliability checks, including three released families, event patches outperform random patches in 39 (sign test p=1.4 x 10^{-7}), with a median gain of +44 percentage points. (2) The remaining error is structured: a complementary patch separates errors at true events from those elsewhere, while an eight-step timing tolerance recovers few events missed by our deterministic models. This structure also guides repair: a rule recorded before four repair outcomes were known predicts when a diffusion model repairs these failures. Event patches improve plan ranking, and the same concentration appears on control tasks with rare reward events.

title: Electronic Inductor-less Parametric Oscillators for Compact Large-Scale Ising Machines
abstract: Parametric Oscillator (PO)-based Ising machines (IMs) are promising candidates for electronic solvers. They are able to solve nondeterministic polynomial-time hard (NP-hard) combinatorial optimization problems that current von Neumann architectures struggle to address. PO-based IMs relying on coupled networks of parametric frequency divider (PFD) circuits have recently been demonstrated, showing the capability to achieve power levels per spin in the hundreds of Nanowatts range. This has created an unprecedented opportunity to realize electronic Ising machines capable of solving NP-hard problems with a million variables while requiring less than 1 Watt. Yet, a major limitation still remains: due to its nonlinear dynamics, a typical PFD circuit requires multiple inductors to enable low-power activation of the period-doubling mechanism that is the basis of its PO-like operation, making it difficult to achieve wafer-scale Ising machines suited to solve problems with millions of variables. To overcome this limitation and enable large-scale PFD-based IMs without passive inductors, we propose a novel inductor-less PFD architecture. This architecture leverages gyrator-based circuits to achieve inductive elements out of active networks of resistors and capacitors, allowing to achieve a low-power threshold for the activation of the period-doubling mechanism without requiring inductors. The design approach creates a path to significantly reduce circuit area and improve integration capability. While being demonstrated using lumped electronic components on a printed circuit board, this architecture can be replicated using Complementary Metal Oxide Semiconductor (CMOS) electronics in the future, providing a promising path toward large-scale, fully integrated PFD-based Ising machines.

title: Causal world models under physical parameter shifts
abstract: World models predict how embodied systems evolve under actions, but their accuracy can degrade when physical conditions move outside the training distribution. We study two components of causal modeling: which inputs a predictor may use, and how its mechanism computes their effects. In a synthetic benchmark with shortcut features, a frozen dependency mask derived from paired interventions reduces mean out-of-distribution (OOD) RMSE from 1.769 for a fully connected predictor to 0.697, close to the generator-oracle mask (0.694). For robot link-mass extrapolation in CausalWorld, with disjoint training and test mass ranges, we develop finger-local world models in which link masses enter inertia and dynamics-bias terms through explicit affine coefficients, actions act through either a learned torque network or the known PD controller, and learned residuals capture contact-related effects. Compared with a separately trained control whose mass inputs are fixed at training means, the known-PD model turns out-of-range masses into a consistent predictive gain: median time-averaged joint R2 over 150-step rollouts rises from 0.609 to 0.727, with improvement in all ten task-seed runs (exact two-sided sign test, p = 0.002). In a shared 100-step forecast, the learned-torque model is competitive with the strongest recurrent robotic world model (RWM) configuration (median joint R2 of 0.755 - 0.768 versus 0.752), whereas supplying out-of-range masses sharply degrades the MLP and recurrent predictors. These results indicate that how a physical parameter enters the dynamics mechanism determines whether its out-of-range value helps or harms prediction.

title: CarBench: A comprehensive benchmark for neural surrogates on high-fidelity 3D car aerodynamics
abstract: Abstract Benchmarking has been the cornerstone of progress in computer vision, natural language processing, and the broader deep learning domain, driving algorithmic innovation through standardized datasets and reproducible evaluation protocols. The growing availability of large-scale Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) datasets has opened new opportunities for applying machine learning to aerodynamic and engineering design. Yet, despite this progress, large-scale standardized benchmarks remain limited for high-resolution three-dimensional automotive aerodynamics, making it difficult to evaluate and compare models systematically. In this work, we introduce CarBench, a large-scale standardized benchmark dedicated to high-resolution 3D automotive aerodynamics, and perform a large-scale evaluation of state-of-the-art models on DrivAerNet++, the largest public dataset for automotive aerodynamics, containing over 8,000 high-fidelity car simulations. We assess eleven representative model configurations spanning multiple modeling paradigms: classical neural operator methods (e.g., Fourier Neural Operator), geometric deep learning approaches (PointNet, RegDGCNN, PointMAE, PointTransformer), transformer-based neural solvers (Transolver, Transolver++, AB-UPT), and implicit field networks leveraging triplane representations (TripNet). Beyond standard interpolation tasks, we perform cross-category experiments in which representative transformer-based solvers trained on a single car archetype are evaluated on unseen categories to probe generalization. Our analysis covers predictive accuracy, pressure-field fidelity relative to the CFD reference, computational efficiency, and statistical uncertainty in evaluation metrics, providing a unified comparison across modeling families and quantifying the robustness of performance estimates under shifts in test geometry distributions. To accelerate progress in data-driven engineering, we open-source the complete benchmark framework, including training pipelines, metric-level uncertainty estimation routines based on bootstrap resampling, and pretrained model weights, establishing a reproducible foundation for large-scale learning from high-fidelity external automotive aerodynamics simulations, available at https://github.com/Mohamedelrefaie/CarBench .

title: Agentic World Action Models
abstract: Recent world action models provide visual foresight and future prediction for robot manipulation, but lack explicit mechanisms for compositional skill reuse. Agentic robotics combines code-based planning and reasoning with reusable skills, but often lacks predictive grounding in physical dynamics. We introduce AW-0, an agentic world action model framework that integrates code-based planning with joint video and action prediction. We jointly model code, future video, and robot actions as three coupled generative streams within a unified mixture-of-transformers architecture. Within this architecture a code expert generates parameterized skill routines and control logic while video and action experts generate future visual states and low-level motor commands. Code serves two complementary roles: it structures multi-step prediction and control within the world model and represents skills as reusable programs for subsequent agentic execution. We further introduce an automated curation pipeline that labels robot and human video trajectories with aligned programs and consolidates recurring routines into reusable skill libraries. Evaluations on RoboTwin 2.0 and physical bimanual manipulation tasks show improved task performance over VLA and WAM baselines, alongside gains in language following, semantic reasoning and robustness, demonstrating that agentic code enables connection between planning, prediction and execution within WAMs.

title: A mechanistic theory of planning in prefrontal cortex
abstract: Abstract Planning is critical for adaptive behaviour in a changing world, because it lets us anticipate the future and adjust our actions accordingly. While prefrontal cortex is crucial for this process, it remains unknown how planning is implemented in neural circuits. Prefrontal representations were recently discovered in simpler sequence memory tasks, where different populations of neurons represent different future time points. We demonstrate that combining such representations with the ubiquitous principle of neural attractor dynamics allows circuits to solve much richer problems including planning. This is achieved by embedding the environment structure directly in synaptic connections to implement an attractor network that infers desirable futures. The resulting ‘spacetime attractor’ excels at planning in challenging tasks known to depend on prefrontal cortex. Recurrent neural networks trained by gradient descent on such tasks learn a solution that precisely recapitulates the spacetime attractor – in representation, in dynamics, and in connectivity. Analyses of networks trained across different environment structures reveal a generalisation mechanism that rapidly reconfigures the world model used for planning, without the need for synaptic plasticity. The spacetime attractor is a testable mechanistic theory of planning. If true, it would provide a path towards detailed mechanistic understanding of how prefrontal cortex structures adaptive behaviour.

title: A PDE-theory-guided neural operator and the long-time relaxation of the two-dimensional anisotropic Boussinesq system
abstract: We design a neural operator for the two-dimensional Boussinesq system with anisotropic dissipation on the periodic box, guided by a rigorous analysis of its long-time behavior. The operator maps a small perturbation of hydrostatic equilibrium, of amplitude $\varepsilon$, to the vorticity at a late time. We prove that the flow relaxes to a stratified shear flow, with the horizontally averaged vorticity staying within $O(\varepsilon^2)$ of its initial value $\barω_0$ and the oscillation about it of order $\varepsilon$. Accordingly, the network outputs $\barω_0$ plus these two parts, each scaled to its size, which grows as $\varepsilon^2$ and $\varepsilon$, respectively. Without this guidance the training either does not converge or misses the $\varepsilon^2$ growth. With it, one network reproduces, sample by sample on $2\times10^3$ test runs over a factor of $23$ in amplitude, the quantity bounded by the theorem to a median error of $2.2$ percent. Being fast and differentiable with respect to the initial data, the network is also used to search the space of initial data, and with every candidate checked by the solver the search finds initial data for which this quantity is $4.4$ times the largest value among the test runs, raising the lower bound for the constant of the theorem by that factor.

title: TRCM: Topology-Aware Route-Consistency Modeling for Robust Neural Vehicle Routing
abstract: Neural combinatorial optimization has enabled fast constructive solvers for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP), yet most autoregressive models still construct solutions through sequential node selection and represent route organization only implicitly. We investigate whether route-level customer co-assignment can be modeled explicitly and used to guide this node-level decision process. To this end, we propose TopologyAware RouteConsistency Modeling (TRCM), which reuses node representations from a standard autoregressive construction pipeline to predict pairwise same-route probabilities and injects them into customer selection as a route-consistency signal. Because sameroute supervision is both class-imbalanced and structurally uneven, TRCM combines structure-preserving augmentation with Topological Entropy (TE)- based reweighting to emphasize locally ambiguous customer pairs. Under matched decoding budgets, TRCM reduces the optimality gap from 3.67% to 3.28% on CVRP50 and from 2.11% to 1.99% on CVRP100; under 8-fold augmented inference, it reduces the CVRP100 gap from 1.61% to 1.49%. On XML100, TRCM*8Aug improves the average objective by 0.24%, with larger gains on several structurally informative factors. A controlled demand-reassignment test over 500 variants further shows more concentrated objective fluctuations. These results support explicit route-consistency modeling as an effective structural principle for autoregressive neural routing.

title: SuperMimic: Scaling Humanoid Whole-Body Control with One Differentiable World Model
abstract: Tracking large human-motion datasets has become the dominant route to general, expressive humanoid whole-body control, but scaling across many motions is expensive. Current pipelines use model-free reinforcement learning, either merging per-motion specialists through lossy distillation, or brute-forcing a single policy with cluster-scale compute. SuperMimic amortizes learning across all motions with one differentiable world model of their shared dynamics, fit from logged transitions of a standard rigid-body simulator. The world model and the tracking policy train together in one loop, and backpropagation-through-time over short imagined rollouts gives the policy analytic gradients. Fast imagined rollouts and analytic gradients make policy learning efficient. In 3 hours on a single GPU, SuperMimic surpasses the return of a state-of-the-art motion tracker baseline trained for 7 days on 128 GPUs. It reduces GPU-hours by more than $1000\times$ and fails on only 25 of 129,514 benchmark motions, versus 179 failures for the baseline. After 9.8 hours on two GPUs, SuperMimic achieves zero failures. From 1 to 264 hours of motion, the world model's prediction error stays stable, and GPU-hours to a target return grow slowly. Our policy transfers to a physical Unitree G1 across diverse and acrobatic motions. SuperMimic removes compute as the bottleneck to scaling humanoid whole-body control, making it practical to measure motion-tracking scaling laws.

title: Spiking Neural Network-Based Neuromorphic Signal Processing for Real-Time Audio Event Detection in Low-Power Embedded Smart Sensors
abstract: The following paper presents the design of a spiking neural network (SNN) based neuromorphic signal processing system that can be used in low power embedded smart sensors to perform real time detection of audio events. In this regard, the aim is to overcome the shortcomings of traditional deep learning frameworks that are both computationally heavy and demanding in terms of power consumption such that they are incompatible with battery-run or energy-limited edge devices. Citing the performance of biological neural systems, the presented framework should utilize event-driven SNNs executed on neuromorphic platforms to identify notable acoustic situations (like alarms, speech commands and ambient environmental sounds). The architecture envisages audio preprocessing part, audio spike encoding, and spike temporally contrast encoding or Poisson encoding, and a multi-layer core SNN trained by surrogate gradient descent. The model is tuned to run on an Intel Loihi and ARM Cortex-M7 microcontroller. The standard datasets were used to assess the performance, such as Google Speech Commands, ESC-10 and UrbanSound8K. Using the experimental results, it can be proven that the SNN-based model has up to 92.7% correct classification accuracy, using < 5mW power with a latency below 20 milliseconds. SNN approach is equivalent in accuracy to conventional CNN baselines in many cases with much lower energy consumption. Results confirm the prospect of SNNs at ultra-low-power, real-time signal processing in future generation edge-AI acoustic systems. The research directions will look at hardware-aware training and learning that can be used to improve on adaptability and scalability of embedded smart sensing systems.

title: Slot-JEPA: Object-Structured Prediction Interfaces for Latent World Models
abstract: As a prototypical latent world model, Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) provide strong semantic representations. However, dense patch representations expose a redundant interface to downstream predictors, which must implicitly infer spatial organization and temporal correspondence, presenting three challenges. First, object information is distributed across patches, forcing each downstream predictor to redundantly recover object structure that could otherwise be reused across tasks before modeling interactions. Second, the lack of explicit entity correspondence across time makes historical transitions expensive, restricting the predictor's flexibility in utilizing context. Third, without explicit transport structure, existing JEPA models typically use pointwise l1/l2 distances, which are insensitive to spatial displacement when predicted and goal supports are largely disjoint. We propose the Slot-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Slot-JEPA), which decomposes dense representations into stable semantic slots and time-varying spatial masks. Pretrained once and frozen downstream, this decomposition exposes a reusable object-structured interface. Building on it, our Transition Memory Predictor (TMP) stores visual transitions as compact masks and retrieves useful context using statistics of corresponding slots. Its two branches separate slot-specific dynamics from shared cross-slot dynamics. We further use Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) to supervise mask prediction and evaluate candidate plans by transporting mass between aligned predicted and goal masks, providing a signal better aligned with spatial progress. Across seven visual-understanding benchmarks, the slot-reconstructed features remain transferable. Slot-JEPA also improves goal-conditioned planning across six planar environments and four robotic arm planning tasks on the REALM-JEPA benchmark.

title: Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to interact with environments and improve their decisions during deployment. However, how anticipating future outcomes and drawing on accumulated interaction experience can jointly support decision-making remains underexplored. We propose a test-time framework, inspired by Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control, that combines multi-branch predictive analysis with experience-based adaptation. At each step, the agent proposes multiple candidate actions and imagines their outcomes with a world model, so that alternatives can be compared without being executed in the environment. Since language environments provide neither explicit dynamics nor costs, the predicted outcomes are evaluated for task progress and risk, and MPPI-style weights over the resulting costs guide the final decision. A dual-branch experience memory enables self-improvement: the planner branch refines candidate generation and action selection, while the world model branch improves next-observation prediction. Experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld across three backbones demonstrate the strong overall performance of our method and the effectiveness of experience-guided predictive control. Our code will be made publicly available.

title: Second Thoughts: Exploring and Planning through Comparative Imagination in World Models
abstract: World models let agents compare imagined outcomes before acting, but an agent must still decide which alternatives to explore and when a proposed plan should replace its learned policy. We introduce SDI (Sibling Disagreement in Imagination), which connects these decisions through a shared actor-based reference. SDI compares action sequences imagined from the same model state, using repeated rollouts of the actor's own sequence to measure variation under fixed behavior. This reference scales both the spread across candidate returns, which provides an exploration signal, and a proposed plan's predicted advantage, which governs action acceptance. The agent executes a planned action when its advantage exceeds the reference variability by a fixed factor; otherwise, it follows the actor. SDI reuses the base agent's world model, actor, and critic without requiring an additional disagreement ensemble. Exploration and planning guide training data collection, while evaluation uses the learned actor alone. Across Meta-World, Adroit, and DM-Control, SDI achieves a higher observed task-average score than every compared baseline in each suite and matches or exceeds the strongest baseline's performance on 15 of 18 tasks. Component ablations and robustness analyses further examine the roles of exploration, planning exposure, and action acceptance. Paired evaluations from identical simulator states show that the gate improves both recovery from actor failures and preservation of successful behavior relative to ungated planning, while substantially reducing return degradation. Together, these results support comparing imagined alternatives against a shared actor reference as a unified approach to exploring and planning with world models.

title: RoboJudge: Multimodal Language Models as Judges for Embodied Video Generation
abstract: Video generation models are promising foundations for embodied world models, but only if their generated rollouts are physically valid and faithful to task instructions. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to judge these properties, yet their agreement with human judgments on embodied videos has not been systematically evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce RoboJudge-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs as judges of embodied video generation. The benchmark measures two fundamental dimensions, Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment, across 800 human-annotated videos from 8 source corpora and 10 video generators, spanning grippers, human hands, and dexterous hands. Experiments reveal uneven alignment between existing judges and human ratings: general-purpose MLLMs show lower agreement on physical adherence, while specialized video judges designed for general-domain physical reasoning do not consistently transfer to embodied scenarios. Motivated by these findings, we construct RoboJudge-Train, comprising 12K videos annotated with 25K human-verified scores and model-assisted rationales for Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment. We fine-tune a 9B MLLM on this dataset with supervised learning followed by reinforcement learning, yielding RoboJudge-9B. Among the model judges evaluated on RoboJudge-Bench, RoboJudge-9B achieves the highest overall agreement, reaching a Pearson correlation of 0.719 with a statistically significant 0.089 gain over Gemini-3.7-Flash, the best-performing proprietary baseline in our evaluation. Training on RoboJudge-Train also yields gains on external benchmarks, including VideoPhy2 and Physion-Eval. We further use RoboJudge-9B as a downstream evaluator to benchmark video generation models according to Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment.

title: Quantum-JEPA: Quantum Born Priors for Latent-Action JEPA World Models
abstract: A single observation can admit several plausible futures, making uncertainty an essential part of world modelling. However, quantum generative models remain underexplored for this task. We introduce Quantum-JEPA, a latent-action JEPA framework that learns distributions of future representations using a conditional quantum Born prior. Circuit measurements generate binary latent actions, which a shared predictor maps to alternative future representations. We train the quantum prior through the quality and diversity of these predictions using a sampled energy objective. Our model learns distinct continuations on constructed multimodal tasks and captures latent-action correlations that support coordinated multi-agent futures. On D3IL, a benchmark of diverse human demonstrations, our trained models generate multiple obstacle-crossing routes from a common starting point without observed motion. On the controlled tasks, our classical and quantum prior implementations improve prediction validity and distributional fidelity over the evaluated variational baselines. Our quantum priors combine competitive predictive quality with a parameter-efficient sampling structure: they avoid an exponentially sized categorical output layer while supporting correlated latent actions. We further validate finite-shot parameter-shift training, including training with readout noise. Unlike most prior work, which focuses on simulation, we also verify the feasibility of inference with trained priors on a real QPU. These results establish a trainable quantum component for JEPA future prediction and a basis for exploring quantum-enhanced world models at larger scales.

title: Quantum-Classical Hybrid Cloud Workflows for Combinatorial Supply-Chain and Fleet Optimization
abstract: Abstract: Global logistics networks, intercontinental air-freight consolidators, and maritime energy fleets continuously solve large-scale Mixed-Integer Linear Programs (MILPs) such as the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows (CVRPTW) and multi-vessel Maritime Inventory Routing Problems (MIRP). When weather disruptions, port congestion, or geopolitical airspace closures invalidate baseline schedules, classical branch-and-cut solvers (Gurobi, CPLEX) experience exponential worst-case tree growth on subproblems exceeding 2,000 binary decision variables, often failing to converge within strict 5-to-15-minute operational re-dispatch windows. Conversely, current Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) processors remain limited to 100-to-1,000 physical qubits with finite two-qubit gate fidelity ($99.2\%-99.8\%$), preventing direct encoding of full enterprise logistics instances. This paper presents a production-grade Quantum-Classical Hybrid Cloud Architecture that bridges enterprise Kubernetes clusters with co-located quantum processing units (QPUs) via AWS Braket Hybrid Jobs and IBM Quantum Qiskit Runtime primitives. Our framework applies Benders and Dantzig-Wolfe column generation on classical cloud HPC nodes to decompose a 25,000-variable global fleet MILP into a continuous master problem and hard combinatorial pricing/routing subproblems of 60 to 140 binary variables. These subproblems are transformed into Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) and Ising Hamiltonians, warm-started from classical linear programming (LP) relaxations (WS-QAOA), compiled with dynamical decoupling and Zero-Noise Extrapolation (ZNE), and executed inside co-located QPU-CPU sessions while a GPU-accelerated Simulated Bifurcation (SB) digital annealer runs in parallel as a deterministic SLA fallback. Evaluated on disruption recovery workloads modeled on ExxonMobil maritime LNG routing and DHL Global Forwarding air-cargo container loading, our hybrid WS-QAOA + Column Generation workflow improves optimality gap closure at a 10-minute SLA cutoff from 6.84% (classical branch-and-bound alone) to 1.42%, reduces emergency re-routing compute wall-clock time by 61.5%, and cuts fleet fuel and charter penalty costs by 4.7%. Research Domain & Specialization Track Master of Science in Information Technology (MSIT) — Quantum Cloud Computing, Hybrid Orchestration, and Operations Research. Core Technical Highlights Empirical Production Case Studies: Rigorous architectural blueprints and telemetry evaluation across enterprise cloud deployments. Four-Tier Reference Architecture: Formal specification from edge ingress to distributed hardware execution pools. Mathematical Formulation: Formally derived algorithmic and optimization models with closed-loop verification. Multi-Modal Benchmarking: Comparative empirical baselines under fault-injection and synthetic workload scaling. Author Information Author: Sonu Kumar SinghRole: Senior Consultant Affiliation: Independent Researcher Publication Status: Preprint / Working Paper (MSIT AI & Cloud Systems Research Series) Reproducibility & Open Science All included architecture diagrams, telemetry schemas, and benchmark curves are open-access under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license.

title: Planning under Noise with Neural Operators
abstract: Planning under uncertain control execution noise requires reliable feedback policies across diverse environments. We introduce Planning Under Noise (PUN), a neural operator that learns noise-aware value fields for planning in unseen geometries. Building on an established screened-Poisson formulation of stochastic optimal control, we address two challenges: specifying boundary conditions that support navigation across varying geometries and efficiently computing fields with reliable gradients. Zero-Dirichlet obstacle boundaries terminate sampled paths at walls, weakening the goal signal along long routes and making it harder to estimate reliably. We instead impose reflecting Neumann conditions on obstacles and a Dirichlet condition at the goal, allowing sampled paths to continue exploring free space until they reach the target. To solve the resulting PDE without a configuration-space mesh, we extend a Monte Carlo (MC) solver, Walk on Stars (WoSt), to higher dimensions. However, local MC fluctuations can reverse estimated gradient directions and cause planning failures, making direct planning require costly sampling. PUN amortizes this computation by learning geometry-to-field mappings from noisy, partially converged Monte Carlo labels, avoiding expensive convergence for every training example. At inference, test-time scaling uses bounded local search guided by the predicted global field. We evaluate PUN on planning tasks across dimensions. Across four noise levels, PUN matches or outperforms all compared planners, achieving 95-100% success on the 4D replanning benchmark while maintaining the lowest runtime. At the highest tested noise level in 4D, PUN achieves 10.7-60.6% relative gains in success rate over other methods while running 3.29-32.15 times faster.

title: Physical Canvas: A Vision Tactile World Model For Robot Policy Evaluation And Learning
abstract: Evaluating and post-training robot policies through physical interaction is costly and difficult to scale, motivating action-conditioned world models as interactive simulators. However, visually plausible predictions can misrepresent contact dynamics, providing unreliable feedback for policy evaluation and learning. We introduce PhysCanvas, a state-consistent visuo-tactile world model for contact-rich robot manipulation. PhysCanvas unifies multi-view RGB, tactile images, marker displacement, task state, and actions within a unified vision space. All modalities share a video VAE and pretrained generative backbone, allowing optical touch to reuse visual and temporal priors. Motion images derived through forward kinematics and camera projection provide spatially aligned action conditioning, while an initial RGB anchor and updated reference observations guide sequential generation. Our consistency-aware post-training uses the frozen Scene Reward Model, Modality Reward Model, and State Reward Model to supervise scene preservation, visual-tactile compatibility, and agreement with real task outcomes. The resulting world model supports closed-loop policy rollouts for evaluation and provides imagined interactions and rewards for GRPO policy updates. Across four real-world manipulation tasks, when policies are rolled out in the world model, State Reward Model supervision increases the arithmetic mean of task-wise Pearson correlations between world-model and real-world success rates from 0.602 to 0.885. Policy post-training in the reward-guided world model further increases $π_{0.5}$'s mean real-world success rate from a 59.1% SFT baseline to 70.8%. These results demonstrate the value of unified multimodal modeling and consistency-aware post-training for robot policy evaluation and learning. title: Neural Operator Splitting for Fluid Dynamics in Complex Geometry
abstract: Solving dynamical systems in complex and diverse geometries remains challenging for both numerical solvers and learning-based surrogate models. We propose Neural Operator Splitting, a framework for learning fluid dynamics while preserving the physical structure of fractional-step numerical schemes. Instead of learning the full-step evolution monolithically, we decompose each time step into physically interpretable steps, and learn each operator separately using intermediate states from the underlying numerical solver. Guided by the linearity properties of the fractional steps, we introduce a conditional-linear Fourier neural operator (CL-FNO) whose linear state mappings are modulated by nonlinear conditioning on inputs such as boundary geometry. We further introduce two complementary strategies, symmetry sampling and corrective cycling, to mitigate error accumulation during autoregressive rollout. Experiments on 2D and 3D fluid flows with varying geometries and initial conditions show that our full model reduces mean relative $L^2$ rollout error by 68\% in 2D and 40\% in 3D compared with a single full-step neural operator. At comparable error levels, neural-operator inference is approximately $10^3$ times faster per step than the Monte Carlo solver.

title: MoDDiT: Simple Token Routing in Diffusion Transformers
abstract: Real-time video generation, interactive world models, and on-device image synthesis are almost a reality. Diffusion Transformers (DiT) achieve excellent sample quality, shifting the bottleneck to the throughput of the models themselves. Natural images are inherently sparse, as large portions of an image are often background, contribute little to the scene content, and are easy to denoise. DiTs fail to exploit this sparsity, as they process image tokens statically and uniformly. We propose MoDDiT, a simple architecture modification that learns to route tokens through both MLP and self-attention operations. By routing tokens through both blocks independently, MoDDiT allows for dynamic compute allocation in MLPs that varies across tokens, images, and denoising timesteps. Using MoDDiT to train image generation models from scratch significantly reduces computational costs of training and inference, processing as few as 12.5% of the tokens. By increasing sparsity and model depth, MoDDiT reduces costs and improves generation performance over unrouted baselines. The learned allocation is interpretable, revealing how computation varies with visual content and noise level. We also use MoDDiT to train video generation models, where allocation correlates with motion, and to distill a dense bidirectional video model into a sparse autoregressive student.

title: LaLa-World: Scaling Latent World Models with Natural Language Actions
abstract: This paper shows that JEPA-style latent world models (LWMs) can learn across diverse domains and data sources by adopting the language-conditioned interface of video generation models. We establish this approach as an effective and efficient basis for planning with imagination and downstream policy fine-tuning. To this end, we introduce LaLa-World, a Language-conditioned Latent World model that learns from simulation and robot trajectories together with broader image and video data. Two designs make this work. First, we describe both numerical actions and visual changes in language, enabling joint training of a single future predictor across heterogeneous datasets. Second, we build the predictor on a language model, allowing it to interpret language conditions while predicting future latent states. The resulting predictor achieves higher average MPC planning performance than existing LWMs trained separately for each domain or task. Adding image and video data further improves average planning performance and robustness to action phrasing. In a matched comparison with an RAEv2-based video generation model baseline, LaLa-World reaches comparable planning performance with $6\times$ less training cost and $13.9\times$ faster planning. Beyond planning, the pretrained LaLa-World serves as an initialization for LaLa-Policy, which jointly predicts actions and future visual representations. LaLa-Policy performs competitively with Cosmos Policy on LIBERO and RoboCasa, with up to $5.5\times$ faster inference.

title: Knowing When to Stop Thinking: A Dissection of Expected Free Energy as a Test-Time Compute Controller for Latent World-Model Planning
abstract: A planner using a learned world model can improve its predicted outcome while choosing a worse action. We study when expected free energy (EFE) can help decide how much computation to spend on a plan. An EFE-inspired objective combines goal distance with disagreement among stochastic predictions. We test candidate scoring, stopping, and online predictor updates separately. Stopping when elite cost stalls reduces refinement on tasks whose success plateaus with depth, with mean success close to fixed-depth references. At the larger tested weights, rewarding disagreement lowers success with a frozen model. Penalizing it helps at some task and weight settings but harms others. When training data omit a region needed to reach the goal, online updates recover part of the resulting loss. The tested cost-stall rule can fail when further optimization exploits model errors, because predicted cost keeps falling after task success peaks. Cost progress can guide computation on a plateau, but protecting performance after a peak requires information about the consequences of the chosen actions.

title: GALA: Geometry-Aware Language Model for Controllable Object Arrangement
abstract: Reasoning about fine-grained placement constraints, such as support and containment, is essential for realistic 3D scene creation. It remains a significant challenge for existing methods that rely on simplified object representations like oriented bounding box (OBB), which are blind to the detailed geometry. To address this limitation, we introduce GALA, a geometry-aware language model with explicit point cloud perception for controllable object placement. Our model performs autoregressively by predicting the 6D pose of one target object at a time conditioned on the scene context and placement instruction. We utilize a two-stage training strategy: the first stage aligns geometric and textual modalities through pretraining tasks, and the second stage fine-tunes the model for placement. To facilitate this task, we also curate a multi-source scene dataset covering diverse room types and fine-grained furniture arrangements, which will be open-sourced for community benefit. Experiments on our benchmark show our model significantly outperforms baselines without explicit geometric reasoning. We further develop a multi-stage plan-place-verify agent pipeline that uses the model for text-driven scene generation. Project Page: https://xccelephant.github.io/paper/gala/
