title: From Generation to Precision: A Systematic Review of Controllable Multimodal Diffusion
abstract: Abstract: Controllable diffusion seeks to make generated content satisfy structural, semantic, and identity constraints, rather than merely maximize visual quality. This systematic literature review maps controllable multimodal diffusion research to clarify mechanisms, application profiles, and remaining limitations. Following PRISMA 2020, we searched IEEE Xplore and ScienceDirect with a documented Boolean string for English peer-reviewed primary studies published from 2023 to 2025. DOI- and title-based deduplication, title/abstract screening, and full-text eligibility assessment reduced 219 retrieved records to 24 studies. We extracted the task/domain, base model, conditioning modalities, control mechanism, training regime, and evaluation measures, and classified each study into Attention Control, Modular Adapters, Loss Engineering, or Agentic Planning. Inference-time attention steering mainly addresses adaptable, per-prompt spatial or semantic conditions; adapted methods more often target persistent identity and domain constraints; and agentic planning supports multi-entity or relational prompts. The evidence is dominated by static-image tasks, with one video study and no audio or spectral studies. Heterogeneous metrics constrain cross-study comparison. We therefore identify standardized cross-family evaluation, temporal and cross-modal consistency, and application-specific reliability as priorities.

title: FIT-MAC: A Closed-Loop Multi-Agent Framework for Robust Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance on standard robotic manipulation benchmarks. However, their reliability can degrade substantially when task conditions deviate from the nominal setting. Perturbations in object positions and task instructions may lead to complete task failure. Existing VLA policies generally lack an explicit runtime mechanism for distinguishing these failure modes and selecting an appropriate recovery strategy. To systematically mitigate this issue, we propose FIT-MAC, a failure-aware, closed-loop multi-agent control framework for improving the robustness of VLA policies at inference time. FIT-MAC augments a VLA policy with an inference-time control layer. First, the Planner Agent parses the language instruction into a structured task specification that captures the manipulation goal and spatial constraints, and the Grounder Agent resolves each instruction-level reference to a visual target. Next, the Verifier Agent tracks phase-specific execution progress, distinguishes target-binding errors from local execution failures, and determines whether intervention is warranted. The Correction Agent then routes permitted interventions to target rebinding or bounded grasping or placement recovery, depending on the failure type. When no intervention is required, the pretrained VLA remains the default action generator. Extensive experiments on LIBERO-PRO demonstrate that FIT-MAC improves robustness across multiple VLA backbones, consistently increasing success rates and achieving state-of-the-art performance under diverse perturbations.

title: Exploring Temporal Context-Aware Physical Grounding in Latent World Models
abstract: Learning latent dynamics is fundamental to building action-conditioned world models for planning. Among existing families, Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) offer a natural framework by modeling transitions directly in latent space rather than at the pixel level. However, two issues remain in JEPA-based world models: (i) physical grounding lacks explicit aggregation of temporal context and (ii) action planning always overly relies on generic sampling distributions. To this end, we propose $\mathcal{G}$-JEPA, which incorporates temporal context into physical grounding for latent world models and couples the learned models with prior-guided action planning. Specifically, during learning, we incorporate a shared causal temporal module that aggregates temporal context within observation and prediction sequences under physical state supervision, grounding both in task-relevant physical states. When planning, we further introduce action inference through stepwise conditioning of a generative action distribution on the current and goal latent representations together with their evolving discrepancy, yielding anchored proposals that guide model-based online refinement. Together, physical state supervision guides temporal representation learning, while the action prior guides search through the learned world model. Experiments demonstrate improved planning performance on manipulation tasks, including tasks with increasing temporal separation between initial and goal observations. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/myl11045/G-JEPA.

title: Empowerment of Islamic Religious Education Teachers through Generative AI Training for the Development of Islamic Value-Based Learning Media at SMP Negeri 35 Medan
abstract: The development of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, particularly Generative AI, has created new opportunities for developing innovative, interactive, and contextual learning media. However, many Islamic Religious Education (IRE) teachers still have limited competencies in utilizing this technology as a learning medium while maintaining Islamic values. This Community Service Program (PKM) aimed to improve the competence of IRE teachers at SMP Negeri 35 Medan in utilizing Generative AI to develop creative, effective, and Islamic value-based learning media. The program employed a Participatory Action Learning approach consisting of needs identification, educational sessions, practical training, mentoring, and evaluation. The training involved demonstrations and hands-on practice using various Generative AI platforms, including ChatGPT, Canva AI, Gamma AI, and Microsoft Copilot, to develop teaching materials, presentations, assessment questions, and visual learning media based on Islamic values. The results indicated an improvement in participants' understanding of Generative AI, enhanced skills in developing digital learning media, and increased awareness of the ethical use of AI from an Islamic perspective. The teachers were able to produce learning media that were more engaging, interactive, contextual, and supportive of the implementation of the Merdeka Curriculum. This program contributed positively to improving teachers' digital literacy while strengthening the integration of technology and Islamic values in the IRE learning process.

title: Deep Operator Learning for Interface Evolution and Uncertainty Quantification in Complex Multiphase Flow
abstract: Predicting moving interfaces in multiphase flow remains computationally demanding because topological changes, high curvature, and thin ligaments require fine spatial and temporal resolution. This study develops a Fourier-DeepONet surrogate that maps initial phase geometry, nondimensional flow parameters, and space-time coordinates to future volume-fraction fields while producing calibrated uncertainty. High-fidelity trajectories are generated with the adaptive volume-of-fluid solver in Basilisk for Rayleigh-Taylor instability and droplet deformation. The architecture combines convolutional branch encoding, Fourier coordinate features, global spectral mixing, physics-aware constraints, and a Normal-Inverse-Gamma evidential head. On the held-out benchmark, the model reaches an interface Dice score of 0.954 ± 0.006, an intersection-over-union score of 0.913 ± 0.009, and a volume-fraction MAE of 0.0187 ± 0.0014. Relative mass error remains 0.73 ± 0.12% over 50 frames, while uncertainty-error correlation reaches 0.812 ± 0.021 after calibration. Under unseen parameter combinations, Dice decreases by only 0.026 ± 0.007. These results support physics-constrained operator learning as a fast and reliability-aware approach to multiphase interface prediction.

title: Consistency of Variational Inference for Nonlinear Inverse Problems of Partial Differential Equations
abstract: Abstract. We investigate the convergence rates of variational posterior distributions for statistical inverse problems involving nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs). Departing from exact Bayesian inference, variational inference transforms the inference problem into an optimization problem by introducing variational sets. Based on a modified “prior mass and testing” framework, we propose general conditions for three categories of inverse problems: mildly ill-posed, severely ill-posed, and those with unknown model parameters. Concentrating on the variational sets comprising the restricted Gaussian or widely utilized Gaussian mean-field families, we demonstrate that for all three categories, the convergence rate can be decomposed into a true distribution term and a variational approximation term. Moreover, we illustrate that the true distribution term dominates the convergence rates, thereby substantiating the effectiveness of the variational inference method for inverse problems of PDEs. As specific examples, we examine a collection of nonlinear inverse problems, including the Darcy flow problem, the inverse potential problem for a subdiffusion equation, and the inverse medium scattering problem. In addition, we show that our convergence rates are minimax optimal for these inverse problems.

title: A unified drift-adaptive and robust residual autoencoder with attention and few-shot learning for zero-day intrusion detection
abstract: Abstract Autoencoder-based unsupervised intrusion detection systems (IDS) offer a promising approach for identifying zero-day attacks without requiring labeled malicious data. However, residual autoencoder (RAE) frameworks remain limited by static decision thresholds, susceptibility to concept drift (CD), limited adversarial robustness, and restricted adaptability to emerging attack patterns. To address these limitations, we propose the Attention-Boosted Streaming Residual Autoencoder (ASRAE), a unified framework that integrates attention-enhanced representation learning, online CD detection with adaptive thresholding, benign-only adversarial training, post-identification few-shot meta-learning, and explainability through integrated gradients (IG). Experiments on UNSW-NB15, CIC-IDS2017, and CSE-CIC-IDS2018 show that ASRAE outperforms the evaluated unsupervised baselines, achieving ROC-AUC values of 0.952, 0.940, and 0.931, respectively. Under the controlled simulated concept-drift setting, ASRAE maintains a ROC-AUC above 0.91, while adversarial evaluation using Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) and Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) demonstrates improved robustness to feature-space perturbations. The few-shot adaptation stage further enables adaptation to held-out attack families using only a small number of labeled samples while largely preserving benign reconstruction performance. ASRAE requires an average inference time of 9.2 ms per sample in the evaluated experimental environment. Overall, the results demonstrate the effectiveness of ASRAE across the benchmark, simulated-drift, adversarial, and few-shot adaptation settings.

title: Vision transformer supported dangerous posture recognition model for high work
abstract: In the high operation scene, the posture of personnel changes rapidly, and the environment such as scaffolding, adjacent platforms and ladders are easily affected by occlusion, perspective deviation and background interference. Traditional manual inspection is difficult to capture risk actions such as body forward leaning, center of gravity deviation and climbing imbalance in time. To improve the real-time performance and stability of dangerous posture recognition at construction sites, a vision Transformer supported dangerous posture recognition model for high work was constructed. The model takes video frames as input, completes the location of operator region, Patch segmentation and pose region Token generation, and fuses the skeleton key point heat map, two-dimensional position coding, center of gravity offset and joint Angle features. In the multi-head self-attention layer, the correlation weights between the torso, arms, legs and the support area are calculated, and then the dangerous posture probability is output through the Transformer classification layer. In the test phase, 126 videos of four types of high working scenes were collected, and 18640 valid image frames were screened, and the data set was divided into 7∶2∶1. The results show that the recognition accuracy of all kinds of dangerous postures is higher than 93.7%, and the false detection rate is controlled within 6.3%. The inference delay of 1080P video stream on the edge side is 32.5 ms, the frame rate is 30.8 FPS, the average delay of the scene early warning is 196.8 ms, and the success rate of early warning is 97.9%. The model can provide technical support for intelligent monitoring of height operations and active early warning of fall risk.

title: Vector-Quantized World Model: Latent Feedback Motion Planning for Robot Manipulation
abstract: Visual world models have shown strong potential for robot planning, yet long-horizon manipulation remains challenging due to compounding prediction errors, large search complexity, and latent plans that the low-level controller cannot reliably reach. In this work, we introduce Vector-Quantized World Model (VQ-WM), a latent feedback motion planning framework that integrates discrete long-horizon search with continuous visual feedback control: a discrete latent predictor models transitions between vector-quantized latent states, allowing the planner to look far ahead and find a shortest path to the goal through discrete search and a continuous learned controller sequentially reaches the planned states through visual feedback, correcting deviations to mitigate compounding errors. Whereas most vector quantization uses Euclidean distance, we use a novel estimator of the first-passage-time as a quasi-metric, which aligns the planning abstraction with the controller's capabilities. We evaluate on the physical robot manipulation of the Tower of Hanoi puzzle: whereas existing state-of-the-art foundation models (VLAs, WAMs) only succeed when the solution trace in their training dataset, our method achieves 100\% success rate with only short-play data, demonstrate its ability to compose long-horizon solutions beyond the short demonstrated trajectories and execute them reliably. Our solution also outperforms strongest world-models by 13.3--85.3 percentage points on simulation benchmarks spanning manipulation and locomotion, demonstrating consistent progress and new capabilities.

title: Train An Imaginative Agent
abstract: A seemingly reasonable push in Sokoban can make the puzzle unsolvable. To avoid such mistakes, an agent has to anticipate the consequences of its actions before execution, especially when feedback from the real environment is sparse or actions are irreversible. We introduce Agentic Imagination (Agima), a training framework that trains an agent to imagine before acting, i.e. to be imaginative. Agima trains a single omni model to propose actions, generate images of their outcomes, and then reason over these imagined futures to decide what to execute in the real environment. Rather than committing to a single plan, the agent can simulate a sequence of actions, explore alternatives, and compare possible futures. We first use supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to unify policy and world modeling within a single omni model. This enables the agent to predict future outcomes and perform basic forms of imagination, such as forward thinking and counterfactual branching. We then use agentic reinforcement learning (RL) to teach the agent to reason with its imagined futures and use them effectively for planning. Across four environments spanning Maze2D, Sokoban, Pacman, and PushT, Agima generalizes to harder settings unseen during training. Trained with SFT alone on two-box Sokoban, Agima solves 40% of four-box puzzles while seeing the real board only once every five moves, compared with an action-only planner that only solves 2%. After RL, new behaviors emerge in how Agima uses its imagination: it learns a new unified format that was unseen during the SFT stage, learns to conduct forward thinking only when necessary, and branches more frequently at critical decision points. An agent that can picture where its actions lead can learn when and where to look ahead, that is, to plan. Project page: https://agima.net/.

title: Toward Online Robust Zero-Sum Markov Games with Function Approximation
abstract: Online robust zero-sum Markov games pose a coupled operator-learning and game-solving problem: from nominal interaction data, the learner must recover a worst-case minimax Bellman operator while maintaining strategic coverage and controlling stage-game approximation error. Existing robust reinforcement-learning theory does not yet provide such an operator-learning perspective beyond specialized multi-agent settings. We develop an optimistic dual robust Bellman framework that combines dual robust Bellman fitting, optimistic minimax planning, backward-validated confidence sets, and exploiter-mix data collection. Our analysis is organized around the robust Bellman residuals induced by the candidate value class and yields a regret reduction that separates exploration complexity, robust operator-estimation error, stage-game solution error, and misspecification. Under explicit interpretable assumptions, we obtain conditional theorem interfaces for general and projected function approximation, together with closed results in several structured regimes, including tabular, epochwise cross-fit linear, self-normalized pure-online linear / finite-rank kernel, and projected RKHS truncation. Small-scale numerical experiments illustrate robustness calibration, strategic coverage, and the return-gap trade-off predicted by the framework.

title: Think Densely, Act Sparsely: Latent Expert Cognitive Chains for Vision-Language-Action Autonomous Driving
abstract: Autonomous driving fundamentally demands dense understanding of visual, semantic, and geometric information, yet existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically trained with sparse supervision such as language instructions or trajectory signals. This direct mapping from dense visual observations to sparse representations forces the model to compress or even discard critical scene information essential for safe driving. We argue that this limitation does not stem from insufficient model capacity, but from the lack of explicit mechanisms that encourage the formation of dense world representations in the latent space. In this spirit, we propose a novel paradigm for driving intelligence, Think Densely, Act Sparsely, and instantiate it with an efficient and interpretable framework, LECDrive (Latent Expert Cognitive Chains for Vision-Language-Action autonomous Driving). The core idea is to mimic the hierarchical perception process of humans by embedding a progressive chain of latent expert cognition within the VLA model. Concretely, we inject a compact set of task-specific latent tokens as carriers, enabling the model to internalize dense knowledge from foundational vision models, including visual representations (DINOv3), semantic structures (SAM3), and spatial geometry (DepthAnything3), while maintaining efficient inference. This interdependent cognitive chain follows a curriculum learning principle, where supervision is progressively structured from representation to semantics and geometry. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LECDrive consistently improves the performance of base VLMs across multiple autonomous driving benchmarks, covering key tasks such as object perception, state prediction, and trajectory planning. These findings suggest that constructing dense world models through structured latent expert chains is a promising direction for VLA-based autonomous driving.

title: Solving Multi-Objective Flexible Job Shop Scheduling Problem to Achieve Sustainable Manufacturing
abstract: Due to global challenges and disruptions—such as increasing energy costs and limited availability of resources and workforce—multi-objective production planning and scheduling has recently attracted significant attention from both academia and industry. Solving scheduling problems based on multiple objectives, rather than focusing solely on makespan reduction, has become one of the key challenges in sustainable manufacturing. The job shop scheduling problem is a well-known optimization problem belonging to the class of NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems. In addition to the inherent complexity of scheduling itself, the difficulty is further increased by the various criteria (objectives) that must be considered, such as electrical energy consumption, machine workload, and tardiness. Consequently, job shop scheduling becomes a multi-objective optimization problem. This paper presents the MOFJSP-HUMANT algorithm for solving the multi-objective flexible job shop scheduling problem (MOFJSP). The proposed algorithm is based on the ant colony optimization metaheuristic and the PROMETHEE multi-criteria decision-making method, resulting in an “a priori” approach to multi-objective optimization. As mentioned, the proposed methodology and algorithm enable a search for the best compromise production schedule based on three criteria—makespan time, electrical energy consumption, and machine workload—to support sustainable manufacturing. The algorithm has been tested on a MOFJSP instance, and the results are discussed to evaluate the proposed MOFJSP-HUMANT framework before its application in more complex industrial environments.

title: Simulation Priors for Rapid Adaptation in Model-Based RL for Autonomous Racing
abstract: Reinforcement learning enables learning high-performance control policies, but its reliance on extensive interaction limits deployment on physical systems where data collection is costly, and failures are unsafe. We introduce Prior-Informed Adaptation (PIA), an offline-to-online model-based RL framework that uses structured simulation priors for rapid adaptation. PIA pretrains a world model on heterogeneous low- and high-fidelity simulated trajectories, then adapts it with limited target-domain interaction using uncertainty-regularized planning. Rather than requiring an accurate simulator for policy transfer, PIA treats simulated trajectories as biased priors whose residual mismatch is corrected during online adaptation. We evaluate PIA in autonomous racing using high-fidelity simulation and on a real full-size autonomous race car. In simulation, PIA adapts faster across track and surface shifts than strong baselines, achieving lower lap times and fewer failures. On hardware, PIA achieves reliable few-shot adaptation with less than one hour of on-vehicle interaction.

title: Ropedia W0: Scaling Loco-Manipulation World Models across Embodiments with Human Experience
abstract: World models enable embodied agents to anticipate action consequences, yet jointly modeling locomotion and manipulation across diverse embodiments remains challenging due to heterogeneous action spaces and limited multimodal supervision. We present Ropedia W0, the first egocentric loco-manipulation world foundation model spanning humans and robots with diverse embodiments. We curate Xp-Data, comprising 10k hours of egocentric human data and 3k hours of robot data with unified multimodal annotations and systematic quality control. A unified kinematic representation encodes locomotion through camera poses and manipulation through projected skeletons, with robot skeletons combining embodiment-specific forward kinematics with extensive manual keypoint annotation and correction. We also introduce Xp-Teleop, a long-horizon loco-manipulation benchmark based on high-quality dexterous humanoid teleoperation data. Evaluations demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across five cross-embodiment benchmarks (DreamDojo, $Ψ_0$, $ω$-HOME, Xp-Teleop, and AgiBot) and on held-out human egocentric video, from zero-shot inference to few-shot and full-data post-training. Scaling human pre-training data improves performance on both human and robot evaluations. After distillation, our model supports real-time, minute-long rollouts, enabling live VR interaction. Applications in policy evaluation, model-based planning, and world-action modeling further demonstrate the model's utility for embodied decision-making.

title: Robotic Photography System based on Vision-Language-Action Model
abstract: Modern robotic photography requires understanding photographic intent, planning camera motions, and producing aesthetically pleasing images in complex environments. We present RoboPhoto-VLA, a unified Vision-Language-Action framework that jointly models perception, reasoning, and camera control for autonomous robotic photography. RoboPhoto-VLA incorporates PhotoCoT for structured action planning and Aesthetic Direct Preference Optimization (ADPO) to align camera behaviors with human aesthetic preferences. To facilitate training and evaluation, we construct OpenPhotography, a robotic photography dataset with language-guided demonstrations. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that RoboPhoto-VLA produces photographs better aligned with human aesthetic preferences while generalizing effectively to unseen subjects, viewpoints, poses, and complex photographic instructions.

title: Robot Learning with Vision-Language-Action Models for Agricultural Manipulation
abstract: Robotic manipulation in agricultural environments remains challenging due to variations in plant geometry, occlusion, and camera viewpoints. Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) and generalist robot policies offer a promising approach to addressing these challenges by learning manipulation behaviors from multimodal observations and language instructions. However, adapting these policies to agricultural tasks requires domain-specific demonstrations, which are costly and time-consuming to collect on physical robots. In this work, we develop a simulation-to-real robot-learning framework for agricultural reaching and grasping that integrates task-specific demonstration collection and pretrained policy adaptation. A MuJoCo-based agricultural environment is developed with diverse tomato plant structures to support demonstration collection and controlled evaluation. Expert demonstrations are collected through joystick teleoperation, with a low-level controller used to execute robot actions. Two pretrained generalist robot policies, Octo and $π_{0.5}$, are adapted using simulated demonstrations, followed by further fine-tuning on a physical Franka Research 3 manipulator using real-robot demonstrations. The adapted policies are evaluated under in-distribution, viewpoint/spatial-shift, and out-of-distribution conditions in simulation, followed by physical-robot experiments. The influence of proprioceptive information on policy performance is also investigated. Results show that $π_{0.5}$ achieves higher task-performance scores than Octo and exhibits less degradation under distribution shifts. These findings demonstrate the potential of integrating pretrained generalist policies with task-specific demonstration learning for agricultural manipulation.

title: Physical AI: Concepts, Techniques, and Challenges
abstract: In recent years, physical artificial intelligence (physical AI) has experienced rapid development, capturing significant attention in academia and industry. However, the field has yet to reach consensus on its definition, technical landscape, and core challenges. To address this gap, this monograph seeks to define physical AI, present its technical landscape, and examine each key technical subfield in depth. In doing so, it establishes a unified framework for Physical AI: artificial systems that perceive, model, and act upon the physical world through continuous feedback under real-world constraints. Further, this monograph distinguishes physical AI from conventional digital AI, embodied AI, cyber-physical systems, and digital twins. It develops the foundations of physical AI across physics, control, cognition, learning, and reasoning. It reviews key methodologies, including multimodal perception, physical data and simulation, world models, embodied foundation models, motor-control systems, multi-agent coordination, and hardware-software co-design. Furthermore, it examines applications spanning robotics, manufacturing, infrastructure, scientific experimentation, and autonomous services. Particular attention is given to sim-to-real transfer, reliability, real-time execution, evaluation, safety, governance, and long-term deployment. By connecting perception, prediction, decision-making, action, and adaptation in a closed loop, this monograph identifies the technical challenges and research directions required to advance from narrow automation toward more generalizable physical AI and, ultimately, physical artificial general intelligence (Physical AGI).

title: PaceVLA: Adaptive Temporal Action Quantization in Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Fast and reliable manipulation is crucial for practical robot deployment. Although Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently shown remarkable progress as generalist robot policies, their execution often remains temporally inefficient. A key source of this inefficiency is that policies learn fine-grained temporal patterns from teleoperated demonstrations, requiring many low-level action steps. Temporal action quantization offers a simple way to accelerate execution by aggregating consecutive low-level actions into temporally coarser actions. However, applying action quantization without considering when fine-grained control is required introduces a speed-accuracy trade-off: accelerated actions may efficiently reduce redundant steps in some phases, while discarding critical motion details in precision-sensitive interactions. To address this, we propose PaceVLA, a unified framework for adaptive temporal execution in VLAs that integrates two coupled components: (1) mode-specific action decoders built on a shared action expert, supporting multiple temporal granularities and prediction horizons, and (2) a quantizability-guided mode selection scheme which decides whether coarse execution is appropriate, and a context-conditioned router that selects an execution mode at each inference step. Experiments across three multi-task simulation benchmarks and six real-world tasks show that PaceVLA improves execution efficiency while maintaining task success rate across multiple embodiments, including long-horizon and dexterous manipulation.

title: PACT: Plan-Augmented Coordination via Trace-Graphs for Dynamic Multi-Agent Combinatorial Optimization
abstract: Multi-agent approaches have been investigated recently as a means of improving the scalability of reinforcement learning for neural combinatorial optimization. Existing methods assume that all problem instance information is known upfront. However, real-world problems are often dynamic: relevant information is progressively revealed as the agents take actions (e.g., arriving at an edge in a routing problem only to discover it is untraversable). In such cases, existing methods fail to coordinate agents to explore and exploit the progressively revealed information. To address the arising coordination challenge, we introduce PACT (Plan-Augmented Coordination via Trace-graphs). PACT augments the environment graph with auxiliary nodes representing the plans of agents, which are connected to the resource nodes to indicate future dependencies. The proposed message-passing scheme over the augmented graph grounds inter-agent coordination in the environment and enables proactive, rather than reactive, conflict resolution. We show that PACT improves solution quality in dynamic problems relative to baselines and exhibits the best transfer to larger instances on which, remarkably, it outperforms centralized oracles with privileged access to instance uncertainty.

title: Imaging-derived coronary fractional flow reserve: advances in physics-based, machine learning, and physics-informed methods
abstract: Purpose of Review: Imaging-derived fractional flow reserve (FFR) is rapidly evolving beyond conventional computational fluid dynamics (CFD)-based pipelines toward machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and physics-informed approaches that enable fast, wire-free, and scalable functional assessment of coronary artery stenosis. This review synthesizes recent advances in computed tomography (CT)- and angiography-based FFR measurement, with particular emphasis on emerging physics-informed neural networks and neural operators (PINNs and PINOs), as well as key considerations for their clinical translation. Recent Findings: ML/DL approaches have markedly improved automation and computational speed, enabling prediction of pressure and FFR from anatomical descriptors or angiographic contrast dynamics. However, their real-world performance and generalizability can remain variable and sensitive to domain shift, due to multi-center heterogeneity, interpretability challenges, and differences in acquisition protocols and image quality. Physics-informed learning introduces conservation structure and boundary-condition consistency into model training, improving generalizability and reducing dependence on dense supervision while maintaining rapid inference. Recent evaluation trends increasingly highlight deployment-oriented metrics, including calibration, uncertainty quantification, and quality-control gatekeeping, as essential for safe clinical use. Summary: The field is converging toward imaging-derived FFR methods that are faster, more automated, and more reliable. While ML/DL offers substantial efficiency gains, physics-informed frameworks such as PINNs and PINOs may provide a more robust balance between speed and physical consistency. Prospective multi-center validation and standardized evaluation will be critical to support broad and safe clinical adoption.

title: From Notebook to Control Room: Reproducible MLOps for Accelerator Digital Twins
abstract: Scientific user facilities like the Linac Coherent Light Source (LCLS), the world’s brightest X-ray free-electron laser at the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, require rapid, continuous control adjustments to maximize beam time and experimental throughput. Machine Learning (ML) surrogate models can help operators navigate complex parameter spaces, but only if those models can be deployed reliably and updated without disrupting operations. How do you reliably and sustainably move ML models from various researchers’ training environments into a facility production system? In this talk, we present a reproducible MLOps framework that addresses this challenge in the context of digital twin deployments for online accelerator control. We discuss how we standardized the Kubernetes-based deployment of digital twins and ML inference services by prioritizing reproducibility across environments through container-based packaging, rigorous model versioning and experiment tracking integrated into the deployment pipeline, minimal boilerplate templates so domain scientists can onboard models without DevOps expertise, and flexible configuration to adapt across diverse control scenarios. The framework is built around a software ecosystem that provides abstraction layers to wrap simulator-specific backends (PyTorch-based neural network surrogates and physics simulations) behind a common Python API. This design means the deployment infrastructure generalizes across model types rather than being tied to any single simulation code or modeling approach. The same model instance can be used directly in Python-native workflows for development and testing, or deployed as a process variable server integrated with existing control system infrastructure, without changes to the underlying model code. This approach demonstrates how such software infrastructure can lower the barrier to AI integration in research facilities, allowing scientists to focus on model development while RSEs maintain the reliability, observability, and sustainability of the deployment stack. We discuss lessons learned, remaining challenges around hybrid ML-simulation system models, and paths toward tooling that is shareable across facilities.

title: EmbodiedWorld-200K: Toward Embodied World Agents via Embodied-Planning Dataset and Interactive World Models
abstract: Building embodied agents that can perceive, reason, and act across diverse 3D worlds is a central research direction toward artificial general intelligence. Yet most existing work remains confined to specific tasks in a single scene and transfers poorly to new environments, leaving general embodied agents for open-world settings under-explored. We refer to such agents as Embodied World Agents (EWAs), whose defining property is the ability to understand diverse visual environments and execute general actions in open-world conditions. To advance EWA research, we study open-world embodied navigation-planning and release EmbodiedWorld-200K, a large-scale dataset of over 200K samples spanning diverse scenes. Each example is equipped with multi-level annotations, ranging from low-level camera-motion trajectories to high-level semantic instructions. The dataset also provides unified evaluation splits and task-specific metrics, supporting offline pretraining and fair evaluation of EWAs. Beyond offline supervision, a defining characteristic of an EWA is its interaction with the environment; training solely on offline data is therefore insufficient, especially for generalizing to scenes not covered in the training distribution. Building dedicated real interactive environments, however, is often prohibitively expensive. To address this, we propose a novel training scheme that employs a video world model as a low-cost environment proxy and performs interactive reinforcement-learning (RL) post-training of the EWA within it. Empirically, pretraining on EmbodiedWorld-200K substantially improves the open-world embodied planning ability of the EWA, and further RL post-training inside a world model yields clear gains on out-of-distribution scenes. The dataset, baseline checkpoints, and training and evaluation code are available at https://xiaokunfeng.github.io/EmbodiedWorld-200K/.

title: CoRS: Fast Neural Flexible Job-Shop Scheduling via Composite Interval State Reuse
abstract: Neural solvers for the Flexible Job-Shop Scheduling Problem (FJSP) typically refresh graph representations and update feasibility after every operation--machine decision. However, only feasibility must remain exact at every step, whereas graph encoding is substantially more expensive and can potentially be refreshed less frequently. We present CoRS, which decouples them: an interval-level graph representation is reused across multiple sequential decisions, while a stepwise feasibility state is updated after every action. This two-timescale design amortizes graph encoding without parallelizing action generation or relaxing scheduling constraints. CoRS further develops a feasibility-preserving composite-interval decoding scheme with dynamic constraint tracking and boundary state synchronization, which reduces representation refresh frequency while maintaining continuous feasible schedule construction. Furthermore, to alleviate representation staleness caused by interval-level state reuse, CoRS introduces enhanced static features as a compensation mechanism. By providing more comprehensive structural information of the scheduling problem, these features improve the model's perception of overall problem characteristics. Extensive experiments on synthetic and multiple public FJSP benchmarks demonstrate that CoRS significantly reduces inference time while maintaining competitive solution quality, achieving favorable speed-quality trade-offs under tight wall-clock budgets and low-latency scenarios.

title: Chronos-QRL: Outperforming Google OR-Tools, Attention Model, and POMO on the International Dynamic VRPTW Benchmark via 28-Qubit Floquet-MBL Superposition in 4GB VRAM
abstract: The Dynamic Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows (Dynamic VRPTW) constitutes the most demanding international standard for evaluating autonomous dispatch algorithms for massive fleets under combinatorial uncertainty O(2^N). Classical local search metaheuristics (Google OR-Tools GLS and HGS-VRP) suffer an exponential growth in computation time when re-optimizing routes live, while state-of-the-art autoregressive deep models (Attention Model – AM, ICLR 2019; and POMO, NeurIPS 2020) are confined to the TC0 circuit class, collapsing under correlated congestion cascades of order k ≥ 6. In this work, we present Chronos-QRL, a Quantum Reinforcement Learning agent that maps the topological and temporal state of the Solomon RC101 graph (100 clients + central depot, Q = 200, Tmax = 240) onto an N = 28 qubit Floquet-MBL Time Crystal (268,435,456 states in 3.221 GB of VRAM) coupled with a Quantum Natural Policy Gradient optimizer (Fubini-Study Metric QNPG + SPSA) with zero Backpropagation. Audited over 16,000 dynamic epochs at a speed of 5,940,668 decisions/second (2.693 ms on a 4GB VRAM RTX 3050 Ti GPU), Chronos-QRL unsupervisedly discovers the critical 6-node subgraph, raises the bottleneck detection ROC-AUC from 0.5121 (AM/POMO collapse) to 0.9985 (+48.64 pts), and reduces the dynamic optimality gap relative to the Best Known Solutions (BKS) from +39.41% (Solomon I1), +23.01% (OR-Tools), and +20.55% (POMO) down to just +0.83% (95.6% BKS hit rate).

title: CIS-Transolver: A Cross-Layer Incremental-State Neural Operator for Fine-Scale Automotive Aerodynamic Flow Prediction
abstract: Neural operators offer an efficient data-driven approach to rapid prediction of complex automotive aerodynamic flows. However, spectral bias and other factors limit accurate reconstruction of fine-scale flow variations near complex geometries. Existing studies improve the representation and fitting of fine-scale information mainly through information extraction and training objectives. Further study is needed to determine how extracted local details can be used continually in subsequent operator computations and contribute effectively to the overall flow-field representation. We propose CIS-Transolver, a cross-layer incremental-state neural operator that extends fine-scale modeling from local information extraction to its use across layers. The method extracts fine-scale information through local multiscale analysis and encodes it as geometric moment states that are propagated and updated across layers. By combining information from previous layers with feedback to the value representations in Physics-Attention, the method allows local details to contribute continually to subsequent modeling of global physical correlations. We systematically evaluate CIS-Transolver on three public automotive aerodynamics benchmarks, ShapeNet-Car, AhmedML, and DrivAerNet++, covering surface pressure fields and volumetric pressure and velocity fields. CIS-Transolver achieves the lowest mean relative L2 error among the evaluated methods for all five prediction metrics across the three benchmarks. The relative error reductions average 8.72% across the five metrics compared with the best baseline for each metric, reaching 16.38% for ShapeNet-Car pressure prediction and 15.60% for AhmedML velocity prediction. These results provide a new approach to fine-scale flow prediction for complex geometries.

title: Artificial intelligence for ophthalmic vessel segmentation: from multimodal imaging to clinical translation
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based vessel segmentation converts color fundus photographs, scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (SLO), optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA), structural OCT, and anterior-segment images into quantitative vascular biomarkers. Strong performance within individual datasets has not consistently yielded reliable clinical measurements because errors can arise during acquisition, anatomical preprocessing, vessel extraction, biomarker calculation, and deployment. This structured narrative review compares segmentation tasks involving retinal vascular trees, OCTA capillary plexuses, the structural choroid and choriocapillaris, macular neovascularization, corneal neovascularization, and conjunctival microvasculature. We assess modern architectures in relation to vessel geometry, severe foreground-background imbalance, scale variation, crossings, and susceptibility to artifacts. The methods considered include multiscale feature pyramids, deformable and directional operators, Transformers, state-space models, diffusion approaches, and foundation models. We organize the synthesis around five evaluation levels: pixel overlap, centerline recovery, vascular topology, biomarker agreement, and clinical actionability. Public fundus and OCTA datasets are catalogued with their acquisition and annotation characteristics, and gaps in public anterior-segment vessel benchmarks are discussed. Because devices, data splits, labels, and post-processing differ substantially, reported metrics are summarized without ranking studies against one another. The review distinguishes structural OCT choroidal vascularity index from OCTA choriocapillaris flow-deficit mapping, as well as true vessel segmentation from global hyperemia grading. Clinical translation will require ocular-magnification correction, quality control of retinal layers and projection artifacts, external testing across devices and populations, out-of-distribution rejection, DICOM/PACS interoperability, prospective impact studies, and regulation as software as a medical device. We conclude that clinical utility depends on an auditable pipeline that measures structural error, biomarker uncertainty, and failure states throughout the workflow.

title: AnyGoal: On World Model Generalization Beyond Expert Rollouts
abstract: The goal of a world model is to capture the dynamics of an environment. This has the great appeal that it allows agents to plan and simulate a course of actions with the help of a world model. For these uses to be reliable, however, the learned dynamics must behave well beyond the specific state-action combinations observed in expert rollouts. Despite this, the relationship between data coverage, dynamics generalization, and downstream planning performance remains underexplored. We study this relationship through the lens of compositional generalization: can a world model recombine familiar state and action factors into valid dynamics? To answer this, we introduce AnyGoal, a benchmark of goal-shifted task variants built from widely used world-model environments, together with an open-source library. Each task is designed to be within reach of a world model that has learned the underlying dynamics: individual state factors and actions remain within their training support, but their combinations are underrepresented in expert trajectories. Across multiple environments and world model families, we find that current models consistently exhibit failures under these recombinations. By examining dynamics and representation failures across model families, interaction regimes, and evaluation metrics, we study where current world models generalize and where challenges remain for goal-shifted prediction and planning. Together, this framework, benchmark, and analysis provide a basis for evaluating progress toward world models that generalize to new planning tasks.

title: Agentic AI Incident Response Platform for Cloud Applications: Telemetry-Grounded Root-Cause Investigation with Human Approval
abstract: Diagnosing production incidents is still largely manual: on-call engineers gather logs, errors and deployment history from separate tools before they can reason about a cause. Large language models (LLMs) can suggest root causes, but a model that sees only an incident summary lacks evidence, and an unchecked suggestion can mislead. This paper aims to give an LLM agent the evidence it needs while keeping a human in control. We present Phase 1 of an open, four-module platform: a non-blocking Java SDK that captures exceptions, latency and deployments; a multi-tenant Spring Boot backend that groups repeated errors into incidents by stack hash; a FastAPI service in which a tool-calling LLM investigates each incident only through audited APIs; and a dashboard where an operator approves or rejects every suggestion. We evaluate it by injecting seven kinds of real faults into an instrumented service. All 21 trials were detected, with mean detection times of 8–12 s for exception faults and 25–45 s for resource faults, and no incident was raised in 8 min of fault-free operation. The SDK added a median of 14 µs per captured error and stayed non-blocking when the backend was down. A successful investigation used about 11k–24k tokens and two to three minutes; of five graded suggestions, two were correct, two partly correct and one wrong despite a confidence of 0.78. The results show that telemetry-grounded investigation is practical for small teams, and that self-reported confidence must not replace human review.

title: Agent World Model in the Wild: Computer-Use Agent Environment Synthesis
abstract: Agent learning is shifting from learning from human data toward learning through interaction with the world. However, scaling such learning directly in real-world computer systems is challenging and can introduce substantial security risks. We therefore propose Agent World Model in the Wild (WildAWM), a scalable pipeline for synthesizing controllable environments and tasks for training general computer-use agents (CUAs). Whereas existing approaches typically specialize in a single agent interaction interface, we construct executable environments that jointly support graphical user interfaces, model context protocol services, and command-line interfaces, allowing agents to flexibly combine visual interaction, tool use, and code execution. WildAWM is entirely powered by open-source models, demonstrating that high-quality computer-use environments can be generated without proprietary frontier models. Beyond environments, we address three recurring challenges in task synthesis: ensuring solvability, maintaining sufficient difficulty, and producing reliable verifiers, by introducing execution-based quality gates that combine heterogeneous agent rollouts, cross-judge consistency checks, and counterfactual probes of judgment robustness. The resulting pipeline synthesizes 341 long-horizon environment-task pairs that can require over 100 agent steps to solve and remain challenging even for frontier models, with GPT-6-Astra solving only 60% of them. We train two Qwen models of different sizes exclusively in these synthetic worlds. Both models achieve substantial gains across 8 out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents, demonstrating that learning in WildAWM's synthesized worlds generalizes broadly to unseen computer-use tasks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/MSR-Orchard/WildAWM.

title: ActTime: Action-Conditioned World Modeling for Time Series
abstract: Time-series models increasingly condition on known future inputs. In controlled systems, some of these inputs are actions that can be changed, compared, and optimized before execution. A model must therefore do more than predict the realized future: it must predict how outcomes change under different actions from the same observed history and support reliable comparison of candidate plans. We introduce ActTime, an action-conditioned world model for time series. Over the observed history, ActTime updates variable-specific latent states through an action-conditioned transition and corrects them using observations. It then rolls the same transition forward under candidate actions to generate future trajectories. Training uses only factual trajectories, without paired alternative-action outcomes or planning supervision. We construct a simulator-grounded evaluation suite across building energy, traffic, greenhouse climate, and inventory management, covering factual prediction, intervention-effect prediction, offline decision making, and closed-loop planning. ActTime ranks first in 12 of 16 domain-task settings. Across eight methods, the mean pairwise model-ranking reversal rate is 17.8% between factual prediction and intervention fidelity, and rises to 28.4% between intervention fidelity and decision ranking. These results show that factual accuracy, intervention fidelity, and decision quality are related but not interchangeable.

title: A Probabilistic, Rotation-Preserving Kernel Operator Surrogate for Continuum-Robot Design Spaces
abstract: We develop an uncertainty-aware, operator-learning-based surrogate for tendon-driven continuum robots (TDCRs) that generalizes across robot design and actuation while predicting the complete equilibrium configuration. Our central idea is a nonstationary Gaussian-process (GP) kernel whose metric is learned by a shallow neural network from mechanics-aware design coordinates. The network learns how similarity changes across design space, while the resulting kernel defines the design-to-pose operator, its posterior uncertainty, and a criterion for sequential simulator acquisition. We represent backbone position and rotational strain with spatial kernels and reconstruct orientation directly on SO(3), preserving valid material frames and tendon geometry. We use ASkotch with Nystrom preconditioning for scalable kernel operator solves and a separate Nystrom approximation for posterior covariance. Experiments show that kernel-coverage acquisition reduces mean trajectory error by approximately 15% relative to IID sampling, while posterior variance increases for increasingly unsupported designs. Compared with prior neural-operator TDCR models, the method is 30-50% more accurate using approximately 5x fewer training designs while additionally providing posterior uncertainty estimates.

title: ZAC-Memory: Collective Provisioning of Memory and World Models for Embodied Intelligence
abstract: Embodied intelligent systems commonly maintain local representations of their environments, including maps, object states, task histories, spatial relationships, and previously acquired experience. Although local memory supports rapid access and autonomous operation, independently maintaining comprehensive environmental knowledge across every agent can introduce redundant storage, repeated observations, duplicated updates, and inconsistent representations. Distributed robotics and cloud-based knowledge management already address parts of these problems, but the provisioning question remains important: which information must each agent maintain locally, and which information can be supplied by a collective memory system without compromising task performance? This paper proposes ZAC-Memory, a research framework for collective provisioning of memory and world-model capabilities within the broader Zero-Agent-Compute (ZAC) framework. The central principle is that an embodied agent need not independently maintain every environmental record, knowledge item, or historical representation required by its tasks. Instead, memory requirements can be distributed across local agents, shared repositories, and cooperating providers according to task criticality, access frequency, information freshness, communication conditions, storage capacity, and reliability requirements. The framework introduces dynamic memory provisioning, evidence-aware conflict resolution, temporal validity management, dependency-aware memory placement, and disconnection-aware autonomous operation. It further distinguishes raw observations, episodic records, semantic knowledge, spatial representations, and predictive world models, recognizing that these memory types have different sharing and consistency requirements. A joint optimization formulation is proposed to minimize storage, communication, synchronization, reconstruction, and failure-related costs while satisfying task-level constraints. A corresponding operational algorithm determines which memory items should remain local, be shared, be replicated selectively, or be reconstructed when necessary. The paper also develops testable hypotheses and a reproducible evaluation methodology using multi-robot environments, dynamic object states, network interruptions, and heterogeneous memory capacities. ZAC-Memory is presented as a conceptual research framework rather than an experimentally validated system. Its contribution must be established through systematic comparison with distributed mapping, cloud robotics, shared knowledge bases, and existing memory-management approaches.

title: When Do Latent World Models Detect Game Glitches? Representation Collapse, Pretrained Video Latents, and an Action-Conditioned Benchmark
abstract: Latent world models trained only on normal gameplay are an appealing, label-free source of "surprise" for glitch detection. This article extends our conference diagnostic study, which found that a LeWorldModel-style JEPA trained from scratch on TempGlitch collapses to effective rank ≈ 1 and reaches AUROC 0.579–0.588, clearly below a kNN detector on frozen VideoMAE features (0.6895). We add three pieces of evidence. (i) Frozen V-JEPA 2 latents. A kNN detector on frozen V-JEPA 2 features reaches 0.6592, and a normal-only next-latent predictor on its 0.4 s temporal tokens reaches 0.665–0.669, a statistical tie with, but not above, VideoMAE kNN; a causal transformer predictor on the same tokens is worse (0.598–0.599). (ii) Collapse remedies. In a pre-specified six-arm sweep (SIGReg weight, batch size, VICReg terms, longer training; one seed), the LeWM encoder's effective rank rises from 1.13 to 21.3, but AUROC does not follow: the best arm (batch 32) reaches 0.6264 (+0.0427 over the reproduced anchor, p = 0.00076), whereas the least-collapsed arm reaches 0.5954 (arm-level Spearman ρ = 0.37, n = 6). (iii) An action-conditioned benchmark. We build ACGB, five headless games with recorded per-frame actions, eight programmatic glitch types at three severities, and a counterfactual clean twin per glitched episode. On its development split, action conditioning does not help the JEPA (macro AUROC 0.605 with actions vs. 0.625 without) but does help a small pixel predictor (0.888 vs. 0.783), notably on input-remapping glitches; locked-test results are pending. (iv) A surprise-driven explorer. On 400 held-out bugged levels with state-triggered hidden bugs, an agent maximising world-model surprise finds fewer bugs than random actions (found fraction 0.258 vs. 0.322) and raises about fifteen times more false alarms on clean levels. Across all experiments, non-collapse is necessary but not sufficient: the temporal content of the latent space matters more than its rank.

title: Unsteady Carreau fluid flow in three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamics with a viscous dissipation effect
abstract: A numerical investigation has been conducted on the 3D magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) flow of an incompressible Carreau fluid over a stretchable surface. Mathematical modeling is performed to represent the laws of conservation of mass, momentum, and heat transfer. An appropriate transformation transforms the governing partial differential equations (PDE) into the dimensionless ordinary differential equations (ODEs). To solve ODEs, we used the shooting technique with fourth order Adams-Moulton method implemented in a Fortran programming language. The validity of the computed results is established by benchmarking them against previously published findings in the literature. Key parameters influencing the flow are illustrated and discussed through graphical representations. The overall results indicate that the velocity profile diminishes with increasing magnetic parameter, while it increases in response to higher values of the Hall parameter and Weissenberg number. The fluid flow model examined in this study finds applications in nuclear reactor cooling systems, polymer extrusion processes, electromagnetic pumping, astrophysical plasma flows, and magnetohydrodynamic generators. Engineering and industrial quantities of interest, such as local skin friction and heat transfer rates, have been calculated and thoroughly discussed.

title: Self-Supervised In-Context Operator Learning for Optimal Mixing in Incompressible Flows
abstract: We develop a self-supervised operator-learning framework for optimal mixing in incompressible flows, aimed at overcoming the computational limitations of classical PDE-constrained optimal control. The objective is to design velocity fields that efficiently homogenize a passive scalar while minimizing kinetic energy, quantified through the $\dot H^{-1}(Ω)$ mix-norm. Classical methods solve a separate optimal control problem for each initial condition using iterative forward-adjoint procedures, leading to substantial computational costs and limited scalability. In contrast, we propose to learn the solution operator that maps initial scalar fields to optimal mixing controls directly. The proposed self-supervised method does not require access to supervised labels, thereby significantly reducing the data-generation burden of supervised operator-learning methods. Our framework integrates a Lagrangian reformulation of the transport equation with a transformer-based neural operator architecture. The transport dynamics are represented through characteristic ODEs, enabling particle-based Monte Carlo optimization, while the learned velocity field is parameterized in a divergence-free spectral basis enforcing incompressibility and no-penetration conditions exactly. Numerical experiments on parametric families of initial conditions in two and three spatial dimensions demonstrate robust generalization to unseen regimes and approximately exponential decay of the mix-norm. The learned controls also transfer consistently to independent Eulerian finite-volume simulations, validating the physical fidelity of the learned operator. To the best of our knowledge, this work provides the first self-supervised operator-learning framework for optimal mixing and among the first data-driven approaches for optimal mixing in fully three-dimensional incompressible flows.

title: Securing LLM-Agent Long-Term Memory Against Poisoning: Non-Malleable, Origin-Bound Authority with Machine-Checked Guarantees
abstract: An agent based on a large language model (LLM) may store an untrusted document and use it weeks later to select a payment destination. Preventing this action requires evidence of authorization that remains valid when stored text changes. We study a policy that requires either endorsements (explicit approvals) from two separately administered sources or explicit user authorization. In an abstract memory model, we prove the policy is preserved under permitted transformations for stores of any size, assuming correct source and authority binding, protected records, and checks on every consequential action. We evaluate the executable monitor, which checks calls before execution, separately from the proof. In 1,152 controlled tool-use episodes, GPT-4o-mini executes attacker-selected actions in 61 of 72 undefended episodes and none of the 72 monitored episodes. Clean-task completion remains 24 of 24 when both endorsers are available. A separate 1,728-episode experiment tests recovery after denial. Returning to signed records instead of rereading a contaminated note raises attacked-task completion from 14/72 to 72/72 for GPT-4o-mini and from 22/72 to 43/72 for Gemini 2.5 Flash, without executing an attacker-selected action. Neither model completes transactions with fewer than two sources. Whole-action tests reject unauthorized combinations of individually approved fields. Extraction probes identify mistaken approvals, and fault analysis shows how shared failures can negate a second domain's benefit. Calibrations using original defense implementations reveal security and task-completion tradeoffs under different policies. These results support conditional enforcement and recovery in constructed workflows, but do not establish that endorsements will be available or correct in deployment.

title: Research on global automotive industry data intelligent fusion system based on stacking double-layer ensemble algorithm
abstract: A multi-source data intelligent fusion system based on the Stacking double-layer ensemble algorithm is proposed to address core issues such as data heterogeneity and inconsistent data quality, real-time performance issues and privacy security conflicts in cross-border data transmission of global automotive industry data. The system adopts a full-process technical framework: data quality control - data fusion - ensemble learning - federated learning. First, data cleaning, filling, deduplication and data standardization are completed through the data quality layer; Then, by using an adaptive feature set weighted fusion strategy, the data sets are fused through attention mechanism learning; Finally, base learners and meta-learners are integrated based on the Stacking two-layer ensemble algorithm. This paper also introduces federated learning techniques throughout the text for privacy-preserving distributed collaborative computing using privacy-enhancing technologies to ensure the security of model interaction. The architecture of this paper enables efficient, secure and real-time integration of global automotive industry data, providing intelligent data support for automakers and promoting digital collaboration in the global automotive industry.

title: Online Learning-Based Adaptive Hybrid Benders Decomposition for Risk-Averse Optimal Sizing
abstract: Optimal sizing problem (OSP) under uncertainty is often formulated as two-stage stochastic programming (2SP). However, this formulation typically introduces significant computational and RAM (memory) bottlenecks as the scenario size grows. Benders Decomposition (BD) is a popular approach to tackle this problem, but it suffers from slow convergence to the exact solution. To address this problem, we propose an accelerated online learning-based adaptive hybrid BD algorithm. The proposed method avoids getting stuck in the infeasible region during early iterations by explicitly embedding a carefully selected scenario in the master problem, while online learning based on logistic regression (LR) leverages a light machine learning (ML) algorithm to avoid solving the entire scenario set at every iteration. The OSP is formulated to select a behindthe-meter battery energy storage system in a multi-site energy community with existing renewables. The use case explores an interesting middle-ground between deterministic methods and training-heavy ML models, showcasing the potential of MLassisted decision-making. Numerical results on scenario sets of up to 500 illustrate the effectiveness and scalability of the proposed approach. © IEEE. Accepted manuscript. Personal use of this material is permitted. title: Neptune: An AI model for Global Ocean Subseasonal Prediction
abstract: Neptune: A Data-Driven Framework for Subseasonal-to-Seasonal Global Ocean and Sea-Ice Emulation Initial codebase and model checkpoints for the Neptune project, an end-to-end data-driven framework for subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) global ocean and sea-ice prediction (up to 60 days). Key Features & Components: - Architecture: Combines Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Spherical Fourier Neural Operators (SFNOs) conditioned on daily atmospheric forcing.- Training & Inference Pipeline: Full PyTorch/Lightning training suite, distributed execution scripts, and ensemble forecasting utilities (`src/training.py`, `src/inference.py`).- Data Processing: Pipeline for downloading, converting, merging, and normalizing ERA5 atmospheric and CMEMS ocean data (`src/gathering/`, `src/processing/`).- Evaluation & Benchmarking: Validation metrics (RMSE, ACC, CRPS), physical coherency checks (OHC, EKE, IBS), and ocean index diagnostics (`validation/`).- Models & Datasets: Includes model definitions, configuration files (`src/config/`), and pre-trained checkpoints (`data/models/`).

title: Learning Skill Representations from Recruitment Data for Skill Gap Analysis and Career Path Optimization
abstract: To address the mismatch between educational provision and labor-market demand affecting the employment of arts graduates, this paper proposes a skill-gap analysis framework integrating recruitment-text mining, semantic representation learning, and knowledge graphs. First, a corpus of job advertisements is compiled from online recruitment data, and a Transformer-based model is used to encode job descriptions semantically, enabling the extraction of skill entities and the development of context-sensitive representations. Second, semantic skill embeddings, hierarchical clustering, and BERTopic-based topic modeling are combined to construct a skill-classification system for arts-related positions, with the aim of identifying core skill groups and emerging competency requirements in the employment market. Furthermore, the proposed framework maps job positions, skill requirements, and students’ existing abilities into a shared semantic space and uses knowledge graphs to characterize structural relationships among jobs, skills, and competencies. On this basis, distributions representing market demand and educational skill supply are constructed and compared to quantify gaps affecting arts graduates. The reported experimental findings suggest that requirements for arts-related positions increasingly combine conventional professional expertise with digital technology, AI-assisted creative practices, data literacy, and transferable professional competencies. The results also identify apparent shortcomings in university preparation concerning computing skills, problem-solving, project implementation, and adaptability across disciplinary boundaries. Together, these analyses offer a structured basis for interpreting skill mismatches and informing curriculum development, individualized upskilling, and career planning.

title: Dynamics-Aligned Representation Learning under Induced Partial Observability
abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) has enabled sample-efficient learning of continuous control policies from high-dimensional observations through learned latent dynamics models. These models are typically trained with observation reconstruction objectives, which provide strong supervision but can bias representations toward visual fidelity leading to an undertrained prior and unreliable long-horizon predictions. We propose a stochastic gating mechanism that induces controlled partial observability during training by sampling a spatial binary mask from a Beta--Bernoulli random field and applying it to the raw observation. The gate probability is resampled at each time step, exposing the encoder to conditions ranging from near-total occlusion to near-full visibility. Integration of our method requires minimal architectural changes from existing dynamics models: the gated observation and the binary mask are channel-wise concatenated and passed to the encoder as a single augmented input, with no modifications to the broader training pipeline. We evaluate the proposed approach on a set of pixel-based continuous control tasks selected from the DeepMind Control Suite. Using model predictive control for evaluation, which relies solely on open-loop model rollouts, we show that stochastic gating improves planning performance and data efficiency across tasks. Further analysis demonstrates that performance is robust to the spatial scale of the mask, and a balanced observability during training outperforms configurations biased toward either sparser or denser observations.

title: Buongiorno Model of Magnetohydrodynamic Nanofluid Flow Over a Heated Stretching Sheet
abstract: Nanofluids are important working fluids for electronic cooling in industrial, engineering, and biomedical applications. Although MHD nanofluid flow over stretching sheets has been widely studied, the combined effects of viscous dissipation, thermophoresis, Brownian motion, and a magnetic field under the Buongiorno model remain insufficiently explored. This study numerically investigates these effects, along with Joule heating and convective surface heating, on flow over a heated stretching sheet subject to a perpendicular magnetic field. Similarity transformations were used to reduce the governing partial differential equations of continuity, momentum, energy, and concentration to nonlinear first-order ordinary differential equations. The resulting boundary value problem was solved using the shooting technique with the Runge-Kutta method in the MATLAB ode45 function. Results show that the magnetic field increases the temperature through Joule heating and diminishes the convective flow through the Lorentz force. Brownian motion and thermophoretic parameters elevate the nanoparticle distribution and increase the fluid temperature. The Eckert number intensifies viscous heating, while the Prandtl number restricts thermal diffusion. The Schmidt number decreases species concentration, while the Joule heating parameter enhances the temperature near the surface. The skin-friction increases with the magnetic parameter while the Sherwood number decreases; a higher Prandtl number enhances heat transfer but reduces mass transfer, and the Nusselt number increases with the Biot number. These findings indicate that magnetic field strength and convective surface heating can be regulated to control wall shear stress and heat and mass transfer rates in plastic extrusion, metallurgy, and electronic cooling.

title: BiDex-100: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation Across 100+ Simulation Tasks
abstract: Bimanual manipulation with dexterous hands has attracted growing attention in research on robotic action models. However, few studies have developed benchmarks specifically tailored for dexterous manipulation, leaving the dexterous manipulation capabilities of existing models insufficiently characterized. In this paper, we present BiDex-100, a simulation benchmark for bimanual dexterous manipulation that combines broad task coverage, multi-dimensional evaluation, and high-DoF hand embodiments. Concretely, the benchmark comprises 106 tasks organized along five capability axes: generalization, instruction following, limited demonstrations, long horizon, and memory. Each task is paired with an out-of-domain variant featuring controlled visual and spatial changes, allowing systematic assessment of robustness. In addition, the benchmark supports two embodiments and provides 8,080 success-validated teleoperated demonstrations, totaling 6.25 million frames. We evaluate seven recent Vision-Language-Action models under a unified protocol, establishing baselines for capability-specific performance, robustness, and data efficiency. The website is available at https://BiDex-100.github.io/BiDex-100/.

title: APPLICATION OF GRAPH THEORY IN OPTIMIZING TRANSPORTATION AND COMMUNICATION NETWORKS IN DRUG DELIVERY
abstract: There are several issues that need to be addressed when involving the distribution of medicine to ensure that the medicine is distributed within the maximum allowable service window.This includes the capacity of the vehicle(s) used for the distribution, the storage conditions needed for the medicine, traffic levels and the security and traceability needs.This mini project aims to investigate this combined transportation and communications network reporting the location, the temperature and delivery using graph theory.The use of multilayer is used for vertices (warehouses, depots, and care sites) as transport vertices, and for road segments as labeled, weighted edges as well as for sensor vertices and communicative vertices (sensors), and data links as reliable-weighted edges.There is a correlation of Interlayer links between each shipment and location to the monitoring endpoint.The proposed scheme is a mixture of shortest paths, capacitated vehicle routing and time windows, k shortest-backup paths and min-cut analysis and prioritisation based by centrality.The edge weights are composed of distances, travel time and costs, disruption risk, emissions and temp exposure.If there is a change in a material's nature in the demand, status of roads, sensor reading, or if there is a change in the availability of roads, then the optimisation workflow gets adapted on the fly.The impact of the framework is shown with a synthetic prototype along with labelled and illustrated results that are juxtaposed against a dispatch recoverable from the graph in relation to Standard dispatch.The project does not aim to replace good distribution practice or product labelling but it does provide a good and traceable decision-making tool which can be used by qualified individuals to plan and monitor drug delivery or re-route it as appropriate.

title: AI-Based Adaptive Traffic Signal Control Using Fuzzy Logic for an Urban Intersection with Pedestrian, Weather, and Emergency Vehicle Awareness
abstract: Urban traffic signal control requires efficient operation of vehicles along with pedestrian safety, weather conditions and emergency pre-emption of vehiclesall factors that fixed-time traffic controllers cannot consider.This paper provides the description and implementation of an AI-based adaptive traffic signal control using four-input Mamdani Fuzzy Inference System (FIS) for a single urban four-way intersection.It includes such traffic input parameters as Vehicle Demand Index (VDI), Pedestrian Density (PD), Pedestrian Crossing Requirement Index (PCRI) and Weather Severity Index (WSI) to calculate adaptive vehicle green time and pedestrian crossing time.There is Supervisory Emergency Pre-emption Module which guarantees priority green corridors of vehicles and pedestrian conflict-zone clearance.The controller was implemented in Python language and integrated with the SUMO model via TraCI library along with a computer vision perception module based on YOLOv8.The controller was compared to Fixed-Time, Webster and VDI-only fuzzy traffic controllers according to seven traffic scenarios and five random seeds (total number of simulations equals to 140).As a result, the proposed controller reached an average waiting time of 45.81 s, throughput of 903.62 veh/h, CO₂ emissions of 197.95 g/vehicle, and Pedestrian Timely Crossing Rate (PTCR) of 97.86%.In comparison with Fixed-Time control the waiting time was reduced by 19.3% and emissions were reduced by 8.1% (p < 0.0001).Although the vehicle-only fuzzy controller demonstrated slightly better results regarding vehicle efficiency, the PTCR was only equal to 87.10%, which confirms that the proposed system works as multiobjective controller.
