title: Same Target, Different Origins: Aligning Latent Rollout for Consistent PDE Emulation
abstract: Neural PDE solvers commonly generate multi-step predictions through autoregressive rollout, recursively applying a learned evolution operator and feeding each prediction back as input for the next step. Approximation errors can therefore propagate through the rollout, causing predictions at a shared target time to depend on their temporal origins and rollout depths. For a well-posed deterministic PDE flow, however, states at different times along the same physical trajectory should, under exact evolution, reach the same target state. To this end, we propose Align Latent Rollout (ALR), a regularization approach that promotes consistency across rollout origins through the neural PDE solver's internal representations. A second-order Taylor analysis of latent discrepancy propagation motivates two objectives: zeroth-order latent state consistency, which aligns representations at a shared target time, and first-order latent dynamics consistency, which aligns local evolution responses to shared perturbations. ALR can be integrated into different neural PDE solvers by regularizing suitable internal representations, without modifying their backbone architectures. Experiments across multiple PDE benchmarks and neural-operator backbones show that ALR improves prediction accuracy while reducing shared-target discrepancies across rollout origins.

title: Quantum-Inspired Reconfigurable Computing for Accelerated Matrix Computations in High-Performance Embedded Systems
abstract: The emergence of data-hungry systems in the form of artificial intelligence, real-time signal processing, and scientific computing systems inside embedded systems has set extremely high requirements to the computational capabilities, electrical energy efficiency and flexibility. The computational backbone of many of these applications is matrix computations, that typically face bottlenecks in traditional processor architectures because of individual resources having no parallelism, and a lack of dynamism in resource allocation. In order to overcome such limitations, this paper introduces a new reconfigurable computing implementation, called Quantum-Inspired Matrix Engine (QIME) that emulates all three of these important quantum computing concepts of superposition, parallelism, and entanglement in a classical hardware setting. The system of the proposal will be applied to the Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs), and here, the system will be used to incorporate a pseudo-quantum state encoding process that enables the representation and processing of multiple matrix states simultaneously. QIME also has dynamic partial reconfiguration (DPR) so as to further have flexibility and efficiency in matching the architecture in real time with the nature and the complexity of the operations performed in the matrix. Also, there is approximate computing, where computational precision is traded off against performance where the tradeoff is allowed to increase energy profiles under workload variability. Experimental analysis of some typical benchmarks on matrices, including multiplication, decomposition, and convolution, shows that for representative operations QIME provides up to 6.3x speedup and 4.1x energy efficiency improvements over typical matrix co-processors and embedded GPUs. These findings will support the viability of quantum-inspired design paradigms in moving forward the performance and scalability of high-performance embedded systems, especially in the edge, and constrained circumstances where conventional quantum hardware is infeasible.

title: Plans Are Not Executions: Adapting Frozen World-Model Planners to Controller-Induced Execution Shift
abstract: World-model planners evaluate candidate trajectories by predicting their future consequences, implicitly relying on the plan-to-motion relationship learned during training. At deployment, a different downstream controller may execute the same planned trajectory differently, creating a planning-execution gap between the frozen model's imagined future and actual execution. A natural remedy is to replace the planned trajectory with its predicted or observed execution. However, we find that better execution fidelity does not necessarily yield better decisions: directly substituting predicted execution trajectories yields only a 0.048 PDMS improvement across 10 unseen controller configurations, far smaller than the gain from our proposed adaptation. This suggests a semantic mismatch between a planned trajectory, which serves as a reference for downstream control, and an executed trajectory, which already describes the resulting post-controller motion. We introduce ExecutionBridge, which infers controller-specific execution characteristics from planned-executed trajectory pairs and uses them to adapt the native ego latent rollout while keeping the original planned trajectory unchanged. The planner, world model, and reward head remain frozen. On NAVSIM, ExecutionBridge consistently improves planning across unseen controller configurations and multiple frozen world-model planners, with substantially larger gains in challenging driving scenes where execution mismatch more strongly affects candidate evaluation.

title: MAIA: Anticipating Interaction Anomalies in Contact-Rich Manipulation via Multimodal World Models
abstract: Reliable contact-rich manipulation requires detecting execution deviations early enough for corrective action. Yet most monitoring methods are reactive, identifying anomalies only after they become observable. Anticipating such anomalies is challenging because visual observations only partially reveal physical interaction, while planned actions describe intended motion rather than their actual physical consequences. We address this problem with MAIA, a multimodal framework for anomaly anticipation. Its vision-action-force world model learns nominal interaction dynamics and predicts the visual and force responses of planned actions, while a lightweight anomaly head predicts impending interaction anomalies. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce CRIA, a real-world multimodal dataset of 2,852 trajectories spanning 18 contact-rich manipulation tasks, with frame-level annotations of anomaly onset and evolution. Experiments on both seen and novel tasks show that MAIA achieves more accurate anomaly discrimination than representative baselines while providing earlier warnings, with bACC scores of 0.765 and 0.710 and median anticipation lead times of 28.0 and 25.1 steps, respectively. Moreover, using these predictions for anomaly-aware action selection improves end-to-end task success from 52.6% to 61.5% without retraining the underlying manipulation policy. These results highlight the value of modeling future physical consequences for proactive anomaly anticipation.

title: Learning and Forecasting Multiscale Spatiotemporal Epidemic Dynamics with Lagrangian-Eulerian Graph Neural ODEs
abstract: Accurate medium- to long-range epidemic forecasting requires extrapolating high-dimensional, heterogeneous and nonstationary dynamics from partial observations. Yet hybrid models often leave implicit which observations inform which epidemic processes and how learned graph interactions modify system state. We introduce LE-EpiGNODE, which replaces generic message passing with process-specific, mechanism-guided neural operators: age-contact information drives Lagrangian infection generation, whereas mobility drives conservative Eulerian population transport within a structure-preserving universal differential equation. We evaluated LE-EpiGNODE across 14 controlled synthetic mechanisms spanning time-modulated, state-dependent, nonlinear and coupled dynamics, three complementary COVID-19 settings, 21 comparator models and five targeted ablations. Forecasting gains tended to become more pronounced at longer horizons; at the longest horizon, LE-EpiGNODE achieved the lowest WMAPE in all three real-world datasets, reducing error by 17.7-40.0% relative to the best baseline. Controlled ablations linked these gains to the Lagrangian-Eulerian decomposition and process-aligned priors, while synthetic ground truth showed that learned operators and induced state fluxes track known generating dynamics. These results support mechanism-organized graph neural dynamics as a route to reliable long-horizon extrapolation with directly testable, process-level mechanistic interpretation beyond trajectory accuracy.

title: Learning Intrinsic Dynamics in Latent World Models
abstract: Learning intrinsic dynamics---the relationship between actions and their consequences---is essential for world models. However, visual variations unrelated to the underlying control process can obscure this relationship in learned representations. We investigate the connection between action predictability, defined as the ability to reconstruct an action from consecutive latent states, and the preservation of intrinsic dynamics. Our central hypothesis is that encouraging action predictability discourages representations from discarding the distinctions between different actions and their consequences. We provide two complementary forms of evidence for this connection. Theoretically, we derive a positive lower bound on squared inverse prediction error when the encoder merges distinguishable outcomes of different actions from the same state and appearance, and show that forward prediction can still be exact on those transitions. Empirically, controlled appearance-diversity comparisons, supervision interventions, and latent probes support the role of action prediction in preserving control-relevant transition information. We instantiate action predictability with Concat IDM, which predicts actions from concatenated latent states and updates the shared encoder using action labels already available in offline trajectories, without changing the test-time planner. Across three independent training runs on Push-T with 24 appearances, Concat IDM increases planning success from 9.1% to 77.2%; its paired improvement is 52.9 percentage points larger than that observed with a single appearance. Together, these findings support action predictability as an inductive bias toward intrinsic dynamics and demonstrate the practical benefits of Concat IDM for latent planning under visual diversity.

title: LTM: Latent Transition Based In-Context Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering interactions that are no longer visible. We introduce Latent Transition Memory (LTM), which stores history as compact latent transitions between consecutive observations. Instantiated on $π_{0.5}$ as LTM-$π$, our method uses a frozen latent action encoder, a lightweight adapter, and causal KV caching for incremental inference without memory-specific semantic annotations or external reasoning-model calls. With DreamDojo transitions, LTM-$π$ achieves 58.54% success on RoboMME and 80.5% on LIBERO-Mem, performing best among baselines without external reasoning models or memory-specific annotations. Ablations support the contribution of transition content beyond temporal cues and the efficiency of delayed memory admission. Scaling RoboMME demonstrations tenfold improves success from 57.67% to 87.50%, while a Cup Swap diagnostic highlights the role of process supervision in temporal composition. Under a 200-token memory budget, success remains 84.00%, versus 87.50% without compression. Finally, real-robot counting success improves from 11.25% to 82.50%. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness, scalability, and efficiency of latent transition memory, highlighting its capacity for complex temporal information, bounded-context operation, and real-world robotic control.

title: Interpolation of unitaries with time-dependent Hamiltonians via Deep Learning
abstract: Abstract Quantum systems governed by time-dependent Hamiltonians pose significant challenges for the accurate computation of unitary time-evolution operators, which are essential for predicting quantum state dynamics. In this work, we introduce a physics-informed deep learning approach based on Physics-Informed Neural Networks to estimate these operators over the full time domain. By incorporating physical constraints such as unitarity and leveraging the second-order Magnus expansion or Trotterization on the evolution operator, the proposed framework enables the estimation of unitary matrices at different time intervals. The model is trained using simulated unitary operators and evaluated on quantum systems ranging from 2 to 6 qubits, governed by a fully non-zero Pauli Hamiltonian. For larger many-body systems, specifically those with 7 and 8 qubits, the same methodology is employed to reconstruct an effective time-dependent Hamiltonian, restricted to nearest-neighbor Ising and XYZ Heisenberg models, from which the corresponding time-evolution operator is computed over the entire temporal domain. Across all system sizes, the framework achieves high gate fidelities using a limited number of unitary samples, with a statistical analysis over independent Hamiltonian realizations confirming mean fidelities close to 0.99 and low variability. Furthermore, once trained, the model interpolates the evolution operator with inference times substantially lower than those of a numerical interpolation baseline, indicating a potential reduction in measurement and data acquisition costs. These results highlight the effectiveness of the approach for data-driven simulation and identification of quantum dynamical systems, with direct relevance to quantum computing and quantum simulation applications.

title: Higher order approximation of nonlinear SPDEs with additive space-time white noise
abstract: We consider strong approximations of 1+1-dimensional stochastic PDEs driven by additive space-time white noise. It has long been proposed (Math. Comp. 70 (2001) 121–134; Proc. R. Soc. Lond. Ser. A Math. Phys. Eng. Sci. 465 (2009) 649–667), as well as observed in simulations, that approximation schemes based on samples from the stochastic convolution, rather than from increments of the underlying Wiener processes, should achieve significantly higher convergence rates with respect to the temporal timestep. The present paper proves this. For a large class of nonlinearities, with possibly superlinear growth, a temporal rate of (almost) 1 is proven, a major improvement on the rate 1/4 that is known to be optimal for schemes based on Wiener increments. The spatial rate remains (almost) 1/2, as it is standard in the literature.

title: Graph neural networks for transmission grid topology control: Busbar information asymmetry and heterogeneous representations
abstract: Factors such as the proliferation of renewable energy and electrification contribute to grid congestion which is a pressing problem. Topology control is an appealing method for relieving congestion, but traditional approaches for topology discovery have proven too slow for practical applications. Recent research has focused on machine learning (ML) as an efficient alternative. Due to their ability to model the graph structure of power grids, graph neural networks (GNNs) are particularly well-suited for topology control applications. This study investigates different graph representations of the power grid for topology control with GNNs. We identify an information flow problem inherent to the popular homogeneous graph representation and propose a heterogeneous graph representation that resolves said problem. We apply GNNs with both graph representations and a fully connected neural network (FCNN) baseline to an imitation learning task. The models are evaluated by classification accuracy and the percentage of successful grid operation days. We find that heterogeneous GNNs perform the best, followed by FCNNs, and lastly, homogeneous GNNs. We also find that both GNN types generalize better to unseen network configurations than FCNNs.

title: GeoState: Learning View-Decoupled Geometry States for 3D World Modeling
abstract: Recent 3D world models increasingly use features from geometry foundation models (GFMs) as predictive world states, benefiting from their rich geometric priors. However, the view dependence of these features entangles scene dynamics with camera-induced variation, making the resulting state evolution harder to predict. We propose GeoState, a view-decoupled geometry representation for predictive 3D world modeling that separates scene-state evolution from camera-dependent observation. Specifically, a scene tokenizer aggregates multi-view GFM features into a view-decoupled scene state, which a geometry decoder queries using camera rays. An autoregressive world model then predicts future scene states, while camera motion is modeled separately. The predicted states can therefore be decoded under either predicted or externally specified cameras, while retaining a single context-derived scale throughout the rollout without per-frame scale alignment. Experiments show that GeoState outperforms prior 3D world models on Waymo, supports geometrically consistent cross-view querying, and generalizes zero-shot to KITTI and nuScenes. title: From Optical Flow to Safety: Visual Safety Certification via Scale-Free Relative Motion
abstract: Safe autonomous navigation using monocular vision remains challenging because explicit obstacle states are not directly observable. This letter introduces a visual safety-certification paradigm that uses scale-free, depth-normalized relative motion encoded by monocular optical flow as the representation for collision-risk certification, without reconstructing obstacle position, velocity, geometry, or a metric world model. Unlike conventional optical-flow-based navigation approaches that rely on image motion to shape avoidance behavior, the proposed framework directly encodes collision-cone geometry and safety constraints in this relative-motion representation. An online Concurrent Learning observer estimates the normalized relative velocity and provides a computable estimation-error bound. This uncertainty is propagated into the collision cone through angular inflation and a monocular robot-footprint margin, yielding a Robust Vision-Based Collision Cone Control Barrier Function (RV-C$^3$BF). An optimal-decay CBF quadratic program minimally modifies the nominal control input to enforce the resulting robust safety constraint under the stated assumptions. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments on a TurtleBot3 in cluttered environments with static and dynamic obstacles demonstrate collision avoidance using only monocular vision and onboard proprioception, with the estimation-error bound containing the measured error in $98.3\%$ of simulation samples and the robot achieving collision-free navigation in $93$ of $100$ real-world trials.

title: FastVLA: Task-Conditioned and Temporally Adaptive Visual Token Compression for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models present a promising paradigm for general-purpose robot manipulation, but closed-loop deployment is often limited by inference efficiency: at each timestep, high-resolution, often multi-view images are encoded into hundreds of visual tokens that dominate transformer computation and latency. Token compression via attention is a natural solution but is challenging for VLA control because (1) decision-critical tokens are determined by the task, not generic visual saliency, and (2) the token budget varies substantially across steps, so static metrics and budgets waste computation or discard control-critical tokens. We introduce FastVLA, a training-free, task-aware, and temporally adaptive visual token compression framework. At each step, FastVLA scores token importance via task-to-vision attention and adaptively sets the compression rate from the importance-distribution uniformity, measured by an inverse-Simpson metric with online sliding-window calibration. We evaluate FastVLA on OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, and CogACT across LIBERO and SIMPLER, and on a physical Franka Research 3 robot. In simulation, it reduces LLM-backbone FLOPs by 35-59\% and action latency by 9-32\% (a 1.09$\times$-1.46$\times$ speedup) while maintaining task success, achieving a comparable or better efficiency-performance trade-off than existing plug-and-play token compression/pruning/reuse baselines. On the real robot, it cuts end-to-end latency by 20\% (1.25$\times$ speedup) at comparable success. Code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/FastVLA.

title: Dexterity from Supervised Play
abstract: How can robots autonomously collect the contact-rich experience needed to learn dexterous manipulation? We present DSP: Dexterity from supervised play, a framework in which a robot learns a play policy from minutes of human play through behavior cloning, then deploys it autonomously to collect hours of interaction data to train a world model. During inference, the same play policy then guides model-predictive control (MPC) by proposing candidate action sequences for evaluation under the learned world model. To accelerate inference, we also introduce a method for distilling a closed-loop, goal-conditioned policy through self-play within the learned world model. We evaluate this framework on underactuated pushing and any-to-any in-hand pose reorientation with a multifingered hand, in simulation and real world. In real world experiment, our method outperforms hindsight behavior cloning by 69.6% in success rate and achieves comparable success to reinforcement learning with 490 times less interaction data. These results demonstrate that supervised play can autonomously collect interaction data, guide model-based planning, and enable policy learning without any task-specific demonstrations or sim-to-real transfer.

title: Controlled rough SDEs, pathwise stochastic control and dynamic programming principles
abstract: We study stochastic optimal control of rough stochastic differential equations (RSDEs). This is in the spirit of the pathwise control problem (Lions–Souganidis 1998, Buckdahn–Ma 2007; also Davis–Burstein 1992), with renewed interest and recent works drawing motivation from filtering, SPDEs, and reinforcement learning. Results include regularity of rough value functions, validity of a rough dynamic programming principle and new rough stability results for HJB equations, removing excessive regularity demands previously imposed by flow transformation methods. Measurable selection is used to relate RSDEs to “doubly stochastic” SDEs under conditioning. In contrast to previous works, Brownian statistics for the to-be-conditioned-on noise are not required, aligned with the “pathwise” intuition that these should not matter upon conditioning. Depending on the chosen class of admissible controls, the involved processes may also be anticipating. The resulting stochastic value functions coincide in great generality for different classes of controls. RSDE theory offers a powerful and unified perspective on this problem class.

title: CoWorld Reasoner: Agentic Multimodal Reasoning with the Evolving Video World Model-Driven Harness
abstract: As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) advance, they are increasingly expected to perform spatiotemporal reasoning over motion, actions, and view changes beyond what the input images show. Video World Models (VWMs) provide a natural unified engine for visual imagination by generating task-relevant visual content as additional evidence. However, existing approaches typically invoke a VWM through fixed pipelines centered on a predefined form of visual imagination, such as novel-view synthesis. To support flexible visual imagination for diverse reasoning tasks, we introduce CoWorld Reasoner, an agentic framework that uses a VWM as a unified visual reasoning engine. Its Video World Model-Driven Harness exposes multiple visual operations through tools and uses skills to guide the VLM in deciding whether to imagine, selecting an operation, constructing a generation request, and interpreting the resulting visual evidence. We further introduce VLM-VWM Harness Co-Evolution, which jointly revises tools, skills, and execution code based on execution feedback while keeping both model weights fixed. Across seven benchmarks spanning spatial intelligence, temporal and causal reasoning, and perceptual reasoning, CoWorld Reasoner outperforms direct reasoning with the same VLM. The strongest variant improves on all seven benchmarks, including relative accuracy gains of 11.8% on MMSI and 13.0% on ERQA, and outperforms all five evolving baselines using the same backbone across five benchmarks.

title: Causal Invariant Bio-Inference: Breaking the Observational Barrier in Rhizosphere Dynamics via Physically-Constrained Edge-GNN Structural Causal Models
abstract: Observational machine learning models (e.g., Transformers, CNNs, Random Forests) fit joint probability distributions P(Y|X) and inherently break down out-of-distribution when spurious correlations fail under environmental volatility. In rhizosphere dynamics, unobserved confounders and micro-climatic shifts frequently lead to catastrophic prediction failures. To break this observational barrier, we introduce Causal Invariant Bio-Inference for RADIUS 0 / MediEEZI, combining Judea Pearl’s do-calculus interventional framework P(Y|do(X=x*)) with structural causal models (SCMs) and decentralized Edge Graph Neural Networks (Edge-GNNs). By embedding a stoichiometric and biochemical constraint matrix (C_bio derived from KEGG/MetaCyc pathways) directly into the adjacency optimization, we restrict the causal search space to thermodynamically allowed interactions and enforce strict directed acyclic graph (DAG) topology via matrix exponential constraints. This physically-constrained architecture enables provably convergent, continuous in-situ causal bio-inference across soil-plant-microbiome interactions, closed-loop environmental control life support systems (ECLS), and non-invasive health monitoring without requiring destructive sampling.

title: A Literature Review on the Sensor Network Design Problem Applied to Chemical Processes
abstract: In the present paper, a comprehensive review of methodologies for the optimal placement of measurement devices in chemical processes, commonly referred to as the sensor network design problem (SNDP), is presented. The SNDP is a combinatorial optimization problem of paramount importance in process design, monitoring, control, and data reconciliation, as sensor placement directly affects estimability, precision, reliability, and fault detectability. In addition to surveying solution strategies for SNDP, this review examines the closely related variable classification problem, which constitutes a fundamental building block in the systematic development of sensor networks. The evolution of the field is analyzed, highlighting early structural search approaches, subsequent optimization-based formulations relying on relaxation and decomposition techniques, and heuristic and metaheuristic strategies. The strengths and limitations of these methodological classes are discussed with respect to problem size and computational complexity. Moreover, this review identified a novel strategy to solve SNDPs based on machine learning algorithms. Finally, future research directions are outlined, emphasizing the growing need for scalable frameworks capable of addressing increasingly large and automated industrial systems. As computational capabilities continue to advance and process plants transition toward highly digitalized environments, research efforts devoted to efficient and robust SNDP methodologies are expected to intensify. In this context, Large Language Models (LLMs) can play a transformative role.

title: What Matters for World Modeling in Vision-Language-Action Models?
abstract: Integrating world models into Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) has emerged as a promising direction, enabling policies to anticipate future dynamics beyond reactive observation-to-action mapping. However, existing approaches vary simultaneously in their world representations, integration paradigms, and policy backbones, making it difficult to determine what truly matters for effective world model integration. To disentangle these factors, we categorize existing efforts into four representative paradigms, namely Implicit Future Alignment, Explicit Future Query, MoT Future Expert, and External World Predictor. We instantiate each within a unified framework and systematically evaluate these paradigms with diverse world representations and policy backbones across in-domain, out-of-domain, long-horizon, dynamic, few-shot, and real-world settings. Our study yields four main findings: 1) world representation effectiveness is paradigm-dependent, whereas 2D semantic representations offer robust, cross-paradigm gains; 2) no single paradigm is universally optimal, yet the decoupled MoT Future Expert offers competitive overall performance, particularly in OOD robustness; 3) world modeling consistently benefits policies built on standard VLMs, while decoupled designs exhibit greater compatibility with pretrained VLAs; and 4) world modeling improves performance over action-only baselines across multiple settings, with notable gains on long-horizon and dynamic tasks. Project page and video demonstrations are available at https://dylanmqs.github.io/WM-in-VLAs/.

title: VLRLA: Deployment-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language-Action Models through In-Context Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual perception and language understanding with robot control, providing a foundation for instruction-conditioned manipulation. However, conventional pretrained VLA policies lack a mechanism for gradual adaptation through accumulated interaction experience during deployment. We therefore propose VLRLA, a general framework that equips existing VLA models with \textit{in-context reinforcement learning} capabilities for deployment-time adaptation. Our approach augments a VLA model with a reinforcement learning module that learns from historical observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals. During deployment, the policy gradually refines its action generation and progressively improves task success while keeping model parameters fixed. Our approach is also designed for general applicability and compatibility with diverse learning history construction strategies and model training pipelines. Finally, through extensive experiments, we systematically investigate the learning properties of VLRLA in simulation and demonstrate its ability to adapt to unseen scenarios during real-world deployment.

title: Towards Agentic Robots: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness
abstract: Foundation models are driving a paradigm shift in robotic intelligence, moving beyond low-level action prediction to goal-directed orchestration of data collection, model training, task planning, and real-world execution. We characterize this emerging paradigm as an agentic robots, in which agents reason over human instructions, interact with robotic environments, rectify execution errors autonomously, and dynamically adjust operational strategies. Although this field develops fast, current studies are not well connected. Researchers have no consistent view of how to combine different agentic functions into a complete robot system. This paper provides a unified overview of existing research on agentic robots. We first trace the development from robot policies to agentic systems, covering vision-language-action models, world models, and world-action models. We then clarify the definition and scope of agentic robots and organize existing research into seventeen categories across four functional domains: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness. Across these domains, we examine how agents shape model learning and robot decisions, collect and curate robot data, construct worlds, tasks, and tests for learning and evaluation, and organize capabilities for robot use. Finally, we discuss open challenges and outline directions for future research. Looking forward, we hope this work contributes to a clearer understanding of agentic robots and supports new approaches to making them more capable, reliable, and adaptive.

title: Tactile-Guided Robot Learning: From Representation Learning to Foundation Models
abstract: Tactile sensing is becoming central to robust, adaptive, and dexterous robotic manipulation. Beyond its traditional role in contact detection and reactive control, touch is increasingly used to learn transferable representations, condition manipulation policies, and support embodied physical reasoning. Yet existing surveys largely emphasize tactile hardware and perception, leaving the rapid shift toward learning-based tactile manipulation insufficiently synthesized. This paper reviews tactile-guided skill learning from a learning-centric perspective, organized by the functional role of touch across the learning and control pipeline. We examine tactile representation and policy learning, tactile foundation models, predictive and adaptive control, and generalization across objects, tasks, sensors, embodiments, and simulation-to-real transfer. Across these directions, we identify common design principles and remaining challenges in learning transferable physical representations, integrating semantic reasoning with contact-level control, and scaling tactile learning across heterogeneous data and hardware. Finally, we outline emerging directions toward tactile foundation and world models that can predict, reason about, and adapt physical interactions. Together, this review characterizes the transition of touch from a task-specific feedback signal toward a core modality for general-purpose embodied intelligence. An accompanying database of the reviewed literature and associated resources is available at https://sites.google.com/view/touch-in-robot-learning-review.

title: StateCraft: Augmenting Video World Models with Abstract-State Reasoning
abstract: Video world models aim to simulate complex environments with realistic appearance and dynamics. Maintaining consistency over long interactions requires tracking past actions and understanding how those actions affect the environment. Video world models can only generate partial observations of the entire world at a time. Remembering past observations alone may not be sufficient in every scenario, as they may no longer reflect the world after a sequence of actions. We introduce a paradigm that decouples a persistent, updatable abstract state from the visual state. The abstract state keeps track of the entities' changes as the world evolves, and is used to condition the visual state, which represents the current view. We propose StateCraft, a novel architecture that pairs a language model with a video diffusion model to evolve the dynamic world. We evaluate our approach on generative interfaces, which pose a substantial challenge because a single action may change parts of the state that are not currently visible. To support training and evaluation, we develop a data collection pipeline that produces informative, densely annotated trajectories at scale without human or agent supervision, together with a benchmark measuring generation quality, memory, and controllability. On this benchmark, our approach improves surpasses the state-of-the-art baselines. We demonstrate that StateCraft maintains high self-consistency and strong generation quality over long trajectories. Because the abstract state is explicit, it can be edited directly, and generation follows edits to states never observed in the data. Finally, a proof-of-concept 3D experiment, in which actions change the illumination of an unobserved room, shows that the paradigm can also be applied to spatial environments. Project page: https://insait-institute.github.io/StateCraft/.

title: Sketches of nonuniformly elliptic Schauder theory
abstract: Schauder theory is a basic tool in the study of elliptic and parabolic PDEs, asserting that solutions inherit the regularity of the coefficients.It plays a central role in establishing higher regularity for solutions to a broad class of elliptic problems exhibiting ellipticity, including those involving free boundaries.In the linear setting, Schauder theory dates back to the 1920-1930s and is now considered classical.Nonlinear extensions were developed in the 1980s.All these classical results are restricted to uniformly elliptic operators and heavily rely on perturbative techniques -freezing the coefficients and comparing the solution to that of a constant-coefficient problem.However, such methods fail in the nonuniformly elliptic setting, where homogeneous a priori estimates break down and standard iteration arguments no longer apply.Here, we give a brief survey of recent progress including the solution to the long-standing problem of proving the validity of Schauder estimates in the nonlinear, nonuniformly elliptic setting.

title: SceneAE: Scene Generation and Reconstruction in Queryable 3D-Anchored Latent Space
abstract: Recent video world models have increasingly adopted 3D memory mechanisms to integrate historical observations into a lightweight and persistent scene representation. This naturally raises a complementary question: if 3D representations can serve as an effective mechanism for memorizing observed scenes, can they also be directly used as the latent space for reconstructing and generating scenes? Motivated by this idea, we represent a scene as a compact and unstructured 3D-anchored latent space (\textbf{SceneAE}). Each latent combines an explicit 3D position with an implicit content feature and is spatially grounded to describe its local scene region, forming a sparse latent point cloud. Unlike conventional video-VAE latents that describe how a scene appears from particular viewpoints, our representation directly describes the scene itself, making it naturally applicable to both reconstruction and generation. For reconstruction, once the scene has been generated, our persistent 3D representation can be projected and decoded into RGB-D observations by different target cameras, without the need to regenerate a video for each new camera trajectory. For generation, we leverage the geometry-content separation to first generate camera-controlled 3D geometry and then synthesize content conditioned on it, reducing camera-appearance entanglement and improving camera controllability. Experiments show that this 3D latent achieves superior generation quality, computational cost, and camera controllability.

title: SafeDriveVLA: Navigation-Conditioned World Model Dreaming for Conflict-Aware End-to-End Autonomous Driving
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are gaining attention in autonomous driving, inheriting commonsense priors from large language models (LLMs) and widening the navigation interface from a fixed command set to free-form natural-language instructions. However, this open-ended interface exposes a new vulnerability surface: an inattentive driver may issue instructions that are unsafe given the current scene, and a malicious user may issue dangerous ones on purpose. We present the first benchmark suite that evaluates navigation following and conflict awareness together, along with adversarial robustness. Existing VLAs fall short on both: SimLingo completes no language-instructed lane change in closed loop, and all models degrade sharply under conflicting signals. We propose SafeDriveVLA, the first driving VLA that (1) explicitly predicts a three-level navigation-compliance mode to decouple conflict reasoning from action generation, and (2) uses navigation-conditioned world model dreaming to inform this prediction. Unlike prior world models that roll out expert or planned actions, ours dreams of strictly following the navigation signal, showing when following is safe. SafeDriveVLA reaches 88.16 Driving Score (DS) and 68.64% Success Rate (SR) on Bench2Drive, lifts closed-loop language following by 49.3% and reduces collisions under unsafe instructions from 60 to 38 compared to the best SimLingo variant. Video demonstrations are available on our project page.

title: SPECTRA-VLA: Base-Fine Hyperspectral Token Transfer at Frozen Vision-Language-Action Interfaces
abstract: Hyperspectral imaging distinguishes RGB-similar objects, but a pretrained vision-language-action model needs a state its frozen decoder can use. SPECTRA-VLA provides a native-width spectral upgrade without retraining the visual encoder or action decoder. A learned continuous residual enriches each target token through its own normalized false-color reference; projection, norm control and validation-calibrated injection regulate the change. Across 86 held-out acquisitions, category balanced accuracy rises from 0.812 to 0.883. With identical residuals and scale, own-token addition improves reuse of an external category-derived probe on frozen decoder logits: 0.701 versus 0.590 with pooled replacement, at similar image-disjoint recognition. Five grouped tests covering the same 86 acquisitions recover within-category spectral shape with $R^2=0.802/0.337$ from continuous and posterior-code states. Category-matched spectral swaps further show that own-token composition approximately doubles the target-specific recovery increment after frozen decoding. Spectral enrichment and receiving-token preservation thus work together at the pretrained interface.

title: Replication Package: When Is Compliance with AI Regulation Evolutionarily Stable? Replicator Dynamics of the EU AI Act and US Soft Law
abstract: This package contains the code and country-level aggregates needed to reproduce every number, table and figure in the article. The article develops a three-strategy replicator-dynamics model in which AI developers choose among hard compliance, self-regulation and unregulated deployment. It treats the EU AI Act and US soft law as two parameterisations of the same game, and anchors detection probabilities in survey data for the 27 EU Member States and the United States. Contents Python code for the evolutionary game model (payoff matrix, regime thresholds, classifier, replicator ODE). Symbolic verification of the propositions with sympy assertions, and numerical checks of the main theorem. Construction of country indices from Eurobarometer 101.4, and validation against Pew Research Center and World Justice Project data. Global sensitivity analysis (Monte Carlo and Sobol indices) and robustness analyses (sampling-error classification, alternative mappings, decomposition of the US counterfactual). Country-level aggregates and all figures. Data not included. The underlying microdata are licensed by third parties and cannot be redistributed. Users must obtain them from the providers and place them in data/: Eurobarometer 101.4, GESIS ZA8844, https://doi.org/10.4232/1.14471 Pew Research Center Spring 2025 Global Attitudes Survey Pew Research Center’s American Trends Panel, Wave 166 World Justice Project Rule of Law Index 2025 Exact file names and sources are listed in README.md. Reproduction. Install the packages in requirements.txt (Python 3.13) and run bash run_all.sh (about 3 minutes). All random draws use fixed seeds, so results are reproduced exactly. Licence. title: Reduced-Order Modeling of Hamiltonian Dynamics Based on Symplectic Neural Networks
abstract: Abstract. We introduce a novel data-driven symplectic reduced-order modeling (ROM) framework for high-dimensional Hamiltonian systems that unifies latent-space discovery and dynamics learning within a single, end-to-end neural architecture. The encoder–decoder is built from Hénon neural networks (HénonNets) and may be augmented with linear G-reflector layers, yielding a structure-preserving symplectic embedding and an associated one-sided symplectic pseudo-inverse between the full and latent phase spaces. Latent dynamics are advanced by a symplectic flow map implemented as a HénonNet. This unified neural architecture ensures exact preservation of the underlying symplectic structure at the reduced-order level, significantly enhancing the fidelity and long-term stability of the resulting ROM. We validate our method through comprehensive numerical experiments on canonical Hamiltonian systems. The results demonstrate the method’s capability for accurate trajectory reconstruction, robust predictive performance beyond the training horizon and strong Hamiltonian preservation. These promising outcomes underscore the effectiveness and potential applicability of our symplectic ROM framework for complex dynamical systems across a broad range of scientific and engineering disciplines. The implementation associated with this work is publicly available at https://github.com/chenyongssss/Symp_NN .

title: ReAl: Refine neural operators via aligning dynamical flow
abstract: Neural partial differential equation (PDE) surrogates trained with mean squared error (MSE) can capture dominant dynamics but often lose high-frequency information and fine-scale structures. Generative models (e.g., Flow Matching) can capture the distribution of fine-scale details, yet stochastic errors may accumulate during autoregressive rollouts and compromise long-term stability. To address these limitations, we introduce Refine and Align(ReAl), a model-agnostic plug-in that augments pretrained PDE surrogates to improve the reconstruction of high-frequency structures associated with complex physical phenomena. In the refinement stage, a conditional flow-matching model learns the residual distribution around the deterministic base prediction, recovering missing fine-scale structures while retaining the dominant dynamics. In the alignment stage, to mitigate the generative discrepancies amplified in the autoregressive rollout, particularly in chaotic systems, we generate multiple trajectories from the same input and reinforce the refiner with trajectory-level rewards, thereby achieving long-horizon dynamical alignment. Experiments across diverse surrogate architectures and PDE tasks demonstrate that ReAl consistently improves high-frequency fidelity, forecasting accuracy, and long-horizon stability.

title: Physics-Constrained Deep Spatiotemporal Surrogate Optimization of Carbon Dioxide Enhanced Oil Recovery Using Bounded Flow-Regime Metrics
abstract: Abstract Carbon dioxide enhanced oil recovery (CO2-EOR) optimization is often driven by field-level targets such as oil production, carbon dioxide retention, economics, and injection schedules. These targets are important, but they do not directly show whether displacement inside the reservoir is stable or whether gas and water are sweeping the reservoir effectively. This work develops a physics-constrained spatiotemporal optimization framework that uses local flow behavior together with field-level performance to guide operating decisions. A compositional reservoir simulator was used to generate CO2-EOR cases under water-alternating-gas (WAG) operation. Three bounded field-scale flow-regime families were developed in this work and resolved locally at every active grid cell and report time: phase mobility, viscous–capillary balance, and gravity–capillary balance. Gas–oil and water–oil forms of these three families provide six bounded regime fields used to describe local displacement behavior. Gas saturation and water saturation were added to give eight spatial targets. A U-Fourier Neural Operator (U-FNO) was trained on 500 simulation cases containing 87,705 case-time samples, with separate validation and held-out sets of 70 and 130 cases. The model also predicts cumulative oil production and retained gas. Differential Evolution was then used to optimize ten production, injection, pressure, and WAG controls while penalizing unfavorable regime behavior cell-by-cell and through time. The final surrogate was evaluated on 100 independent unseen OOB cases containing 17,494 case-time samples. Across the eight spatial targets, the mean absolute error was 0.028 and the root mean square error was 0.102 in the processed output space. The gas–oil viscous–capillary and gravity–capillary fields, which have very low target variance, had mean absolute errors of 0.005 and 0.008, respectively. Mean absolute errors for cumulative oil production and retained gas were 0.043 and 0.031. On the 100 unseen cases, physics-constrained optimization increased average cumulative oil production by about 42%, improved the displacement-efficiency proxy by about 52%, and increased retained gas by about 130% relative to the original operating cases. Oil production improved in 96% of the unseen cases and displacement efficiency improved in 100%. Similar behavior was observed across the additional 130 held-out cases. In comparison, conventional optimization based mainly on field-level objectives favored more gas-dominated solutions and gave less consistent sweep improvement. The main contribution is the direct use of newly developed bounded flow-regime fields inside the optimization objective. The framework therefore does not ask only how much oil is produced or how much carbon dioxide is retained; it also evaluates how displacement is occurring throughout the reservoir. This provides a physics-aware and interpretable way to screen WAG operating strategies for recovery, carbon dioxide retention, and sweep.

title: PAWA: Panoramic Action-conditioned World Modeling for Multiple Agents
abstract: A multiplayer world model must predict how the independent actions of several players change a shared environment, including changes outside a player's current field of view. A point-of-view (POV) video captures such changes only after they enter its field of view, whereas panoramic video records the surroundings in every viewing direction and has served as an intermediate representation of the world state in recent world models. Learning this task therefore requires synchronized POV and panoramic videos of interacting players together with their actions, yet no existing dataset provides this combination in Minecraft, an established testbed in which players act independently in a shared, modifiable 3D world. We present PAWA, a dataset and framework for action-conditioned panoramic multiplayer world modeling. The dataset pairs each player's POV video with world-stabilized panoramic video and aligned actions. Its distributed pipeline decouples CPU gameplay capture from GPU rendering, scales beyond 64 simultaneous players, and re-renders each recorded session under new observation configurations without replaying the gameplay. On this dataset, we develop a dual-tower model that jointly predicts POV and panoramic video and couples the two streams through cross-attention that aligns tokens observing the same direction in a shared world frame. We further introduce a quadratic-phase player encoding that provides many more player codes than existing rotary codes at the same embedding dimension. Experiments show that PAWA outperforms state-of-the-art multiplayer world models in POV prediction quality while also producing high-fidelity panoramic predictions. The dataset and collection pipeline are open source to support further research on multiplayer world models.

title: ObjDream: Guiding Vision-Language-Action Models with Object-Level Understanding and Future State Prediction
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation, enabling robots to generate actions from visual observations and language instructions. However, most existing VLA models still operate on image-level visual representations inherited from pretrained vision-language backbones, while lacking fine-grained object understanding for manipulation. As a result, their robustness can degrade under out-of-distribution object layouts, clutter, and background variations. To address these limitations, we introduce ObjDream, an object-centric VLA framework centered on object-level understanding and future object state prediction. ObjDream uses a spatio-temporal object encoder to organize visual observations into temporal object slots, where persistent object identity and dynamic object state are represented through separate channels. These structured object representations are inserted into the token sequence of the vision-language model (VLM), where identity-guided routing modulates VLM attention to the corresponding object tokens. In addition, an action-conditioned object dynamics module predicts compact future object states relevant to manipulation during training, explicitly supervising object state evolution under robot actions without requiring future prediction at inference. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0 show that ObjDream improves generalization under diverse distribution shifts and scene perturbations. Real-world robot experiments further demonstrate that ObjDream transfers to physical manipulation settings with novel object arrangements and background changes.

title: Neurosymbolic Learning of Interpretable World Models
abstract: World models aim to learn compact representations of an environment from observations, enabling agents to predict future states and plan their behaviour. However, most existing approaches learn black-box representations, with limited ability to incorporate prior knowledge about the world. We introduce Concept-Grounded World Models (CGWMs), a neurosymbolic world model design that instead learns interpretable concept representations. We learn these concepts from observations using explicit and complete knowledge, expressed in temporal logic, that specifies the valid world states and the temporal relations governing their dynamics. Furthermore, we directly use this knowledge by formulating planning as differentiable reasoning, optimising the agent's actions by gradient ascent to satisfy a goal. We experimentally compare CGWM with a purely neural baseline and a neurosymbolic baseline on two game environments. We find that CGWMs ground concepts much more accurately, even over long horizons, resulting in significantly more robust planning both in and out of distribution.

title: Machine Learning‐Assisted Optimization for Dynamic Supply Network Design in the Additive Manufacturing Platform
abstract: ABSTRACT Distributed manufacturing enabled by additive manufacturing (AM) allows supply chains to rapidly adapt to changing market conditions through flexible facility relocation and capacity adjustment. However, existing studies largely overlook the logistical aspects of AM‐based supply chains and typically treat facility location and logistics decisions separately. This study addresses this gap by developing a novel AM supply network design model that simultaneously considers the dynamic relocation of AM facilities, the adjustment of production capacities, and delivery routing decisions over multiple periods. We formulate the problem as a mixed‐integer linear programming model (MILP). Given the computational challenges associated with the delivery routing component, we propose a machine learning genetic algorithm (MLGA) approach to solve the problem efficiently. MLGA incorporates a machine learning surrogate to estimate the cost of the capacitated vehicle routing subproblem (CVRP), thereby significantly accelerating the convergence of the genetic algorithm (GA). We train two different machine learning surrogates: One based on a neural network model and the other on an XGBoost model. The MLGA solution methodology, under both surrogate models, performs satisfactorily in terms of solution quality and computation time across a set of randomly generated instances. Extensive sensitivity analyses are also conducted on a realistic use case to evaluate the model's applicability under varying service area, demand, and cost scenarios, offering valuable managerial insights and practical implications.

title: Learning-enabled collaborative intelligence in search and rescue robotics: a survey of paradigms, models, and challenges
abstract: Search and Rescue (SAR) robotics increasingly depends on collaborative intelligence to operate effectively in dynamic, uncertain, and time-sensitive environments. Modern SAR missions require coordinated interaction among heterogeneous robotic agents as well as structured collaboration between humans and intelligent systems for perception, decision-making, and adaptive mission execution. This paper presents a structured narrative review supported by a systematic literature search of learning-enabled collaborative intelligence frameworks in SAR robotics, organized around three paradigms: human-to-machine (H2M), machine-to-machine (M2M), and machine-to-human (M2H) learning. The review examines recent developments in reinforcement learning, federated and decentralized learning, knowledge distillation, swarm intelligence, semantic communication, and the growing integration of large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) for knowledge grounding, transfer, and explainability. Beyond algorithmic advances, the analysis emphasizes deployment-oriented challenges including partial observability, communication constraints, uncertainty management, model reliability, and real-time operational requirements. Rather than conducting a fully PRISMA-compliant systematic review, this work synthesizes representative and influential studies to identify emerging trends, architectural trade-offs, deployment limitations, and future research directions for scalable and trustworthy collaborative SAR systems.

title: HRTF Upsampling and Personalization via Neural Operators
abstract: Head-related transfer function (HRTF) spatial upsampling from sparse measurements is a fundamental challenge in personalized binaural audio. We formulate HRTF upsampling as an operator learning problem and introduce SPARO, a neural operator that maps sparse measurements at a set of spatial directions to the HRTF field, a continuous representation that can be queried at arbitrary positions. SPARO projects the measurements onto a learned set of spherical latent modes, processes the latent modes with Transformer blocks, and decodes the resulting representations at query directions. On SONICOM, using the LAP24 measurement configuration, SPARO attains the best log-spectral distortion (LSD) and interaural level difference (ILD) error at every sparsity level from 3 to 100 measurements (18% lower LSD and 43% lower ILD error than the strongest baseline at 100 measurements) while remaining competitive in interaural time difference (ITD) error. It reconstructs a dense HRTF 15 to 373 times faster than the leading neural-field method RANF. We further validate the approach on HUTUBS, demonstrating its effectiveness across HRTF datasets.

title: Fractional is Better: Learnable Derivative Orders in Neural Operator Learning
abstract: Neural operators learn mappings between function spaces, enabling fast surrogate solutions to partial differential equations. Despite remarkable architectural diversity, these methods often share a common input representation: raw coordinate-value pairs $(x, u(x))$. We ask whether inputs aligned with PDE differential structure can improve learning. Through Picard iteration on mild solutions, we show that derivatives of the input appear explicitly in the solution operator, suggesting that providing derivative features should reduce the network's implicit differentiation burden. We prove this intuition: providing derivative features improves approximation bounds from $O(W^{-(s-m)/d})$ to $O(W^{-s/d})$, where $W$ is parameter count, $s$ is input regularity, $m$ is the PDE order, and $d$ is spatial dimension. Our central finding, however, is a surprise: the optimal derivative order $β^*$ is strictly less than the PDE order $m$. This gap arises from a bias-variance tradeoff in spectral space that we characterize in closed form. Learning $β$ from data achieves automatic spectral regularization. We introduce $\partial$-NO (del-NO), for derivative-augmented neural operators, an architecture-agnostic augmentation that provides learnable fractional derivative features to any neural operator backbone. Across benchmark problems and architectures, $\partial$-NO consistently improves prediction accuracy, with learned orders that reflect a representation of known physics modulated by noise and finite-sample constraints.

title: F-equivalence for parabolic systems and applications to the stabilization of nonlinear PDE
abstract: We consider the $F$-equivalence problem for parabolic systems: under which conditions a control system, governed by a parabolic operator $A$ and a control operator $B$, can be made equivalent to an exponentially stable system with arbitrarily large decay rate through an appropriate control feedback law? While this problem has been resolved for finite-dimensional systems fifty years ago, good conditions for infinite-dimensional systems remain a challenge, especially for systems in spatial dimension larger than one. Our main result establishes optimal conditions for the existence of an $F$-equivalence pair $(T,K)$ for a given parabolic control system $(A,B)$. We introduce an extended framework for $F$-equivalence of parabolic operators, addressing key limitations of existing approaches, and we prove that the pair $(T,K)$ is unique if and only if $(A,B)$ is approximately controllable. As a consequence, this provides a method to construct feedback operators for the rapid stabilization of semilinear parabolic systems, possibly multi-dimensional in space. We provide several illustrative examples, including the rapid stabilization of the heat equation, the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, the Navier-Stokes equations and the quasilinear heat equation.

title: Dynamic fund protection in markets with stochastic volatility and frictions: a double Heston model with transaction costs and its applications
abstract: This paper develops a pricing framework for Dynamic Fund Protection (DFP) contracts with lookback features under a double Heston stochastic volatility model with proportional transaction costs. The valuation leads to a multidimensional nonlinear partial differential equation (PDE) involving the underlying price and two variance factors, where a nonlinear term captures the impact of trading frictions. To solve this PDE efficiently, we employ a Random Feature (RF) method (a mesh-free, machine-learning-inspired technique) that approximates the solution in a randomly generated feature space via least-squares minimization of the PDE residual. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the RF solver achieves higher accuracy and faster computation speeds compared to conventional grid-based schemes for the same model. Calibration exercises using equity index and foreign exchange market data show that with transaction costs fixed at representative market levels, calibrating the multifactor volatility dynamics fits implied volatility surfaces significantly better than single-factor benchmarks. We also present novel application case studies, including cross-border digital goods pricing under exchange-rate exposure. The results confirm that our integrated volatility-friction framework offers a robust and computationally tractable approach for pricing and hedging lookback-style protections in realistic market settings.

title: Digital Self-Interference Cancellation for In-Band Full-Duplex Systems Based on Transformer Neural Operators
abstract: Digital-domain self-interference cancellation is essential in in-band full-duplex radios after passive suppression and analog cancellation. It is particularly challenging when the desired signal is strong relative to the residual self-interference. In this regime, conventional iterative digital cancellers update their coefficients from desired-signal-contaminated received samples and may suffer substantial performance degradation. This paper reformulates digital-domain self-interference cancellation as an operator-learning problem. The proposed framework learns the temporal evolution of the residual self-interference channel from historical observations and uses the learned operator together with the known local transmit signal to reconstruct the current residual self-interference. A Transformer neural operator is used to realize this framework. The resulting method is trained in a desired-signal-free setting and then applied in the presence of a desired signal. A continuity-based analysis characterizes the sensitivity of the learned operator to the resulting input perturbation. Numerical experiments in static and time-varying channels, including time-varying SIR conditions, demonstrate stable cancellation performance over a wide range of interference levels. At 30 dB SIR, the proposed method improves the cancellation performance by 5--15 dB over the considered conventional methods.

title: Deterministic Quantum Mechanics of Transformer In-Context Attention: Wavefunction Dirac-Delta Collapse via Optical-Mechanical Dual-Chassis
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) governed by softmax-based self-attention inherently suffer from non-deterministic token drift, attention dispersion, and cumulative hallucination. In this paper, we formalize in-context attention dynamics through a quantum mechanical perspective, modeling the attention distribution as a statistical probability density over the discrete token Hilbert space. To eliminate attention drift without model fine-tuning or external orchestration wrappers, we introduce an In-Context Virtual Machine (ICVM) operating via an Optical-Mechanical Dual-Chassis control system. The Optical Chassis partitions the softmax partition function into an immutable static core basis (collimated by 10 core persistent grounding assets) and a dynamic token basis, inducing a non-zero potential energy barrier that contracts the continuous probability wavepacket into a deterministic Dirac-delta function centered precisely at the target attractor state. Concurrently, the Mechanical Chassis executes direct POSIX kernel system calls (stat()) to enforce monotonic physical byte and line growth, halting the hardware tool bus whenever zero-tolerance engineering bounds are violated. Spanning extensive multi-turn empirical evaluations across complex reasoning domains, the dual-chassis system achieves a 0.00% hallucination rate, zero token drift, and O(1) state convergence with zero recurring cloud API overhead. This work provides an axiomatic mathematical proof and deterministic computing framework bridging theoretical attention thermodynamics and production-grade cybernetic autonomy. title: CTIA-ODE: Continuous-Time Inter-Variable Attention for Long-Term Time Series Forecasting
abstract: Although multivariate time series forecasting has broad application prospects, effectively incorporating exogenous variables remains challenging. Prevailing discrete-time architectures often impose rigid temporal alignment across heterogeneous variables, which may limit their ability to capture continuously evolving external effects. To address this limitation, we introduce CTIA-ODE, a continuous-time forecasting framework centered on Continuous-Time Inter-Variable Attention (CTIA). Specifically, CTIA is embedded within an ordinary differential equation (ODE) solver, enabling the continuously evolving endogenous trajectory to dynamically query a static exogenous context along the integration path without requiring explicit temporal alignment. To improve the stability of the continuous latent dynamics, we further introduce a dual-stabilization strategy: architecturally, a Linear Residual Augmentation (LRA) module provides a macroscopic trend anchor, while an Outlier-Robust Hybrid Loss (ORHL) mitigates the influence of heavy-tailed anomalies during optimization. Extensive experiments across eight real-world datasets demonstrate that CTIA-ODE achieves state-of-the-art forecasting performance across diverse datasets and prediction horizons, while maintaining a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off with a compact memory footprint and low inference latency, particularly under long-horizon forecasting settings. Anonymous code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CTIA-ODE-15A6/.

title: Beyond Optimization: A Multi-Agent Systems and Human–Agent Collaboration Perspective on Decentralized Multi-UAV Task Allocation
abstract: Decentralized task allocation among multiple Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) is a critical NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem for enabling autonomous swarms to operate without central supervision. Multi-UAV research has advanced distributed algorithms to manage physical constraints, dynamic networks, and battery limitations. However, previous work frequently reduces task allocation to abstract numerical cost minimization, largely overlooking the critical socio-cognitive coordination dynamics both among UAVs and with human partners. Furthermore, previous surveys often blend centralized and decentralized architectures, leaving a gap for a dedicated, decentralized multi-agent systems (MASs) perspective. This review addresses these limitations by framing decentralized multi-UAV task allocation as a cooperative coordination problem rather than a simple optimization task. First, we establish a taxonomy that categorizes the literature into four foundational approaches—market-based, learning-based, distributed optimization, and clustering—comprehensively mapping their characteristics and trade-offs. Second, we bridge the multi-UAV literature with broader MAS research, highlighting how socio-cognitive models can address the current optimization-versus-coordination mismatch. Third, we contrast the dominant supervisory control approach of human–UAV collaboration (HUC) with the reciprocal, peer-level teaming models found in human–agent collaboration (HAC). We advocate for the integration of socio-cognitive factors present in cooperative coordination, such as dynamic trust calibration, shared mental models, hybrid intelligence, and ethics, within the allocation loop. Finally, we present a future research roadmap focusing on richer task structures, socially aware rational agents, mixed-initiative allocation, and multi-dimensional process-level coordination metrics. This review provides a holistic understanding for investigating how decentralized multi-UAV task allocation can evolve from rigid supervisory hierarchies toward resilient, adaptive, and human-aligned cooperative teaming models.

title: Back on Track: Deployment-time Policy Improvement via World Model Planning
abstract: State-of-the-art visuomotor policies are increasingly capable of executing complex tasks, yet can fail during deployment in ways they cannot predict or recover from on their own. Improving their performance and robustness typically requires collecting more data, retraining, or modifying the policy architecture, all of which are time- and resource-intensive in practice. We instead propose an offline-trained monitoring-and-intervention framework that improves a policy during deployment using only black-box query access. From a limited set of labeled on-policy rollouts, we learn a policy-conditioned liveness value that measures the nominal policy's progress toward task completion; we additionally train a compact latent world model using these rollouts together with play data. At deployment, the liveness value continuously monitors execution. When it detects a loss of progress, a short-horizon planner searches the world model for corrective actions using the same value as its planning objective, after which control returns to the nominal policy. We evaluate our method on the LIBERO-Goal task suite and on a Franka Panda manipulator, using the vision-language-action model $π_{0.5}$ and a diffusion policy as nominal policies, and demonstrate significant improvements in task success rates, while supporting real-time control. Additional results and videos are available on the project website (https://policy-improvement-wm.pages.dev/).

title: Are We Overthinking One-Step Generation?
abstract: Diffusion and flow matching are now dominant frameworks for generative modeling in continuous domains, but they typically require multiple network evaluations at inference. This has motivated extensive research on one-step generative modeling primarily built on diffusion and flow, though existing approaches often rely on complex training machinery. In this work, we introduce Priming Models, a simple two-stage framework for training one-step generators. Motivated by the difficulty of distributional training from scratch, Priming Models are first trained on a reconstruction objective, e.g., pixel-space denoising at a fixed noise level, before undergoing feature-space distributional post-training. Our central scientific finding is that this simple reconstruction stage is already enough to entirely alleviate the difficulty of distributional training. Empirically, across class-conditional image generation, text-to-image generation, and world modeling, Priming Models significantly advance the Pareto frontier of training compute vs. generation quality. On ImageNet at $256 \times 256$ resolution, we achieve a state-of-the-art FID of $1.19$ among one-step generators using approximately one-tenth the training compute of prior methods with comparable FID. We open-source our codebase at https://github.com/JaeyeonKim01/priming.

title: Accelerating droplet-laden Stokes flow simulations with hierarchical surrogate modeling
abstract: We present a surrogate modeling strategy for Stokes flows with liquid droplets suspended in a carrier fluid. Our approach is based on a multi-fidelity framework. At the lowest fidelity, droplets are treated as passive tracers, neglecting their influence on the ambient flow field. Building on this approximation, we derive a PDE that represents the current modeling error. This error equation is then solved approximately to correct the flow field and the procedure is iterated. Two fidelities are employed in an alternating fashion: Stokes flow in the absence of droplets and flow around a single droplet in free space. By systematically combining these models, the method captures droplet-flow, droplet-boundary, and droplet-droplet interactions. In this work, the framework is developed and validated for circular, non-deforming droplets in two spatial dimensions. The geometric self-similarity of the droplets allows us to construct an efficient offline-online strategy based on the reuse of precomputed single-droplet solutions. Extensions to deformable droplets are also discussed. Numerical experiments demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed surrogate in a variety of tests, including scenarios with up to $10^4$ droplets. Notably, we show that the proposed surrogate achieves substantially reduced computational cost compared to fully resolved multi-fluid simulations with state-of-the-art software.

title: Accelerating Field Development Planning with Generative AI: A Transformer-Based Framework
abstract: Abstract Field development planning for oil and gas reservoirs is becoming increasingly complex, making traditional simulation-based optimization prohibitively costly in time and compute. This research explores a generative AI transformer that directly predicts optimal well locations, aiming to maximize net present value (NPV) while reducing planning time by orders of magnitude. A custom transformer was built to ingest reservoir fields (pressure, porosity, permeability, fluid saturations) together with wellbore production and injection rates. Raw voxel data are first projected into dense embeddings, then passed through stacked multi-head self-attention blocks that encode both spatial and temporal dependencies via sinusoidal positional encodings. To keep memory footprints tractable for full-field models, we partition the volume into overlapping chunks before feeding them to the network. The model was developed using 200 Brugge simulation scenarios using a mean squared error loss on well locations and well production/injection rates, with model parameters optimized using the Adam optimizer. The transformer architecture successfully accommodated scenarios with varying numbers of wells and achieved stable training convergence after 100 epochs. We used the trained transformer to optimize well placement in different scenarios from the test dataset, achieving instantaneous inference times and acceptable accuracy. The NPV obtained from the transformer-inferred wells achieved 87% of that obtained from traditional simulation-based stochastic optimization, which is a significant improvement considering the substantial reduction in computational time and cost. Additionally, comparison with several AI-based surrogate-assisted optimization workflows demonstrated that the generative framework achieved higher economic performance while eliminating the iterative optimization process. These results demonstrate that a transformer-based generative model can deliver near-optimal well placement with negligible computational cost, opening the door to rapid and iterative field development studies. This work applies a full-field transformer to generative well placement, learning high-dimensional spatial and temporal reservoir relationships directly from data. The model delivers instantaneous, optimization-free predictions, enabling rapid scenario screening and substantially accelerating field development decision cycles.

title: A discontinuous Galerkin method for the three-dimensional heterodimer model with application to prion-like proteins’ dynamics
abstract: Neurocognitive disorders, such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, have a wide social impact. These proteinopathies involve misfolded proteins accumulating into neurotoxic aggregates. Mathematical and computational models describing the prion-like dynamics offer an analytical basis to study the diseases' evolution and a computational framework for exploring potential therapies. This work focuses on the heterodimer model in a three-dimensional setting, a reactive-diffusive system of nonlinear partial differential equations describing the evolution of both healthy and misfolded proteins. We investigate traveling wave solutions and diffusion-driven instabilities as a mechanism of neurotoxic pattern formation. For the considered mathematical model, we propose a space discretization, relying on the Discontinuous Galerkin method on polytopal/polyhedral grids, allowing high-order accuracy and flexible handling of the complicated brain's geometry. Further, we present a priori error estimates for the semi-discrete formulation and we perform convergence tests to verify the theoretical results. Finally, we conduct simulations using realistic data on a three-dimensional brain mesh reconstructed from medical images.
