title: A Bregman Proximal Viewpoint on Neural Operators
abstract: We present several advances on neural operators by viewing the action of operator layers as the minimizers of Bregman regularized optimization problems over Banach function spaces. The proposed framework allows interpreting the activation operators as Bregman proximity operators from dual to primal space. This novel viewpoint is general enough to recover classical neural operators as well as a new variant, coined Bregman neural operators, which includes the inverse activation operator and features the same expressivity of standard neural operators. Numerical experiments support the added benefits of the Bregman variant of Fourier neural operators for training deeper and more accurate models.

title: WorldOracle: Benchmarking Action-Conditioned World Models against Real-World Executions
abstract: We introduce WorldOracle, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) against paired real-world executions. Given the same initial observation and low-level action sequence, WorldOracle asks whether a predicted rollout reproduces what happens in the real world, including physical consequences and task-state transitions. We evaluate models along four complementary dimensions: physical state correctness, interaction spatial alignment, key interaction area fidelity, and multi-view action coherence. To support this evaluation, we curate real-world training and evaluation suites that cover different interaction dynamics and embodiments. The evaluation suite contains long, multi-segment episodes with both successful and failed executions, enabling evaluation across varied action outcomes and behavior distributions. Experiments on seven representative ACWMs reveal distinct model strengths and failure modes. WorldOracle provides a systematic foundation for measuring and advancing action-conditioned world modeling for manipulation. We will release the datasets, evaluation code, and leaderboard.

title: Wong--Zakai Convergence and FNO Learning for Stochastic Volterra Equations
abstract: This paper studies Wong--Zakai convergence and Fourier neural operator learning for stochastic Volterra integral equations (SVIEs) describing random systems with memory. A Wong--Zakai theorem establishes convergence of pathwise solutions driven by piecewise linear approximations of Brownian motion to the corresponding SVIE solution. This convergence provides a foundation for using mirror-padded Fourier neural operators to learn the solution operator mapping initial conditions and driving noise to entire solution trajectories. Numerical experiments demonstrate competitive prediction accuracy and generalization to temporal grids finer than those used for training, while assessing the influence of padding and computational cost. As a follow-up to \citet{LKP:26}, this study extends their operator-learning framework to SVIEs through separate convergence and approximation analyses tailored to convolutional memory.

title: WAVE-0: Bridging VLA Policies and WAMs with Lightweight Latent Future Prediction
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies excel at generalist robotic manipulation but generate actions without explicitly modeling their environmental consequences. World action models (WAMs) incorporate future prediction, yet most rely on costly video generation, while latent alternatives either use predicted futures only as auxiliary targets or infer latent actions from suboptimal visual transitions through costly large-scale video pretraining. We introduce WAVE-0 (World-model-Augmented VLA Execution), a framework that bridges VLAs and WAMs through a lightweight latent world model. By connecting the semantic understanding of pretrained VLAs with explicit future prediction, WAVE-0 allows anticipated action consequences to directly guide action generation. Built on a pretrained VLA, its 257M world model translates VLM-generated latent action plans into predicted future representations that condition the action expert, unifying latent planning, future prediction, and action generation. The world model is trained directly on ground-truth robot actions with a counterfactual ranking objective, requiring neither pixel reconstruction nor large-scale video pretraining. WAVE-0 achieves success rates of 91.47% on RoboTwin 2.0 and 98.7% on LIBERO, along with 88.0%, 61.4%, and 75.0% on LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro, and LIBERO-Para, respectively. On real-world tasks, it improves the success rate of $π_{0.5}$ from 38.3% to 73.3%. These results demonstrate strong manipulation performance and generalization across diverse distribution shifts.

title: UniW(A)M: A Unified Mixture-of-Experts Framework for World and World-Action Models
abstract: World models (WMs) and world-action models (WAMs) focus on future world prediction and executable action generation, respectively. Although these models learn shared physical dynamics and interaction semantics from embodied trajectories, they are typically trained in isolation, which restricts knowledge reuse between prediction and control. The central challenge is therefore to develop a unified learning framework that shares these dynamics while preserving the distinct modeling capabilities required by each paradigm. We propose UniW(A)M, a mixture-of-experts world-(action) model built upon diffusion Transformers that unifies action-conditioned world modeling and diverse WAM variants. Shared experts capture common dynamics, while atomic capability experts are reused across interfaces so that each interface keeps its own conditional pathway. At deployment, a plug-in adaptive interface router (PAIR) learns from a small subset of target-task chunk scenarios to select a suitable WAM interface for each execution chunk, balancing task success and execution efficiency while keeping the backbone frozen. We evaluate UniW(A)M on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and three real-world manipulation tasks, where it achieves 88.3% average real-world success versus 76.7% for the strongest baseline. On WorldArena, it leads action-conditioned world modeling on all three tasks. AC-WM co-training contributes to action generation on every action interface and PAIR raises OOD success from 63.3% to 76.7%.

title: Toward human-centered AI-assisted terminology work
abstract: Abstract Generative AI is likely to transform terminology work by creating new opportunities for automation. At the same time, it raises concerns about the future of terminologists and terminological resources, as efficiency pressures may encourage excessive automation based on the perception that human expertise can be replaced by AI. However, large language models remain unreliable for terminological purposes due to errors, hallucinations, and various forms of bias, making terminologists indispensable for ensuring the accuracy and reliability of terminological data. This paper argues that human-centered AI, an approach that emphasizes that AI’s primary goal should be to contribute to human well-being, provides a framework for maximizing the benefits of generative AI while mitigating its risks. It contends that high levels of automation and meaningful human control are compatible and desirable, and that AI should enhance terminologists’ capabilities while preserving their agency and decision-making authority. The implications of AI-assisted terminology work are examined through three interrelated dimensions: the augmented terminologist, ethical AI, and human-centered design. In particular, the paper addresses how AI integration reshapes the role of the terminologist, affects professional values and working conditions, requires the management of AI-generated bias, and calls for the design of AI tools around the terminologist’s needs. The paper concludes that a human-centered orientation is necessary to ensure that AI strengthens, rather than undermines, the essential role of terminology work in supporting specialized communication and the accurate transmission of knowledge across languages and cultures.

title: Sampled-Based Guided Quantum Walk: Non-variational quantum algorithm for combinatorial optimization
abstract: We introduce SamBa-GQW, a novel quantum algorithm for solving binary combinatorial optimization problems of arbitrary degree with no use of any classical optimizer. The algorithm is based on a continuous-time quantum walk on the solution space represented as a graph. The walker explores the solution space to find its way to vertices that minimize the cost function of the optimization problem. The key novelty of our algorithm is an offline classical sampling protocol that gives information about the spectrum of the problem Hamiltonian. Then, the extracted information is used to guide the walker to high quality solutions via a quantum walk with a time-dependent hopping rate. We investigate the performance of SamBa-GQW on several quadratic problems, namely MaxCut, maximum independent set, portfolio optimization, and higher-order polynomial problems such as LABS, MAX- k -SAT and a quartic reformulation of the travelling salesperson problem. We empirically demonstrate that SamBa-GQW finds high quality approximate solutions on problems up to a size of n = 30 qubits by only sampling poly( n ) states among 2 n possible decisions. Furthermore, SamBa-GQW compares in par with classically optimized variational approaches, such as the variational guided quantum walk and QAOA (the latter when run on deep circuits). This places Samba-GQW as a promising heuristic to tackle combinatorial problems beyond the NISQ regime.

title: RoboFQE: Rollout-Free Evaluation of Visual Robot Policies from Offline Trajectories
abstract: Evaluating robot policies before deployment typically requires producing new trajectories through real-world execution, simulators, or learned world models. These rollout-based approaches impose infrastructure requirements; simulator and world-model evaluators additionally face prediction errors that can compound over the evaluation horizon. In this paper, we study off-policy evaluation as an alternative to rollout-based robot-policy evaluation methods. Specifically, we introduce RoboFQE, an evaluator that estimates the discounted expected return of a target policy from offline robot trajectories without estimating a behavior-policy density, combining fitted Q-evaluation with a pretrained vision foundation model and learned terminal success annotation to bridge the gap between standard OPE benchmarks and continuous-control visual manipulation. Controlled experiments across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks show that RoboFQE produces accurate discounted-return estimates and preserves policy rankings even on long-horizon manipulation tasks where video world-model evaluators are degraded by autoregressive prediction errors. Ablation experiments show that pretrained vision encoders substantially outperform from-scratch alternatives, particularly on long-horizon tasks, and that learned terminal success annotation enables evaluation without ground-truth reward labels with only slight reduction of accuracy.

title: PINNeAPPle: A Python platform for physics-informed machine learning with physics-based trust checks
abstract: PINNeAPPle: Physics-Informed Machine Learning and Scientific Computing PINNeAPPle is an open-source framework for physics-informed machine learning (Physics AI) and scientific computing, designed to facilitate the development, integration, and evaluation of machine learning methods for physical systems governed by ordinary and partial differential equations (ODEs and PDEs). The framework aims to bridge scientific computing, numerical simulation, physical modeling, and machine learning through a composable and extensible software architecture. Rather than replacing established numerical solvers or promoting a single model family, PINNeAPPle provides a foundation for combining physics-based knowledge, computational methods, and learning-based models within reproducible scientific workflows. Key capabilities Physics-informed learning: Tools and abstractions for incorporating governing equations, physical constraints, and differential operators into machine learning workflows. Multiple model paradigms: A framework designed to accommodate physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), neural operators, and other learning architectures for scientific problems. Composable scientific workflows: Reusable components for connecting data, physical representations, models, transformations, and training procedures. Scientific computing integration: An extensible foundation for connecting machine learning methods with numerical simulation and domain-specific computational tools. Reproducible experimentation: A software-oriented approach to organizing computational experiments, evaluating methods, and supporting systematic comparisons. Open-source extensibility: Modular design intended to support research, collaborative development, and application-specific extensions. Motivation Scientific machine learning increasingly requires more than isolated neural network architectures. Practical applications must account for governing equations, boundary and initial conditions, data representations, numerical methods, computational constraints, and evaluation protocols. PINNeAPPle addresses this integration challenge by providing reusable software components and a common framework for developing physics-aware learning systems. Its broader objective is to make scientific machine learning more accessible, composable, and reusable across scientific and engineering domains. Applications Potential application areas include computational fluid dynamics (CFD), heat transfer, solid mechanics, inverse problems, parameter estimation, surrogate modeling, reduced-order modeling, uncertainty quantification, and engineering design optimization. Intended audience PINNeAPPle is intended for researchers, scientific software developers, computational scientists, and engineers working at the intersection of machine learning, applied mathematics, physics, and numerical simulation. Availability and citation Source code, installation instructions, documentation, and development resources are available through the project's GitHub repository. This record identifies the PINNeAPPle software release archived in Zenodo. For reproducibility, cite the specific version used in your research and consult the corresponding release documentation for implementation details and supported functionality.

title: Order-Consistent Latent Geometry for Reliable Short-Horizon Planning in World Models
abstract: Latent planners often rank candidate action sequences by terminal Euclidean distance to a goal latent. Exact agreement with transition distance would make this score ideal, but is stronger than planning requires: along a transition-shortest rollout, the essential requirement is that latent distance does not reverse true transition progress. We show that this pathwise no-reversal requirement is precisely the classical self-approaching condition. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to identify self-approachingness as a planner-facing compatibility condition for terminal Euclidean latent planning and to connect its violation to an exact finite-horizon candidate-order reversal. Because visual world models predict discrete latent sequences, we analyze their polygonal interpolation. We prove that an acute bend creates a nonempty region in which terminal Euclidean distance ranks a transition-worse candidate ahead of one that makes genuine progress, even under exact rollouts. We further interpret latent dimension as angular capacity through a classical spherical-code bound. A controlled six-branch experiment, including a zero-padded three-dimensional baseline, validates the predicted ordering failure and separates angular arrangement from ambient dimensionality.

title: Operator Surrogates
abstract: This chapter provides a mathematical introduction to operator surrogates, which are finite-parametric maps approximating complex (typically nonlinear) operators between infinite-dimensional (function) spaces. A typical approach to constructing operator surrogates is the encoder-approximator-decoder paradigm, whereby infinite-dimensional inputs are mapped to a finite-dimensional latent space, processed, and then mapped back to the infinite-dimensional output space. We discuss various methods for creating efficient representation systems, including stable linear frameworks like Banach frames and data-driven techniques such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Active Subspaces, and nonlinear autoencoders. Subsequently, we survey key surrogate architectures, contrasting spectral methods, based on polynomial chaos expansions and related technologies, with more recent neural network approaches. We further discuss architectures that do not rely on representation systems, such as Fourier Neural Operators and transformers. We elaborate on their relationship and how they relate to other neural network operator surrogates, particularly those obtained by so-called "algorithm-unrolling". Additionally, we provide an introduction to the theoretical analysis of approximation and generalization errors. We explain how underlying low-dimensional structures, provided for example by holomorphy, are essential to overcome the so-called "curse of dimensionality": this refers to the fact that the complexity of numerical algorithms tends to increase exponentially in the problem dimensionality. We present convergence rate bounds for holomorphic operators that depend on the number of trainable parameters and the regularity of the input and output data. Throughout, we prioritize intuition over detailed technical proofs and provide precise pointers to the literature for detailed arguments.

title: Model-adaptive simulation of moment models with applications in shallow free-surface flows and rarefied gases
abstract: Many complex physical systems are described by high-dimensional partial differential equations (PDEs), whose numerical simulation can be computationally expensive. Lower-dimensional moment models offer a way to reduce this cost by retaining the essential physical behaviour while representing the system with a smaller number of variables. Their hierarchical structure makes them particularly suitable for adaptive simulations, in which the model resolution is varied in space and time according to the local physical complexity. This thesis develops a general framework for space- and time-adaptive simulation of moment models with a hierarchical structure. The framework includes methods for estimating the error introduced by reducing the model order and for coupling moment models of different orders within a single computational domain. It is applied to two classes of multiscale physical problems: shallow free-surface flows and rarefied gas dynamics. For shallow free-surface flows, a hyperbolic radially symmetric moment model is first developed, providing stable and increasingly accurate results with increasing model order. Next, an adaptive framework for hierarchical shallo water moment models is described. The adaptive framework is then used to dynamically select the model order in space and time, achieving accurate simulations while reducing computational cost by up to 60%. For rarefied gas dynamics, the adaptive framework is applied to a nonlinear hyperbolic kinetic moment model, with model selection based directly on the difference between successive model orders. The resulting simulations remain accurate compared with high-order models and benchmark solutions while reducing computational cost by up to 40%. Overall, the thesis demonstrates that adaptive moment models can provide an effective balance between physical detail and computational efficiency for multiscale simulations.

title: LoopWAM: Closed-Loop Generalist Policy Improvement from Deployment Rollouts
abstract: Scaling expert demonstrations alone does not enable generalist robot policies to improve from deployment. Real-world rollouts contain successes, suboptimal behavior, and failures: imitating every recorded action can reinforce poor behavior, while filtering out failures discards evidence of physical interactions and their consequences. We introduce \textbf{LoopWAM}, a closed-loop world-action model that learns directly from this full quality spectrum, using rollouts from both itself and other deployed policies. Source-dependent noise sampling unifies behavior learning and action-conditioned world modeling, while quality steering and quality-weighted supervision retain full video supervision across qualities and regulate action imitation. Video and action tokens interact throughout parallel denoising, allowing learned consequences to inform action generation directly. On RoboChallenge Table30-V2, three deployment-and-training rounds raise success from 23.67\% to 43.33\%, a 19.7-percentage-point gain, with a final score of 56.80. LoopWAM also achieves 94.5\% average success on RoboTwin~2.0 and 49.5\% overall success on RoboCasa365 without additional embodied pretraining, obtaining the best overall results among the compared methods across all three benchmarks. On challenging shirt folding task, two rounds of deployment-driven improvement after single-task post-training raise success from 13.20\% to 55.56\%. These results demonstrate closed-loop improvement from mixed-quality experience under both multi-task learning and single-task post-training. \href{https://loop-wam.github.io/}{\textcolor{orange}{Project Page}}

title: Higher-Order Boundary Conditions for Atomistic Dislocation Simulations
abstract: Abstract. We present a higher-order boundary condition for atomistic simulations of dislocations that address the slow convergence of standard supercell methods. The method is based on a multipole expansion of the equilibrium displacement, combining continuum predictor solutions with discrete moment corrections. The continuum predictors are computed by solving a hierarchy of singular elliptic PDEs via a Galerkin spectral method, while moment coefficients are evaluated from force-moment identities with controlled approximation error. A key feature is the coupling between accurate continuum predictors and moment evaluations, enabling the construction of systematically improvable high-order boundary conditions. We thus design novel algorithms, and numerical results for screw and edge dislocations confirm the predicted convergence rates in geometry and energy norms, with reduced finite-size effects and moderate computational cost.

title: High-fidelity Three-Dimensional Flow Field Reconstruction Driven by Turbulent Fluid Dynamics
abstract: High-fidelity three-dimensional turbulent flow fields are essential for scientific and engineering analyses, yet obtaining them through direct numerical simulation or high-resolution measurements remains expensive. Super-resolution reconstruction from coarse-grained data therefore offers a promising alternative, but remains fundamentally challenging because fine-scale structures are intrinsically three-dimensional and dynamically coupled across scales. Existing data-driven approaches still struggle to recover multiscale volumetric structures and their coherent temporal evolution. To address these limitations, we propose a turbulence-aware framework for time-resolved three-dimensional flow reconstruction. The framework couples a multiscale neural operator, designed to recover volumetric structures, with a state space model to promote temporal consistency in the reconstructed dynamics. In addition, Navier-Stokes residuals are incorporated as soft constraints to regularize the reconstruction toward physically plausible dynamics. A mixture-of-experts mechanism is also introduced to support unsupervised adaptation to unknown coarse-graining. Across evaluations on canonical turbulent systems and atmospheric reanalysis data, the proposed framework reduces reconstruction errors relative to learning-based and classical baselines, while better preserving multiscale spatial structure and coherent temporal evolution. These results validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in reconstructing high-fidelity three-dimensional flow fields from coarse-grained data.

title: Grid or Nodes? Probing Object Memory in World Models Under Partial Observability
abstract: A robot's world model must remember objects that leave the camera's view. FloWM, a learned world model, keeps them in a spatial grid of features that it moves with five built-in velocities. A node memory instead keeps each object's position and velocity as numbers. We compare them in FloWM's own block world, with an oracle-fed Kalman tracker as the node memory. How the grid is read changes its score: a single-cell probe finds 66% of out-of-view blocks, while FloWM's own probe 89%. FloWM also scores 8 points higher in view although no frame is shown, which we attribute to its write-back of its own predictions. Out of view, the tracker reaches FloWM's range in 14KB against 5.6MB, with no probe. On diagonal motion, outside its five velocities, FloWM finds 11% of blocks even after fine-tuning, while the unchanged tracker keeps 93%. Faster blocks defeat both until one more allowed speed takes the tracker to 94%, where FloWM's built-in shifts would need 25 copies of its grid. A learned node memory must still replace the oracles and handle velocity under noise, long gaps, and the bounce.

title: GreenWAM: A World Foundation Model for Robotics
abstract: A robot needs a world model that predicts how its actions will change the scene and a policy that chooses those actions. Models are usually built and evaluated for only one of these roles, and every robot records its actions in its own format. We ask whether one robot world model can serve both roles across different bodies, and what makes this work. We present GreenWAM, a world foundation model for robotics, together with the recipe that produces it: (1) a shared anatomical action space that describes 20 robot families, from bimanual arms to dexterous humanoids, in common joint coordinates; (2) joint training on these families in visual, action-conditioned and world-action modes; and (3) policies that split an action expert off the generator. As a world model, GreenWAM attains top-tier trajectory, depth and 3D accuracy on WorldArena 1.0, ahead of every world-action model and video generator in our comparison. As a policy, it scores among the top entries of the RoboTwin 2.0 leaderboard, reaches the highest zero-shot LIBERO-plus success among the compared methods and is competitive with dedicated vision-language-action and world-action policies on CALVIN and LIBERO. We further adapt GreenWAM to a real humanoid, where it succeeds more often than policies adapted from $π_{0.5}$ and from Cosmos 3 Edge, and distill it into a single-step policy for real-time control. Controlled experiments yield three findings: robot specialization improves world prediction and control together; an action expert helps when split off at the start of adaptation; and keeping world-model modes during policy adaptation preserves robustness to scene changes.

title: Global-in-time Spectral Duhamel-Picard Method for Post-Exposure Bake Simulation and Physics-Informed Neural Operators for EUV Lithography
abstract: We present a global-in-time spectral Duhamel-Picard method with polynomial expansions for post-exposure bake (PEB) simulation. The coupled acid-quencher reaction-diffusion equations are reformulated as nonlinear Volterra integral equations using the Duhamel principle. Full trajectories are represented by finite polynomial expansions, with temporal coefficient fields determined over the bake interval by Anderson-accelerated Picard iteration, thereby avoiding sequential time marching. In 3-D PEB simulations, we employ Chebyshev and Legendre temporal bases while evaluating the Duhamel integrals using the corresponding Gaussian quadrature rules. We demonstrate that the proposed method simulates a large domain of $1200\times1200\times100$ voxels on the order of one minute. The representation is further incorporated into a physics-informed neural operator (PINO) with a mixed-transform variant of a factorized Fourier neural operator, which is trained without precomputed solution trajectories. Together, the integral formulation and its PINO extension enable accelerated, time-marching-free prediction of concentration fields at arbitrary times within the bake interval.

title: Generative Quantum Search for Combinatorial Optimization: Learning Shallow Quantum Samplers for Classically Refined Solution Subspaces
abstract: Abstract We port the Generative Quantum Eigensolver + Quantum-Selected Configuration Interaction (GQE+QSCI) architecture from quantum chemistry to combinatorial graph optimization. Our framework, GQO+QSS (Generative Quantum Optimization + Quantum-Selected Search), follows the same principle: ML generates circuit programs, quantum samplers produce bitstrings, classical recovery repairs and expands them into a restricted subspace, and a classical solver finds the optimum within that subspace. We formalize the key quantity as the recovery-basin mass pr(qθ,G) = Prx∼qθ [x ∈ Ar(G)], where Ar(G) = {x : Er(R(x))∩X∗(G) ̸= ∅} is the preimage of the optimal set under repair R and r-flip expansion Er. Under B independent shots, success probability becomes Psuccess = 1 − (1 − pr)B. The quantum-benefit question reduces to: does pr(qquantum,G) > pr(qclassical,G)? We test this on MaximumWeighted Independent Set (MWIS) with a preregistered, frozen protocol. All 150 ground truths are certified with CBC + brute-force verification. Exact recovery-basin masks are enumerated for all n ≤ 20 instances. Nine samplers are compared on a held-out test set: uniform, greedy, simulated annealing, tabu search, multi-start local search, Metropolis, warm-start QAOA, oracle QAOA, and a matched learned classical policy. Key findings: 1. Tabu search dominates at all sizes (pr = 0.82–0.94), followed by simulated annealing. All quantum samplers and the learned classical policy lose to both at every problem size under the frozen test protocol. 2. Oracle QAOA loses to SA under fair evaluation: With random QAOA configurations (not per-instance optimized), oracle QAOA achieves pr = 0.014 at n = 28 vs SA’s 0.088. The earlier positive result (pr = 0.185 vs 0.130) required per-instance best-of-50 configuration selection—an oracle upper bound, not a deployable method. 3. Learned classical policy matches oracle QAOA: A matched 140K-parameter classical policy achieves pr = 0.005–0.101, comparable to oracle QAOA’s 0.014–0.113. The quantum circuit’s proposal distribution provides no structural advantage over a matched learned classical model in this setting. 4. Recovery-basin masks reveal the phase structure: At r = 2, uniform-sampling Precover drops from 0.975 (n = 16) to 0.775 (n = 20) at B = 200, identifying the regime where sampler quality matters. 5. Hardware robustness without advantage: 136 cores on Piast-Q show 93.4% recovery consistency between QPU and simulator, but no basin-mass advantage. This is a falsification study: Under rigorous, preregistered evaluation with matched learned baselines, shallow QAOA-derived proposal distributions do not outperform matched classical proposal models, and both lose to strong classical baselines (SA, tabu). The earlier positive oracle result was an artifact of per-instance configuration selection. We claim no quantum advantage.

title: Generalized Forcing Method: Generation of diverse data for training linear transport PDE closure models
abstract: This archive contains the reproduction data, reduced models, plotting scripts, and precomputed figures for the paper “Generalized Forcing Method: Generation of Diverse Data for Training Linear Transport PDE Closure Models.” The archive includes five model-evaluation cases: two homogeneous parallel-flow cases, two inhomogeneous-flow cases, and one homogeneous random-flow case. The provided scripts evaluate the reduced models against the included test solutions and reproduce the RMSE convergence plots and eGFM dataset-summary plots reported in the manuscript. The release is intended for figure reproduction and model-evaluation verification. It does not include the full simulation code or the model-fitting code.

title: ForkCast: Predictive Recovery for Vision-Language-Action Policies via Counterfactual Futures
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies perform manipulation tasks using camera images and language instructions, but object slip or visual occlusion can disrupt execution. Recovery is typically learned during policy training or delegated to a monitor that triggers a scripted repair after detecting a failure. We introduce ForkCast, a predictive recovery framework that compares counterfactual futures to determine whether and how to intervene in a frozen VLA policy. At each decision point, ForkCast evaluates three candidates: executing the policy's nominal action chunk (Commit), adjusting the camera viewpoint (Reobserve), and replanning the arm trajectory (Replan). A candidate-conditioned world model forecasts the latent outcome of each candidate at a common future horizon, and a shared task-progress head scores the predicted outcomes. By evaluating the policy's own continuation alongside the repair candidates, a single comparison based on task progress determines both whether and how to intervene, without a failure detector, an intervention threshold, or updates to the VLA backbone. On five simulated RoboTwin 2.0 tasks with injected occlusion and object slip, ForkCast increases pooled success from 13.3% for the frozen $π_{0.5}$ policy to 30.0% and transfers to two additional VLA backbones without updating ForkCast. After adaptation on real-robot candidate rollouts, ForkCast also improves success over the base policy under both clean and visibility-limited conditions. Code will be released to benefit the research community.

title: ForceWAM: Decoupling Future and Response Learning from Demo and Play Data for Contact-Rich Manipulation
abstract: Expert demonstrations show how to complete contact-rich tasks, but provide limited coverage of how interaction forces respond to different actions. Task-agnostic play provides broader experience of contact dynamics without specifying task goals. To fully leverage these two types of data, we introduce ForceWAM, a force world action model that decouples knowledge of task-compatible interaction outcomes from knowledge of how local actions change contact. A world model learns from successful demonstrations to jointly predict future video and six-axis force/torque trajectories. Together, these futures describe the expected evolution of motion and contact during the task. A separate inverse dynamics model (IDM) learns from both task and play, mapping current observations and recorded visual-wrench futures to their associated robot actions. Play data thus provide knowledge of force responses for goal-directed execution. At deployment, the IDM reactively translates generated futures into actions, reusing them with fresh wrench feedback between world-model updates. Across real-robot force-regulated sliding, box flipping with and without disturbances, and ring placement, ForceWAM achieves $85$-$95\%$ mean success, surpassing world-modeling and reactive baselines. Our experiments further show that adding task-agnostic play data improves success by $15$-$45$ percentage points, demonstrating its value for learning contact-rich execution. Project page and code are available at https://force-wam.github.io/.

title: Educational Recommender Systems for Metacognitive and Self-Regulated Learning Support: An Algorithmic Systematic Review
abstract: Recommender systems (RSs) increasingly support self-regulated learning (SRL) through personalized resources, feedback, and strategy recommendations. However, traditional content based and collaborative filtering approaches suffer from cold start problems, while machine or deep learning methods raise interpretability concerns and LLM-based recommenders require evaluation of explanation faithfulness and hallucinations. This systematic review examines SRL-oriented recommender algorithms from an algorithmic and pedagogical perspective. Six databases were searched using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, yielding 25 eligible studies published between 2020 and 2025. The review traces the evolution from traditional filtering methods to machine or deep learning and emerging LLM-based approaches. Three major challenges were identified: cold start, limited explainability, and LLM hallucinations, alongside gaps in learner system interaction and metacognitive scaffolding. Future SRL-RS research should compare algorithms under controlled data sparsity, evaluate explanation faithfulness and source curation, preserve learner agency, integrate SRL strategies across three phases, and longitudinally assess SRL skill maintenance and transfer.

title: Constrained bilinear optimal control of reactive evolution equations
abstract: We consider constrained bilinear optimal control of second-order linear evolution partial differential equations (PDEs) with a reaction term on the half line, where control arises as a time-dependent reaction coefficient and constraints are imposed on the state and control variables. These PDEs represent a wide range of physical phenomena in fluid flow, heat, and mass transfer. Existing computational methods for this type of control problems only consider constraints on the control variable and lack global convergence guarantee. In this paper, we propose a novel optimize-then-discretize framework for computing constrained bilinear optimal control with both state and control constraints. Unlike existing methods that derive optimality conditions directly from the PDE constraint, this framework first replaces the PDE constraint with an equivalent integral representation of the PDE solution and then derives optimality conditions for the reformulated problem. The integral representation, derived from the unified transform method, does not involve differential operators, and thus explicit expressions for necessary conditions of optimality can be derived using the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions for infinite-dimensional optimization. Discretizing the optimality conditions results in a system of finite-dimensional smooth nonlinear equations, which can be efficiently solved using existing algorithms with guaranteed global convergence at a quadratic rate. This is in contrast with discretize-then-optimize methods that discretize the PDE first and then solve the optimality conditions of the approximated finite-dimensional problem. Computational results for two applications, namely nuclear reactivity control and water quality treatment in a reactor, are presented to illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

title: Benchmarking time-series foundation models for multitask predictive maintenance in digital twins
abstract: Digital twins provide a comprehensive virtual representation of physical assets, distinguishing themselves from traditional control systems through long-term diagnostic and prognostic capabilities. However, current digital twin architectures face a critical scalability barrier: they rely on dedicated, single-purpose models for every distinct query, task, physical scale, and operating context, resulting in unsustainable engineering overhead. To address this limitation, there is an urgent need for flexible, general-purpose analytical backbones capable of interpreting diverse time-series data without constant reconfiguration. While time-series foundation models (TSFMs) offer a potential solution through large-scale pre-training, their capacity to generalize beyond forecasting to the complex, multi-objective downstream requirements remains largely unverified. Addressing this challenge, this study utilizes the Commercial Modular Aero-Propulsion System Simulation (C-MAPSS) dataset to benchmark three representative multi-task TSFMs (MOMENT, UniTS, and FFTS) across four downstream tasks (imputation, anomaly detection, classification, and regression) within a predictive maintenance context. We frame this evaluation as a rigorous test of generalization, assessing whether architecturally distinct TSFMs can adapt to distinct downstream tasks such as regression for remaining useful life estimation. Our benchmark reveals that although TSFMs generalize across all evaluated tasks, they do not yet match specialized baselines trained only on the C-MAPSS dataset. We further find that the three backbones separate most clearly when adaptation is restricted to a small set of parameters, where the model combining channel-mixing with explicit task tokens adapts best to multi-objective use, including regression, a task absent from all three pre-training objectives; in the zero-shot regime no single backbone leads across tasks. Because the models differ simultaneously in architecture, capacity, pre-training corpus, and patch size, we report these as patterns observed under one shared benchmarking framework rather than as isolated causes. The evaluation is conducted on raw sensor series alone, without the semantic or physics-based components of a mature digital twin, so these findings provide an empirical baseline for the analytical layer such a system would host rather than an evaluation of digital twin integration itself.

title: Adjoint method versus physics-informed neural networks in PDE-constrained inverse problems
abstract: Inverse problems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs) are central to computational mechanics and are commonly solved by adjoint-based optimization, while physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a flexible alternative. Their relative performance remains difficult to assess because the two approaches are often compared under different formulations, parameterizations, optimizers, and regularization choices. We present a controlled comparison of adjoint optimization and PINNs for PDE-constrained inverse problems. From a common abstract formulation, we instantiate both methods on identical domains, governing equations, observation models, and regularization terms, while matching the optimizer, unknown parameterization, and arithmetic precision wherever applicable. The benchmarks include unsteady Burgers, noisy Darcy permeability inversion, three-dimensional Allen–Cahn reaction identification, and unsteady Navier–Stokes viscosity identification. The results show that the representation of the unknown largely determines the preferred method: grid-based fields favor the discrete adjoint, whereas neural representations are native to PINNs and relevant for closure and constitutive modeling. For time-dependent problems, adjoint inversion can be dominated by trajectory storage and differentiation, while PINNs provide satisfactory reconstructions at lower cost. A PINN-warm-started adjoint strategy then recovers adjoint-level accuracy at about half the cost.

title: The field equations of penalized non-parametric regression
abstract: Abstract We view penalized risks through the lens of the calculus of variations. We consider risks comprised of a fitness-term (e.g. MSE) and a gradient-based penalty and search for the minima of such risks. After establishing the Euler-Lagrange field equations as a systematic approach to finding minimizers of risks involving only first derivatives, we proceed to exemplify this approach to the MSE penalized by the integral over the squared $$\ell ^2$$ ℓ 2 -norm of the gradient of the regression function. The minimizer of this risk is given as the solution to a second order inhomogeneous partial differential equation, where the inhomogeneity is given as the conditional expectation of the target variable conditioned on the features. We discuss properties of the field equations and practical implications thereof, which also apply to the classical ridge penalty for linear models, and embed our findings into the existing literature. In particular, we find that we can recover the Rudin-Osher-Fatemi model for image-denoising, if we consider the features as deterministic and evenly distributed. We proceed to derive the minima of the population-MAE and the Cramer Distance using the calculus of variations. Last, we exemplify the usage of the field equations for post-training regularization in a simulation study.

title: Sampling from Neural Operator Priors to Solve Partial Differential Equations
abstract: Guided sampling with sparse observations and PDE residuals has recently been combined with neural operator priors to solve partial differential equations in function space, their natural setting. We pair such a prior with pseudo-bootstrap sequential Monte Carlo (pBS SMC), a guided sampling framework that accommodates proposals without tractable densities, and introduce a new proposal by adapting the DPM++ algorithm to the guidance setting. Across five benchmark PDE systems this proposal attains the best error--time trade-off at every step count tested, and wrapping it in pBS gives the lowest error on most inverse-problem settings, with the largest gains when few sampling steps are used.

title: Same Problem, Different Field: Cross-Domain Solution Import via Domain-Stripped Computational Fingerprints
abstract: The same underlying computational problem is solved across unrelated fields under different names: recursive Bayesian state estimation appears as a “Kalman filter” in control, “Bayesian forecasting” in pharmacokinetics, and “data assimilation” in geoscience. Topical and citation-based scientific embeddings cannot see this shared problem. We distill each paper once into a domain- and method-name-stripped faceted computational fingerprint, a free-text mechanism skeleton plus controlled computational facets. We define a tunable, facet-selectable similarity over it. The goal is solution import: surface cross-field pairs solving the same problem, so a bespoke implementation can be swapped for another field’s standard, specialized solver. On a benchmark of 18 method families across 109 papers, the skeleton lifts cross-domain retrieval average precision over the abstract from 0.222 to 0.513, and the whole fingerprint reaches 0.557. Strikingly, four trained scientific embedders all fall below plain abstract+TF-IDF: they encode topical and citation similarity, the wrong signal for this task. The gain is the representation: the abstract-to-skeleton swap lifts every embedder, and the pipeline is one cached LLM call per paper plus a cheap embedder. An interventional re-skin / math-edit test shows the fingerprint tracks the computation, not the field. On a 501-paper wild corpus, known twins dominate the top of the ranking (23 of the top 30); with planted pairs excluded from the results, three blind LLM judges rate 3 of the top 5 and 8 of the top 30 pairs genuine import candidates, and 0 of 30 random ones. The human verification is the four executed imports: in one, an open standard solver reproduces a bespoke clinical dosing engine’s output. We release the benchmark, the code, and the distillation prompt.

title: SPLICE: Sparse Physics Library Identification and Compositional Expansion
abstract: Neural operator splitting composes a library of neural operators, one per physical mechanism, into zero-shot simulators of new equations. Existing approaches, however, require these mechanisms and their labels to be specified in advance. We ask whether a pretrained library can instead be adapted and grown from unlabeled trajectories in which multiple mechanisms act simultaneously. We introduce SPLICE, a framework that discovers operators without mechanism labels on mixture data. The contributions of the candidate operators to each trajectory are inferred by solving a convex optimization problem. A calibrated test then assigns each discovered operator the mechanism it implements. Failure cases are also detectable, when the library lacks the required physics or when mechanisms are insufficiently separable. Across one and two dimensional systems, the discovered operators recover mechanisms from unlabeled mixtures and compose into zero-shot simulators of unseen equations; a frozen library can also grow an operator for physics absent from pretraining, without labels and without forgetting. On Navier-Stokes, the discovered operators compose about as accurately as their supervised counterparts.

title: Niet-intrusieve parametrische modelreductie voor niet-lineaire structurele mechanica met behoud van de onderliggende fysica
abstract: High-fidelity Finite Element (FE) models enable accurate simulation of nonlinear structural systems but remain computationally expensive for many-query and Digital Twin applications. Model Order Reduction (MOR) provides efficient Reduced Order Models (ROMs), although conventional nonlinear and parametric approaches often require intrusive access to the underlying FE solver. Conversely, non-intrusive data-driven methods offer greater flexibility but generally lack guarantees on the preservation of physical and numerical properties. This PhD develops Physics-Augmented, non-intrusive MOR methodologies for nonlinear and parametric structural mechanics. The proposed POD-TD-pICNN frameworks combine Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) with Physics-Augmented Neural Architectures (PANNs) that learn the reduced potential energy while enforcing relevant physical properties by construction. Internal forces and tangent operators are obtained through differentiation, preserving important properties such as equilibrium consistency, symmetry, positive semi-definiteness, and hyperelastic structure. The methodologies are validated on nonlinear academic benchmarks and a large-scale industrial structural application, demonstrating the potential of Physics-Augmentation to bridge classical physics-based MOR and data-driven Machine Learning.

title: Intelligent Pre-Drill and Real-Time Optimization of Drilling Parameters
abstract: Abstract Optimizing drilling parameters throughout the drilling process is essential for improving drilling efficiency, extending bit life, and advancing drilling automation. This paper presents an intelligent closed-loop drilling parameter optimization framework that integrates Pre-Drill planning with Real-Time optimization to enable coordinated decision-making for bit selection, drilling parameter control, and wear risk management in complex formations. A drilling database containing approximately 17,500 records from 61 bit runs was established after removing non-drilling intervals. The database integrates bit design parameters, operational parameters, and formation characteristics, including lithology and unconfined compressive strength (UCS). To overcome the lack of continuous downhole wear observations, a three-stage wear reconstruction method was developed to generate continuous cutter wear evolution, and a unified wear index was defined by combining inner-row and outer-row wear grades. An Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model was trained to predict the rate of penetration (ROP) under varying drilling conditions, while a Transformer-based sequential model was developed to predict bit wear evolution. Based on these predictive models, a dual-mode optimization strategy was established. Bayesian optimization was first applied to optimize bit selection and drilling parameters before drilling and was subsequently extended to real-time optimization of weight on bit (WOB), rotary speed (RPM), and flow rate. Simulation case studies demonstrate that the optimized solutions can increase average ROP by approximately 10% under field-oriented operating conditions. This work also provides a practical and interpretable solution for intelligent drilling parameter optimization, supporting drilling automation and reducing reliance on experience-based decision making.

title: Inductive bias and out-of-distribution generalization in deep learning surrogates for 2D PDE dynamics
abstract: Abstract Partial differential equations (PDEs) are a foundational tool for modeling physical systems. However, high-fidelity numerical simulations are often computationally intensive, which has prompted the development of surrogate models in the field of scientific machine learning. While recent approaches have achieved high predictive accuracy by employing complex architectures and extensive datasets, many scientific applications offer only a limited number of simulation trajectories. In this study, we examine the impact of architectural inductive biases on the learning of two-dimensional PDE in data-limited settings. Instead of proposing a highly expressive model, we deliberately adopt a simple multi-channel U-Net modified to enforce periodic boundary conditions. In this study, we compare this architecture with transformer-based and UNet variants such as vision transformer (ViT), adaptive fourier neural operator (AFNO), PDE-Transformer (PDE-T), and UNet with Kolmogorov-Arnold Layers (KAN-UNet) under a common training setup across five PDE families. To keep comparisons uniform and to mimic partial observability in real measurements, we train all models on rollouts of a single representative scalar field per system. Despite its simplicity, the adapted U-Net consistently matches or outperforms these more complex models in forecasting accuracy, spectral similarity, and physics-based metrics while requiring substantially less training time. The findings of this study demonstrate that, in scenarios where data is limited, the judicious selection of inductive biases can often prove to be more advantageous than increasing the model complexity for the purpose of learning the dynamics of PDEs.

title: Identifiability of a dissipative knowledge-dynamics model: exact recovery under designed excitation, degeneration on observational data
abstract: Human learning is a dissipative dynamical process: mastery accumulates through practice, decays through forgetting, and propagates across interdependent concepts. We model it as a nonlinear dissipative system of ordinary differential equations whose parameters are mechanistically meaningful (a concept-transfer matrix encoding prerequisite coupling, per-concept forgetting rates, and a saturating practice-response gain), and we study when those parameters can actually be recovered from data. We prove a structural identifiability theorem for the associated inverse problem under explicit excitation conditions, with constructive closed-form recovery for the two-concept case, together with monotonicity, robustness and L-stability results. We derive a semi-implicit L-stable scheme for the dissipative subsystem and a batched solver numerically equivalent to the per-trajectory formulation (bit-exact predictions, gradients to 10−10) yet two orders of magnitude faster, making estimation feasible on cohorts of 105 learners. The empirical study is two-sided. Under the theorem's excitation conditions, synthetic recovery is exact: parameters to machine precision, prerequisite structure at F1=1.0. On large observational benchmarks it is not. An apparently strong recovery, with forgetting rates correlating with topic difficulty at Spearman ρ=0.83, is refuted by four independent controls: it survives destroying the temporal order of the data, is matched by a classical Bayesian baseline, and is unaffected by removing real timestamps. We trace this to the stationary structure of the model and show that it is the degeneration the theorem predicts in the absence of designed excitation. The result delineates a sharp boundary between identifiable and unidentifiable regimes and yields a validation protocol for interpretability claims.

title: Do large language models keep the hedge? Uncertainty preservation when large language models summarize aviation and maritime incident reports
abstract: Safety-incident reports are written with deliberate epistemic caution: A reporter marks what was seen, what was inferred, and what remains unsure, and a dropped hedge can turn a tentative observation into an apparent cause. As large language models take over summarizing such reports for triage, indexing, and search, whether they preserve that caution becomes a property of the safety record itself. This study asks whether models keep a reporter's expressed uncertainty when they summarize, testing two hypotheses fixed before any summary was generated: that models systematically harden uncertainty by default and that an explicit instruction to preserve it overcorrects into softening. Six open-weight models summarized 42 real incident reports, 30 from the United States Aviation Safety Reporting System and 12 from the United Kingdom Marine Accident Investigation Branch, under a plain prompt, a preserve prompt, and a paraphrase of it. Uncertainty change was measured two ways: at the passage level, by a deterministic epistemic-marker lexicon, and at the claim level, by aligning those markers between source and summary, each validated against manual annotation and cross-checked against two independent language-model judges. Under plain summarization, all six models hardened the reporter's uncertainty (claim-level hardening 0.59–0.85), dropping explicit hedges almost entirely (retention about 0.08) while epistemic modal verbs survived far better. The preserve instruction reversed the pattern into over-softening: In a cluster-robust logistic regression, it carried an odds ratio of 0.12 (95% CI [0.03, 0.49], p = 0.003) and held once summary length was controlled, so the change reflects expressed certainty rather than compression. In practical terms, the instruction lowered the predicted probability of hardening from about 0.43 to 0.13 (Cohen's h = 0.69), and the effect held in mixed-effects models and under adverse imputation of the missing outputs. The pattern was directionally consistent across the tested models and both instruction wordings. Automated safety triage that relies on model summaries should measure epistemic fidelity directly and not treat a single preserve instruction as a solution.

title: Digital-Twin-driven textile classification and foreign object recognition in automated sorting systems
abstract: The increasing demand for sustainable textile recycling requires robust automation solutions capable of handling deformable garments and detecting foreign objects in cluttered environments. This work presents a digital twin–driven robotic sorting system that integrates grasp prediction, multi-modal perception, and semantic reasoning for real-world textile classification. A dual-arm robotic cell equipped with RGB-D sensing, capacitive tactile feedback, and collision-aware motion planning autonomously separates garments from an unsorted basket, transfers them to an inspection zone, and classifies them using state-of-the-art Visual Language Models (VLMs). We benchmark nine VLMs from five model families on a dataset of 223 inspection scenarios comprising shirts, socks, trousers, underwear, foreign objects (including garments outside of the aforementioned classes), and empty scenes. The evaluation assesses per-class accuracy, hallucination behavior, and computational performance under practical hardware constraints. Results show that the Qwen model family achieves the highest overall accuracy (up to 87.9 %), with strong foreign object detection performance, while lighter models such as Gemma3 offer competitive speed–accuracy trade-offs for edge deployment. A digital twin combined with MoveIt enables collision-aware path planning and integrates segmented 3D point clouds of inspected garments into the virtual environment for improved manipulation reliability. The presented system demonstrates the feasibility of combining semantic VLM reasoning with conventional grasp detection and digital twin technology for scalable, autonomous textile sorting in realistic industrial settings.

title: Deadline-Aware Virtual Machine Optimization and Task Scheduling in Cloud Computing
abstract: Cloud computing infrastructures in contemporary times were very dependent upon effective task scheduling, smart workload management, and proper VM allocation for offering reliable, high-performance computing services and at the same time achieving optimal operational cost, energy footprint, and physical data centre utilization.Since multi-processor job scheduling among heterogeneous distributed processing nodes is an NP-hard problem of combinatorial optimization without any polynomialtime solution, cloud management systems will be required to use heuristic, meta-heuristic, and hybrid approximation approaches to find nearly optimal mappings of tasks onto the available resources within finite time.In this study, the underlying cloud scheduling structures and their taxonomies (differently analysing compile-time static allocation in contrast with run-time dynamic allocation, independent batch of tasks vs. dependency-based scientific workflows) are explored and multidimensional performance assessment parameters are analysed.In particular, the emphasis is put on QoS provisions, Service Level Agreements, execution cost, makespan, and resource utilization in the cluster.Besides that, operational issues in distributed virtualization platforms are also considered.Among others, these are the complex latency and throughput overheads resulting from runtime VM live migration such as the iterative dirty-memory pre-copying process, secondary storage disk I/O overheads, and uninterrupted network connectivity, along with the critical challenges in multi-tenancy environment, that is, the threat of unapproved VM hopping, noisy neighbour VM's resource poaching behavior, and divergence in cloning configurations on shared network infrastructure.This paper attempts to solve the ongoing conflict between end-user's requirement of deadline guarantee and the provider's requirement of resource optimization through introducing the theoretical and mathematical formulation of a new framework referred to as Deadline-Based VM Optimization (DBVO).DBVO combines dynamic slack-time analysis with earliest completion time metrics to emphasize time-critical tasks, achieve system-wide load balancing, avoid schedule bottlenecks, and SLA violation fines.Moreover, an experimental roadmap to test performance of this new method using CloudSim simulator is outlined.

title: CLNO: Conservative Local Neural Operator for Compressible Flow Prediction
abstract: We propose a conservative local neural operator (CLNO) for accurate and generalizable autoregressive prediction of compressible flows. Building upon the locality and translation invariance of the local neural operator (LNO), CLNO introduces a conservative evolution framework based on local subdomains of fixed physical size, separating local mean-state evolution from fine-scale reconstruction. The flow is encoded into subdomain-integrated conservative states and fine-scale features, while a shared local network predicts interface fluxes for finite-volume updates that enforce discrete conservation. A convolutional reconstruction network recovers fine-scale structures using zero-mean basis functions, preserving the updated local means and providing information for subsequent evolution. To accommodate different physical parameters, Reynolds--Mach number conditioning modulates the encoding, flux-prediction, and reconstruction networks, enabling a single model to learn parameter-dependent dynamics and generalize to unseen parameter combinations without retraining. CLNO supports prediction across spatial resolutions, computational domain sizes, and boundary conditions. Numerical experiments demonstrate improved generalization and competitive or higher accuracy compared with LNO, including order-of-magnitude error reductions in representative cases, at approximately three to five times the inference cost on periodic benchmarks. These results demonstrate accurate, generalizable, and physically consistent flow prediction through conservative local evolution and fine-scale reconstruction.

title: An Efficient Mixed‐Integer Formulation and an Iterative Method for Optimal Control of Switched Systems Under Dwell Time Constraints
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper presents an efficient mixed‐integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) formulation for systems with discrete control inputs under minimum dwell time (MDT) constraints. By viewing such systems as switched systems, the problem is decomposed into a sequence optimization (SO) and a switching time optimization (STO)—the former providing the sequence of the switched system, and the latter calculating the optimal switching times. By limiting the feasible set of SO to subsequences of a master sequence, this formulation requires a small number of binary variables, independent of the number of time discretization nodes. This enables the proposed formulation to provide solutions efficiently, even for a large number of time discretization nodes. To provide even faster solutions, an iterative algorithm is introduced to heuristically solve STO and SO. The proposed approaches are then showcased on four different switched systems, and the results demonstrate the efficiency of the MINLP formulation and the iterative algorithm.

title: A physics-coupled graph neural operator for mid-plane six-component stress tensor field prediction in concrete penetration
abstract: The penetration-resistant design of concrete structures requires the spatiotemporal evolution of the stress field within the target, whereas in design only the strength grade, the geometry and the projectile parameters are known, and the aggregate arrangement is not. Empirical formulae and scalar-output surrogates serve design screening, and mesoscale finite element models resolve the aggregate-scale response, but one solution cannot cover random aggregate samples at scale, and no framework links mesoscale heterogeneity to field-level prediction. A physics-coupled graph neural operator (PC-GNO) is proposed, which learns in function space the evolution of the mid-plane six-component stress tensor field. The training data are generated by full-scale, aggregate-resolved finite element models and comprise 359 cases at the impact velocities of 100, 135 and 165 m/s, corresponding to compressive strengths of 14, 23 and 48 MPa; the data source is verified by laboratory measurements. The coupling strength of message passing is constructed from the impedance contrast across the material interface, and the update is constrained by spectral normalization. Under the single-step primary setting, the mean accuracy of the three levels is 80.16% (91.45%, 77.80% and 71.22%), i.e. 27.81, 42.46 and 34.16 percentage points above the preceding-frame field of the same window; with 20 664 parameters it exceeds the 87.9% of the best Fourier neural operator configuration (about 812 times as many parameters) and the 71.0% of the closed-form linear regression. The output is the complete six-component tensor field rather than a fixed engineering quantity, so that strength criteria and energy indicators follow from one set of weights. For field-level response prediction in concrete penetration, this result provides a data-driven route, with conditions of applicability defined by the training and the evaluation.

title: Shape Optimization for Incompressible Fluid Flows With Diffuse Domain Method
abstract: ABSTRACT Shape optimization plays a central role in scientific and engineering design, where one seeks to improve the performance of a system by altering its geometries subject to the governing partial differential equations (PDEs). This setting poses challenges for traditional numerical methods, as the optimization process may involve grid regeneration on evolving and irregular domains. The diffuse domain method (DDM) provides a flexible alternative by embedding complex geometries into a rectangular background domain using a smooth phase‐field function and then extending the governing PDEs to the new domain. This eliminates the need for re‐meshing and facilitates the implementation of standard finite difference or finite element discretization. In this work, we develop a DDM‐based method for shape optimization for fluid flows governed by the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations. The method incorporates variational formulations of the PDEs, the associated adjoint problem, sensitivity analysis, and gradient‐based optimization strategies within the diffuse domain setting. Numerical experiments show that the DDM approach achieves robust convergence in space. Furthermore, efficient handling of topological changes by the proposed DDM‐based shape optimization method is demonstrated through several benchmark problems. The results highlight its potential as a versatile tool for solving complex shape optimization problems in fluid flows and related applications.

title: RCTs & Human Uplift Studies: Methodological Challenges and Practical Solutions for Frontier AI Evaluation
abstract: Human uplift studies, or studies that measure the effects of AI access on human performance via randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or similar methodologies, increasingly inform frontier AI governance and deployment decisions. While RCT methods are robust in other fields, their interaction with the distinctive properties of frontier AI systems remains underexamined, particularly when results are used to inform high-stakes decisions. We present findings from interviews with 16 expert practitioners with experience conducting human uplift studies in domains including biosecurity, cybersecurity, education, and labor. Across interviews, experts described a recurring tension between the standard causal inference assumptions upon which human uplift studies rely and the object of study itself. Rapidly evolving AI systems, shifting baselines, heterogeneous and changing user proficiency, and porous real-world settings strain assumptions underlying internal, external, and construct validity, complicating the interpretation and appropriate use of uplift evidence. We contribute (1) a synthesis of methodological challenges in human uplift studies, mapped to risks to study validity and classified by their degree of specificity to large language model (LLM) systems, and (2) a mapping from challenges to proposed solutions. By collating expert-identified challenges and solutions, we seek to clarify the interpretive limits and appropriate uses of human uplift evidence, to align evaluation practice with the decisions it informs, and to support more coordinated methodological foundations for AI governance.

title: Open Science, Closed Models: How Funding Shapes AI in Science
abstract: How funding shapes AI engagement in science is poorly understood despite its structural importance. We analyze 104,226 papers (2018–2025), linking funding acknowledgments to how each paper engages with foundation models: whether it extends a model (fine-tunes or builds on it), uses one without modification, or references models only peripherally. We report three findings. First, both private and public funding are associated with greater AI engagement. Public funding is associated with more off-the-shelf and open-weight use, while private funding is associated with greater model extension. Industry cloud credits are associated with less open-weight use, consistent with greater reliance on closed models. Second, industry involvement is associated with model extension, suggesting that corporate resources reach science through coauthorship, though this channel is concentrated in Computer Science and Global North collaborations. Third, the gap across research systems is not one of AI adoption but of control. Off-the-shelf use is rising across fields and country groups, and the least publicly funded group, the Global South, now has the highest share of API-only engagement (0.4% to 10.0% of engaged papers). China shows the opposite profile: the highest public-funding share and lowest API-only engagement, with extension remaining stable as it declines across the Global North. Standard capacity indicators show convergence in AI adoption even as dependence on proprietary infrastructure diverges

title: Mesh-Free Convolution: Learned Spectral Attenuation and Transport
abstract: Learning solution operators for partial differential equations (PDEs) requires models that can represent spatial structure across grids and scales. This becomes especially important in time-dependent problems, where the learned operator is often used autoregressively: each predicted state is fed back as input to predict future states. In this setting, small spatial errors can be repeatedly propagated through the learned dynamics, leading to instability and drift, vitiating long-term solution fidelity. We propose Mesh-Free Convolutions (MFCs), filters defined in continuous space and discretized only at evaluation time. This allows the same learned filters to be applied across resolutions. Rather than imposing a grid-dependent stencil or a fixed spectral cutoff, MFCs learn smooth scale-dependent filtering and include directional terms for transport-like behavior. Across fluid-dynamics and weather-forecasting benchmarks, MFC-based models produce stable long-horizon rollouts, transfer reliably across resolutions, and better preserve long-time statistics. These results suggest that continuous, mesh-free filtering is a useful inductive bias for PDE operator learning, especially in autoregressive prediction.

title: Learned Graph Bases for Neural Operators on Power-System Transients
abstract: Fourier neural operators predict power-system transient trajectories with high accuracy. We extend this line of work by examining the choice of spatial spectral basis, studying both the graph Fourier transform derived from the grid's own coupling network and learnable bases trained from that starting point and from a Fourier control. Evaluated in one controlled pipeline across three protocols spanning unseen fault locations and shifted operating regimes, the learnable bases improve on a parameter- and budget-matched DFT variant by 7-14% in distribution, with per-case significance on both in-distribution protocols and no loss on the third; the gain comes from adaptation rather than from the coordinates alone. We further characterize the regime dependence of this gain, identifying its cause, locus, and continuity, and show that a resolution requires no new model: averaging the learned and frozen variants gives the best shift-robust predictor, while their disagreement provides a label-free alarm that flags every shifted case with no false alarms.

title: LLMs as Representation Generators for Gradient‐Free Scientific Optimization: A Case Study in Battery Fast Charging
abstract: Scientific optimization problems are often characterized by slow, expensive, and non-differentiable evaluations, which severely limit efficient exploration of rich design spaces. In these settings, performance depends not only on the optimizer itself, but also on whether the chosen search space can represent good solutions and whether important design requirements are effectively incorporated into the search. Here, we introduce a gradient-free optimization framework based on large language models (LLMs) that enables the generation and refinement of executable control policies directly from natural language. We propose two complementary paradigms: Prompt-to-Optimizer (P2O), which combines LLM-based structural generation with gradient-free parameter optimization, and Prompt-to-Protocol (P2P), which directly synthesizes fully specified control policies. We apply this framework to battery fast-charging protocol design, a representative slow-feedback optimization problem. Across multiple case studies, our methods outperform conventional approaches restricted to predefined functional forms. In a realistic fast-charging scenario, both approaches improve battery state of health by approximately 4.2% over a representative baseline, with P2P achieving this under matched evaluation budgets. More broadly, our results suggest that LLMs can serve as representation generators that expand the hypothesis space of scientific optimization, enabling efficient search in domains where evaluations are costly, and gradients are unavailable.

title: Grounded but Misleading: Evaluating Semantic Alignment in AI-Generated Security Explanations
abstract: Online scams increasingly leverage fluent and context-aware social-engineering strategies, creating growing demand for AI systems that explain why a message may be risky. However, explanations that cite detector-derived evidence may still semantically weaken or redirect the intended risk interpretation. We introduce VEXA (Verifying Semantic EXplanation Alignment), a controlled testbed for studying the gap between lexical grounding and semantic risk alignment in AI-generated scam-risk explanations. VEXA generates ungrounded, risk-aligned, and risk-diluting explanations by independently controlling evidence grounding and semantic framing. Across LLM-as-a-judge and human evaluations, explanations can remain comparatively grounded even when their interpretations weaken the detector’s intended risk assessment. In human evaluation, risk-diluting XAI-grounded explanations retained comparatively elevated Perceived Evidence Grounding scores (3.66 ± 1.02) despite lower Helpfulness (3.00 ± 1.41) and Reasoning Support (3.14 ± 1.05) scores. These findings provide controlled evidence of grounding-illusion effects and suggest that trustworthy explanation evaluation must verify not only whether evidence is cited, but also how it is interpreted.

title: Full Waveform Inversion with a Learned Preconditioner
abstract: Full-waveform inversion (FWI) is a powerful approach for reconstructing subsurface velocity models, but its practical performance is limited by ill-conditioning, sensitivity to the update direction, and the high cost of curvature-based methods. In this project, we investigate whether a neural operator trained on reverse-time-migration (RTM) images can provide a useful learned preconditioner for FWI. We compare projected FWI against neural-preconditioned FWI using either a standard Fourier neural operator (FNO) or a Jacobian-informed FNO (JI-FNO). The neural preconditioner applies the normal operator of the learned RTM map to modify the true Devito FWI gradient. Our experiments show that the JI-FNO preconditioner achieves the lowest model error while maintaining data-residual decay comparable to baseline projected FWI. In contrast, the standard FNO preconditioner is unstable and gives worse model recovery, despite using the same neural-preconditioning framework. We also identify a failure mode of a nonlinear neural Gauss Newton-type inner solve: directly matching the neural RTM output to the FWI gradient creates an objective-space mismatch and does not yield a reliable descent direction. These results suggest that forward RTM-image prediction alone is insufficient for learned preconditioning; accurate learned derivatives and objective-consistent use of the neural operator are critical for producing useful inversion updates.
